events.title: Nvidia’s turmoil is prompting a rotation across chip stocks. Here's what we know
events.summary: Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its rivals — and a major partner. AMD to Broadcom and even TSMC sees greater investor interest as they rotate out of Nvidia. Nvidia 's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals as well as partners, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated. From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC , chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead. "What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management. That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy . Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks. Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil. "Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC. Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit , irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme. The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said. Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively. Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis. Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals. That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production. The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers. "If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said. The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market. Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom. Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit. The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said. For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors. Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery. He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis.

events.title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services
events.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company said it did not suspect malicious activity was the cause and it was attempting to restore operations. Amazon Web Services said it was "operating normally" and noted inaccurate reports of outages on its platforms. Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, as engineers scrambled to fix server issues that caused disruption to millions of its customers around the world. Connectivity issues began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. External services that connect with Outlook features such as Calendar were also hit. Email and other tools were unavailable for Microsoft users through much of the Asian business day and into the European morning, though some access to Teams was restored. In an update just before 7:30 a.m. in London (2:30 a.m. ET), Microsoft said users may still be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook on either web or desktop. It did not give a timeline for restoring full service but said it was seeing "positive results for server stability" after applying a new patch fix to some infrastructure. "As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident. We will continue to treat this incident with urgency and priority until full resolution," Microsoft said, adding that it would provide a full report with further details once the problem was mitigated. Microsoft said on Thursday the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more, Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data." At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online. "We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses." events.title: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
events.summary: Watch: What we know about the Microsoft global outage overnight Published 13 November 2026, 07:12 GMT A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products. Reports of problems with the email provider Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Follow live updates: Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting tens of thousands but says fixes not going 'as expected' Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems". While customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. Some users have been able to use Teams as normal and are using messaging and online meeting functions as usual. How many people have been affected? The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The software is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected. Government agencies and services, including the Singaporean government and Australia's spy agency, have also said they have been affected. Several GP practices across the UK have warned of potential problems, with some instructing patient to make urgent queries over the phone instead of by email or web form. Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure. The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do. In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these. On Friday morning, Microsoft said it had observed "marginal success" in its efforts to treat the incident. The company said in its latest update that is it continuing to monitor activity across regions to evaluate server status and determine what actions it can take to improve capacity. In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected". Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. Paul Spain from New Zealand-based advisory firm Gorilla Technology said that with e-mails and services offline, companies have practically "lost a business day", which is "frustrating" users". events.title: Microsoft outage live: ‘positive results for server stability’ reported, amid global disruption
events.summary: Microsoft outage may persist as fix is 'not taking as expected' It is anticipated the outage may persist for some time, as efforts to fix the issue are not “taking as expected”. In an update to its website, Microsoft said: We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected. We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances. 2m ago Microsoft outage: The state of play 20m ago Microsoft outage has "major impact" in Japan 34m ago Microsoft: we're seeing positive results for server stability 1h ago Microsoft: seeing 'marginal success' patching servers 1h ago Tech giants and international airlines say they’ve been hit by outage 2h ago Microsoft’s global outage will cost Australia billions, expert says 5h ago Microsoft outage may persist as fix is 'not taking as expected' 6h ago Victorian government warns of opportunistic scammers amid outage 7h ago 'Looks like we will have to talk to people’: Australians on their email-free day 7h ago WA government: 'Microsoft are prioritising life, safety and Government services' 8h ago What we know so far about the global Microsoft outage 8h ago Microsoft having issues bringing servers back online 8h ago Microsoft ‘do not believe they are dealing with a cyber event’, Tony Burke says 8h ago Schools, courts and public service staff affected 8h ago Thousands of Australians report issues with Microsoft 365 Microsoft outage: The state of play Across Europe, millions of Microsoft customers will have woken up to the news that the company is strugging to get its services back online. The disruption, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, has disrupted key Microsoft services such as Outlook , Teams and Copilot . Initially mainly affecting US users, it has gone on to cause disruption across the Asia-Pacific region. Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. It says it doesn’t believe it is suffering a cyber attack. And it became clear that the problem was pretty serious when the company admitted that the fix was “not taking as expected”. The outage hit government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States, as well as companies including two massive AI companies – OpenAI and Anthropic. In Japan, the economy, trade and industry minister said the disruption had had a “major impact,” on the world’s fourth-biggest economy. Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations reporting disruption there, with billions of dollars of damage predicted . The latest word from Microsoft is that it is seeing “positive results for server stability” after applying a software patch. But despite that, the company still reports “Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise) and Microsoft consumer products”. Microsoft outage has "major impact" in Japan The Microsoft outage has caused disruption among companies and government ministries in Japan, forcing staff to turn to analogue methods to distribute information and contact clients, our colleague Justin McCurry reports from Tokyo. The digital minister, Toshiharu Furukawa , said the government’s email services had become unavailable and that it would temporarily use other formats, including text messaging, as an “emergency measure”. The economy, trade and industry minister, Ryosei Akazawa , conceded that the disruption had had a “major impact,” on the world’s fourth-biggest economy. “Since this software is used by a vast number of people, we will closely monitor the situation and take every possible measure to address it,” he said, according to the Asahi Shimbun newspaper. The realisation that something was wrong hit as soon as employees tried to log on this morning, with social media flooded with complaints from users who were unable to check work emails. The government confirmed the outage had disrupted a shared network the digital agency uses to send information to ministries and other official bodies. The chaos also seeped into the private sector. The shipping firm Sagawa Express , which uses Outlook, said it was unable to accept online reservations for its hands-free luggage service at airports and train stations, according to the Kyodo news agency. Taisho , a major pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone. Outlook is also used by Japan’s defence ministry and the cabinet office, which said it would pin notices on bulletin boards to notify media organisations of upcoming press conferences. The meteorological agency said it does not use Microsoft to issue special weather and earthquake warnings to local governments.

events.title: NBA: Cunningham scores 52 as Pistons win double OT thriller against Wizards
events.summary: Cunningham became the first NBA player to record a 50-point, 10-assist game without committing a turnover since 1977-78. Cade Cunningham racked up 52 points as the Detroit Pistons edged a double-overtime thriller 144-140 against Washington on Thursday. The Wizards twice extended the game with clutch scores in the dying seconds but could not repeat the trick a third time as the Pistons held their nerve to claim an epic road win. list 1 of 3 Harry Kane breaks caps record as England reach Nations League knockouts list 2 of 3 ‘Utter nonsense’: Australia’s Cummins denies involvement in Sandpapergate list 3 of 3 WTA Finals: Pegula wins thriller as compatriot Gauff eliminated Cunningham became the first player in NBA history to score 50 points and add 10 assists with zero turnovers, while Ausar Thompson had a triple-double with 17 points, 11 assists and 11 rebounds. The Wizards had three starters scoring 30-plus points – Trae Young, Anthony Davis and Alex Sarr – but it was not enough to prevent Washington’s sixth defeat in a row. “Two overtimes, it was just going to come down [to] who wanted it more, who had more in the tank,” said Cunningham. “I’d bet on my team any day. So great win for us.” In a back-and-forth game featuring 20 lead changes, Detroit started slow but built a double-digit lead early in the second half. It was slowly whittled down by Washington, but the Pistons were clinging to their lead when Cunningham was fouled at 119-118 with less than two seconds remaining. Cunningham sank both free throws, but Trae Young made a nerveless try right at the buzzer to force overtime. The Wizards raced 128-121 up, but Cunningham would not quit. He made a three-pointer with 30 seconds left to level the score, then set up Duncan Robinson for what appeared to be another. A video replay ruled Robinson’s toe was on the line, and Detroit had only a two-point lead. That proved crucial as Young set up this year’s top draft pick AJ Dybantsa , who forced a second overtime period with a pull-up jump shot. Cunningham made a fadeaway shot for a four-point lead with 25 seconds left, and this time the Wizards could not conjure a third comeback. Young missed two three-point efforts, with Washington settling for two free throws, but unable to score in their final possession. Tyrese Maxey powered Philadelphia to its latest comeback victory, scoring 27 points as the Sixers shrugged off a slow start and the absence of LeBron James to beat the Toronto Raptors 123-112. Maxey added eight assists, linking up seamlessly with Joel Embiid, who briefly left the court early with a knee injury but returned to add 20 points. The Sixers had trailed by 17 points in the first quarter, immediately following Embiid’s absence, but rallied for their fifth double-digit comeback this season. “We’ll take it. I mean, extreme professional win by us. We stayed with it. Didn’t start out great, but it was a good win,” said Maxey. “We played together the last seven years, so I kind of know where he’s going to be, he knows where I’m going to be at, and it’s good for us,” he said of his partnership with 2023 MVP Embiid. Veteran James, who turns 42 next month, was ruled out of Thursday’s clash to manage a lower back issue. Philadelphia moved to 10-3, just half a game back from the 10-2 Boston Celtics atop the Eastern Conference. The Minnesota Timberwolves thrashed Dallas 133-94, while Devin Booker’s 30 points helped the Phoenix Suns overcome Charlotte 101-96.

events.title: Banks in Singapore offer alternative contact channels amid Microsoft outage: ABS
events.summary: ABS said banks affected by the disruption, particularly those providing retail banking services, had also put up notices across various channels to alert customers to the outage. SINGAPORE – Banks in Singapore affected by Microsoft’s global outage have reached out to customers with alternative ways to access help, including customer service hotlines and relationship managers. The Association of Banks in Singapore said banks affected by the disruption, particularly those providing retail banking services, had also put up notices across various channels, including their websites, to alert customers to the outage. ABS director Ong-Ang Ai Boon said banks were making alternative contact arrangements available to customers while the disruption persisted. They were advised not to click on unknown or unsolicited links and messages relating to the disruption, as these could lead to phishing attempts, scams, credential theft and malware infections. The advisory comes amid concerns that cybercriminals could take advantage of the disruption to impersonate banks or send fraudulent messages to customers seeking information or help. Microsoft suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill. ABS/Association of Banks in Singapore

events.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
events.summary: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup , who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel . Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal ( P2900 ) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested , and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig , a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post . The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adpot Rust . Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language . Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”) ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final. According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy , the group faces a number of choices. They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts. Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology. Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

events.title: The real winner in Poland’s constitutional battle is Putin
events.summary: As Poland’s political camps fight for control of the Constitutional Tribunal, they risk eroding public trust in the state itself. Political scientist (Warsaw University) and theologian (University of Nottingham). President of Reform & Solidarity Centre. Poland’s two main political camps are locked in an escalating fight for control of the Constitutional Tribunal, each claiming to defend the rule of law. In the process, they are undermining the legitimacy of the Polish state in the eyes of its own citizens, playing directly into Putin’s playbook. The roots of the dispute go back more than a decade. In 2015, the outgoing centre-right Civic Platform-controlled parliament attempted to appoint judges to the Constitutional Tribunal for vacancies that should have been left to the incoming parliament. The newly elected conservative Law and Justice government used this controversy to intensify its efforts to pack the Tribunal with party nominees rather than independent judges. Now back in power, Civic Platform is trying to bring new judges into the Constitutional Tribunal. But President Karol Nawrocki and the Tribunal’s leadership, both aligned with Law and Justice, have blocked several of the newly appointed judges from taking office. Last month, one of the newly elected judges ordered the suspension of the Tribunal’s president and deputy, and police were deployed to the building. Nawrocki denounced the move as a forcible takeover, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended it as an effort to restore the rule of law. Moscow has already seized on the confrontation to cast doubt on the legitimacy of Poland’s institutions. On November 3, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described the intervention as a “coup”. A decade ago, it was the conservative Law and Justice government that sought to pack the Constitutional Tribunal with party nominees, disregarding legal constraints. Today, it is the coalition of the centre-right Civic Platform and the liberal Left that is acting unlawfully. We see the main parties becoming mirror images of one another. Conservative Law and Justice is calling on its supporters to take to the streets to defend the rule of law, a slogan previously used by the liberal opposition when Law and Justice was in power. Now it is the liberal Prime Minister Donald Tusk who is playing the strongman, with police carrying shields and wearing helmets deployed around the Constitutional Tribunal during the operation. He presents himself as an effective leader who gets things done, with little regard for legal subtleties and doubts raised even by some liberal-leaning experts. Against this backdrop, a photograph of Tusk reading an issue of the philosophical journal Kronos devoted to Carl Schmitt has recently circulated widely on social media. Schmitt, a theorist of decisionism, famously declared, “Sovereign is he who decides on the exception.” Law and Justice’s efforts to politicise the Constitutional Tribunal pushed middle-aged supporters of the liberals in big cities onto the streets a decade ago. It seems, however, unlikely that Poles will again take to the streets in their millions to support either political bloc. The public is tired of the tug-of-war between politicians, not only because both main blocs demonstrate considerable hypocrisy when invoking the rule of law over force, but also because the fight does not speak to people’s chief everyday concerns: the cost of living and the safety of a country with an aggressive neighbour waging a hot war on its border and a hybrid and cognitive war inside the country. What has changed drastically compared to the protests that took place a decade ago, when the main forces occupied mirror-image positions, is the geopolitical context: Russia’s full-scale war in neighbouring Ukraine, alongside its hybrid and information warfare aimed at weakening Poland’s position on the global stage. In the worst-case scenario, this struggle over the legitimacy of state institutions could extend to elections. A precedent can be found in Romania, where, on December 6, 2024, the Constitutional Court annulled the presidential election following intelligence reports of alleged foreign interference, social media manipulation and campaign financing irregularities, and ordered the electoral process to be repeated. What we might see in other Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland if the situation deteriorates, is, on the one hand, the liberal establishment adopting measures that override electoral outcomes, such as courts annulling elections in response to genuine foreign interference through social media campaigns. On the other hand, the opposition could become increasingly anti-establishment, effectively delegitimising the institutions of the state. The problem will be aggravated by the fact that foreign interference may be real rather than invented by the establishment.

events.title: Why Singapore keeps turning up in the fight over Nvidia chips and China
events.summary: Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026 after authorities said she provided inaccurate information about her role in Megaspeed. The country repeatedly sought intelligence on Super Micro from U.S. authorities, but received "limited information or assistance," the ministry said. Singapore has faced international scrutiny over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight. The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country. A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year. The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday. Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday. Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development. Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue. Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up. Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year. Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering. Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added. "Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said. Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators. Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation. Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement. The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said. Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025. In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.

events.title: The Gulf must build security that can outlast this war
events.summary: Trump’s latest statement should accelerate the region’s move towards a layered and networked security architecture. Vice President of the Center for International Policy Research. On November 10, Gulf defence ministers approved the establishment of a forward command in Kuwait under the Gulf Cooperation Council’s Unified Military Command, with forces to be allocated to it. The decision marks another step towards Gulf states taking greater collective responsibility for their security. One day earlier, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, US President Donald Trump had said: “Iran militarily is effectively over.” He also said the US blockade would continue and left open further military action. His remarks fell short of announcing an agreed end to the war. Any opening for diplomacy deserves support. But even a lasting agreement would leave the Gulf’s underlying security problems unresolved. The Kuwait command’s value will depend on implementation and on how it connects with the region’s other security partnerships. The answer requires abandoning the expectation that one grand security arrangement can resolve every threat facing the region. That expectation assumes a degree of agreement about enemies, priorities and acceptable risks that does not exist. Iran’s attacks on Gulf states during this war, together with Israel’s September 2025 strike on Qatar, demonstrate the breadth of the challenge. A security architecture designed around only one adversary will leave serious gaps. Armed militias and terrorist groups add other risks, alongside cyberattacks, maritime disruption and the consequences of state failure in the neighbourhood. The erosion of international restraints on the use of force makes all of these problems harder to manage. The most credible response to this complex set of threats is a security architecture that is both layered and networked. Gulf states are already moving in this direction. The task now is to make those arrangements work together and sustain the effort when the immediate pressure of war recedes. Layering starts with the recognition that different partnerships do different jobs. National capabilities and cooperation within the Gulf Cooperation Council provide the foundation. The relationship with the United States remains central, while additional arrangements address needs that a single partner cannot meet. Cooperation with US Central Command supplies an operational layer. The air and missile defence coordination cell opened at Al Udeid in January, for example, was designed to improve regional coordination, share threat warnings and prepare for contingencies. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan, adds a collective defence commitment among its members. The Badr memorandum, signed in October by Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia, sets out cooperation in defence manufacturing, research and technical training. These arrangements should be judged by the gaps they fill. Collective defence, operational coordination and industrial capacity reinforce one another, but none can substitute for the others. Buying an interceptor, producing its components and deciding who will use it in a crisis are separate problems. The next step is to connect these layers so that capabilities developed through one partnership strengthen what countries can do through another. This is what makes the architecture networked. Qatar offers a useful example. It shares GCC membership with Saudi Arabia and participates in Badr alongside Turkiye and Pakistan. It therefore connects to all three Mecca signatories through other arrangements, despite not being a party to Mecca itself. Those connections create opportunities. Stronger production capacity or better coordination among shared partners could improve the capabilities available to Qatar through its own relationships. A more effective deterrent against attacks on a neighbour could also improve the wider security environment. Such benefits depend on deliberate cooperation. Qatar acquires no automatic Mecca guarantee through association. Information, equipment and expertise travel through a network only when governments agree to make that possible. The connections need as much attention as the agreements themselves. This is also where the Gulf’s interests converge with those of a wider group of countries. European states, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia and Pakistan all have reasons to resist a world in which force routinely overrides sovereignty and access to trade depends on political coercion. Energy exporters and importers face different consequences when shipping is disrupted, but both need these routes to remain open. Countries need not share a political system or an identical relationship with Washington to recognise the costs of an international order becoming less predictable. There is already a diplomatic basis for cooperation.

events.title: Jessica Pegula wins thrilling contest at WTA Finals, Coco Gauff eliminated
events.summary: Pegula’s win, in the final group one round-robin match, meant Gauff was knocked out of the season-ending championships. Jessica Pegula saved a match point en route to a gritty 7-6 (7/2), 4-6, 7-5 win over Linda Noskova on Thursday to advance out of ⁠her round-robin group at the WTA Finals and send fellow American Coco Gauff packing from the season-ending championships. Pegula had a career-high 16 aces while Wimbledon champion Noskova had a career-high 15 double faults in a see-saw battle that spanned two ⁠hours and 45 minutes at the tournament, which was moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells due to the United States-Israel war on Iran . list 1 of 3 ‘Utter nonsense’: Australia’s Cummins denies involvement in Sandpapergate list 2 of 3 Harry Kane breaks caps record as England reach Nations League knockouts list 3 of 3 Manchester United sack Michael Carrick after worst league start in 40 years “I’ve learned that sometimes the serve feels good and sometimes it doesn’t, and how to manage the days when it doesn’t and to ride it when you are serving well,” Pegula told reporters. “I don’t think I served that well in my first ‌couple matches and I served great today. Sometimes there’s no rhyme or reason.” In the end, Noskova, Gauff and Pegula all finished 2-1 in the group while alternate Marta Kostyuk went 0-3. Noskova went 5-2 in sets to win the group, followed by Pegula at 5-3 and Gauff at 4-3. The win sets up a first meeting between Pegula and Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva in the semifinals on Saturday. “It’s the match people wanted; well now you are going to get it,” said Pegula. Pegula had earlier called Andreeva “ a diva ” who “needs to be humbled”, but didn’t realise that ⁠her remarks were being livestreamed during a practice session before the tournament. In the same ⁠comments, Pegula also praised the World No 3, and she apologised afterwards to those involved. “She’s fast, she has a great serve, she’s strong, she hits the ball pretty hard, and she’s smart,” Pegula said on Thursday. Gauff rallies past Kostyuk, but eliminated Earlier, Gauff rallied to beat ⁠Kostyuk 6-4, 7-5 on a sun-soaked Stadium Two. After sealing the first set with a stab volley that sent fans leaping to their feet under sunny California desert skies, Gauff ⁠rallied from 1-5 down in the second, winning six games in a row. “I ⁠was fully prepared to play a third set there,” said Gauff, who needed treatment on her back during the second set. “It’s the last tournament of the season, so I just wanted to finish it on a high note and give myself the best chance to play the semifinals. Either way, ‌I didn’t want to be sad walking off the court.” Kostyuk, who won the Madrid title and reached the French Open semifinals , was already eliminated coming into her match against Gauff, having lost to Noskova and Pegula. Kostyuk, who joined the ‌eight-player ‌tournament as an alternate after top-ranked Elena Rybakina withdrew due to illness, failed to win a set in her three matches as she struggled with a wrist injury.

events.title: Oil on track to post second weekly decline as Trump eases fears of renewed war with Iran
events.summary: Oil prices were on course to post a second weekly decline as supply concerns eased, after US President Donald Trump signalled that he is not keen to restart the Iran war. But further attacks on ships in the region mean prices remain volatile. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was down 0.24 per cent at $95.59 a barrel at 8.53am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 0.54 per cent lower at $88.26 a barrel. Both Brent and WTI are set for decline of more than 2.5 per cent decline for the week, after plunging about 13 per cent last week. Mr Trump this week indicated that he is not planning to resume the war with Iran after his Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. He also said on Thursday that the US was no longer looking to reach an agreement with Tehran. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we’ve got their strait,” Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social. But attacks continue on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for two thirds of global crude supply and liquefied natural gas, putting upward pressure on oil prices amid supply risks. This week, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed there were explosions on two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels of oil in the strait. A tanker was also struck by a projectile while travelling east in the Arabian Gulf, with casualties reported, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said yesterday. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure by Yemen's Houthis also pushing prices higher. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that a pumping station on the kingdom's East-West oil pipeline and the Yanbu oil installation on the Red Sea coast were hit on Thursday. Saudi Arabia has been exporting much of its crude through the pipeline since the beginning of the war, owing to disruption in the strait. Meanwhile, gold rose on ⁠Friday after prices ​reached a more than one-year low in the previous session. Spot gold climbed 1 per cent to $3,917.70 per ounce at 9.55am UAE time. Gold prices dropped below the $4,000 level as markets expect a December increase by the US Federal Reserve.

events.title: US reports record number of deportations and arrests in 2026
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? ICE carried out 483,200 deportations in 2026. Democrats prepare to investigate tactics used. Asylum seekers caught in US immigration crackdown The United States government has reported a historic high in deportations and arrests this fiscal year, surpassing previous records. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Wednesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out 483,200 deportations and more than 491,000 immigration arrests in 2026. list 1 of 4 Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data list 2 of 4 On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote list 3 of 4 US lawmakers ask Trump administration to stop deportation of Afghans list 4 of 4 Surging ICE raids shadow final weeks of California congressional race The total number of deportations breaks all records in ICE’s 23-year history, including the previous record of 442,640 deportations made in 2025. The report comes days after US President Donald Trump acknowledged his administration’s immigration crackdown may have been “too tough”. “Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE’s history in terms of arrests,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. ICE said it made more than 48,000 arrests in September, ending a two-month run of record highs that reached 50,925 in August. “There is no question the administration has increased enforcement more than any prior president. There’s also evidence that the illegal immigrant population has declined significantly because of increased out-migration due to a fear of enforcement,” Steven Camarota, director of research for the Washington, DC-based Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), told Al Jazeera. However, he highlighted ambiguity in the figures DHS released. “Of course the data is always incomplete and it’s difficult to measure. On the specific numbers released today, the big issue that I have not been able to determine is what percentage of these individuals are interior enforcement and what percentage are removals from the interior of the United States and what percentage are those turned around at the border or at airport. “Increased removals, sometimes called deportation, certainly can encourage more people to go home, and clearly that is a central goal of this administration,” Camarota concluded. Trump has acknowledged that his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough”. “A lot of people would say it is great but a lot of people would think it is too tough,” Trump said in a recent interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes. Trump, however, defended his performance. “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out; I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law that was they came into the country illegally.” Trump’s immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability , with his approval rating on the issue falling to 38 percent from 50 percent at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling. The Democrats appear to be gearing up to halt Trump’s immigration crackdown when they take control of Congress next year. They plan to target ICE tactics ⁠and expand paths to legal status, despite limits on ⁠how much they can achieve. “We will investigate the administration weaponising DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies,” Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told the Reuters news agency in a statement. At a news conference in the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, ‌said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals. “We’re not going to be extreme,” Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the US who cast their votes for Democrats. But a number of Democratic voices sounded firmer. “We will rip ICE apart,” Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two people during an enforcement surge in January. Two US citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, were killed in Minneapolis, in incidents that were caught on bystander video. Their shooting deaths have gone viral, prompting international outrage. Other footage shows masked agents deploying chemical agents and beating civilians who were documenting their activities or protesting – activities protected under the US Constitution.

As The Register reported yesterday , the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services. The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional. The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.” In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service. It’s also using changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility a cyberattack is the reason for the outage. As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.” Microsoft’s status page preserves only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order: We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online; We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected; We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability; We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances; We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery; Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected. Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon. “We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.” Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend.

events.title: Nvidia scandal sparks US national security furore and calls to take tough line on China
events.summary: Former CEO Jensen Huang and US commerce secretary to appear before Congress amid bipartisan concern that America’s security was put at risk Analysis: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached? Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China. Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge . The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported . On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia. The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist. “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News. Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.” Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy. The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded. House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony. House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China. Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them. “The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“ Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters . Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models. Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday. On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades. News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo. Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.

Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script. He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP). "Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote. This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases. "In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the struct proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code." Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe. "It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained. The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night. After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague. But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot. So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions. How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? events.title: Politicians back focus on cost of living
events.summary: Targeted action on the cost of living is among the Government of Jersey's priorities for the next political term Politicians have backed the Government of Jersey's key priorities for the next political term which includes action on the cost of living. States members adopted the Common Strategic Policy , external which lays out the Council of Ministers' priorities for the political term until 2030. The priorities are centered around four pillars including targeted action on the cost of living, restoring Jersey's competitiveness, investing in homes and infrastructure and maintaining financial stability. Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was determined "to make Jersey a more affordable place to live" but Reform Jersey co-leader Lyndsay Feltham said the policy lacked "real action". The policy was backed with 31 votes in favour, 10 against and two abstentions. Ministers first published the proposed policy in September and this week politicians debated a number of amendments proposed by backbenchers. This included adding a priority about government transparency and promoting democracy , bringing the total number of priorities up from 11 to 12. Reform Jersey co-leader deputy Lyndsay Feltham does not support the government's Common Strategic Policy Listen to the latest news for Jersey Deputy Feltham's amendments to add actions to the policy about household affordability and employment rights were rejected and members also voted not to include reference to rental stress. The Reform Jersey co-leader said she was worried about the gaps this left behind. "What I really wanted to see from government was something more sustained and a sustained commitment to reduce everyday cost of living," said Feltham. "They've committed to a review of household affordability. A review doesn't put food on the table or a roof over somebody's head. "I am really concerned that ministers aren't going to actually take any action." Chief Minister Senator Lyndon Farnham believes the Common Strategic Policy reflects islanders' interests However, the chief minister said the policy recognised islanders' concerns such as affordability, housing, economic growth, investing in infrastructure and protecting the environment. In his closing speech, Farnham said their contributions "reflected a shared commitment to securing the best possible future for our island". He said the policy "will send an important message to islanders that we are putting their interests before our political disagreements". events.title: Cider makers fear future for orchards as costs grow
events.summary: Cider maker Matilda Temperley said the budget had been "disappointing" Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses. Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset. The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers. Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs. Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider. She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it. "We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020." "The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said. "That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards". Isaac Stell says ultimately it will be the consumer who pays Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole." He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage. "Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. " Matthew Showering said like his apples - his business is growing The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations. "Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said. "We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing." While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention. "We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible." Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider with his apple picker Johnny Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings. Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs. "We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county." A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks. "But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief." events.title: Australia captain Pat Cummins denies involvement in ‘Sandpapergate’ scandal
events.summary: Cummins says Khawaja was ‘100 percent wrong’ in claiming the whole team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Australia captain Pat Cummins ⁠has again denied any involvement in ⁠the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in a Test against South Africa in 2018, describing the allegations in Usman Khawaja’s autobiography as “utter nonsense”. Former Australia batsman Khawaja, whose autobiography was published on Tuesday, said last weekend that all the players in the team knew about ⁠the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing. His latest comments triggered calls for a new investigation into the incident. list 1 of 3 Harry Kane breaks caps record as England reach Nations League knockouts list 2 of 3 Italy fight back to give Zidane first defeat as France coach list 3 of 3 Manchester United sack Michael Carrick after worst league start in 40 years The scandal centred around the third Test in Cape Town, but Khawaja also claimed the tactic was used in the second Test at Port Elizabeth. “When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100 percent wrong. I’ve said that consistently for the last eight years,” Cummins told a news conference in Sydney on Friday. “I did not know that was happening, but I think ⁠Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. “He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense. “There was no master plan around using illegal methods,” he added. “There’s no grand plan. There’s no team meeting. There’s no bowlers saying ‘this is what must happen’.” Cummins and fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in a 2021 statement that they were aware of the plan. Darren Lehmann, who was the Australian head coach at the time, has also denied any knowledge, as has former batting coach Graeme Hick, who called Khawaja’s allegations “absolutely false”. Cummins spoke for 68 minutes on Friday, taking every question from the media and saying he would never discuss the ball-tampering incident again. The Australia skipper also took exception to Pakistan-born Khawaja’s contention in the book that the colour of his ‌skin and background had prevented him from becoming Australia captain. “I think of all the things that I’ve read this week, I think that’s actually the most serious,” he said. “Him saying that if you’re Australian captain, you have to be a certain skin colour, I couldn’t disagree with that statement any more.” Steve Smith and David Warner, the then-Australia captain and vice-captain, were banned by Cricket Australia from elite cricket for a year for their roles in the ball-tampering. Opening batter Cameron Bancroft, who brought a piece of sandpaper onto the field, received a nine-month suspension for his part in the ball-tampering. “I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam to be careful when using sandpaper. That’s not the Usman that I know,” Cummins said. “It’s not the Usman that has helped rebuild the Australian cricket ⁠culture over the last eight years.” Later on Friday, Warner said the trio had paid a heavy price for the incident and revealed ⁠that his wife Candice had lost a baby in the aftermath of what became known as “ Sandpapergate “. “I still stick by Uzzie and what he has written in that book. It is the truth,” the former Test opener said in TV commentary ahead of a one-day international between Australia and England. “I actually feel for [Khawaja] at the moment. I actually feel that the captain today threw Uzzie under the bus and I’m very disappointed ⁠by that.” ‘Casual with lives and reputations’ Cummins was asked about Khawaja’s recollection that two players had rejected the batsman’s call for the team to take collective responsibility for the ball-tampering. “I don’t remember any conversation around collective responsibility,” he said. “So then, I’ve got no idea who ⁠those two people would be because I don’t remember ever being asked or having a conversation about it.” Khawaja and ⁠Warner have also been critical of the Cricket Australia investigation in 2018 that found the three punished players solely responsible for the plot. “I got asked to be part of that review,” Cummins said. “I was totally truthful. I’ve been very consistent since then at that event till now. Nothing’s changed.” Earlier this week, the head of Cricket Australia ruled out opening another investigation into the 2018 incident. Cummins said he respected the right of Khawaja to tell ‌his story in the autobiography but felt some of the allegations were very serious and had to be addressed. “Usman’s a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,” he said. “In his book, Uzzie has been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.

events.title: The Microsoft outage is disrupting email. These business leaders barely use it anyway.
events.summary: These CEOs say they limit their use of email. Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic; Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg; Daniel Delgado Jr./Disney A major Microsoft 365 outage sparked jokes and complaints as workers lost email and Teams access. Microsoft said overloaded infrastructure and unresponsive servers led to the disruptions. These business leaders say they hardly use email at all. A widespread Microsoft outage on Thursday left thousands of users struggling to access their emails, disrupting workplaces and government operations around the world. The outage affected Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 services. In updates on X, Microsoft said overloaded infrastructure and unresponsive servers were contributing to the disruptions, which continued into Friday. "We regret that today's outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue," Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said in a Thursday post on X. " We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity." The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Some employees around the world are celebrating the outage, saying they can't possibly work without their Teams and emails, and are jokingly suggesting their bosses give them Friday off. Others, in angry social media posts, are calling on Microsoft to resolve the issue soon so they can get back to work. But for some of the world's most successful business leaders, going without email is already a way of life. Several CEOs and entrepreneurs have previously told Business Insider that they rarely use email, preferring phone calls, text messages, or even handwritten letters. Kevin O'Leary "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary said in a December interview with Business Insider that he had given up on email after being inundated with thousands of messages daily. "I don't do emails anymore because I get anywhere from 2,000 to 4,000 a day," he said. O'Leary said he had tried different filtering systems but couldn't escape the constant stream of messages. People who need to reach him now use messaging apps instead, he added. Brian Chesky Brian Chesky says email is one of the most inferior forms of communication. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Airbnb The Airbnb CEO is another email skeptic. "I don't know if I write an email a week," Chesky told Time in a September interview. He said he responds to emails daily but rarely initiates them, preferring texts, calls, and in-person conversations. "I just find it inferior to almost every other form of communication," Chesky said, explaining that texts feel more personal and faster. John Paul DeJoria DeJoria, the billionaire cofounder of haircare brands John Paul Mitchell Systems and Patrón Tequila, takes things further. "I don't even own a computer," DeJoria told Business Insider in a June interview . The 82-year-old entrepreneur said he doesn't have an email address. Instead, he uses his assistant's computer when necessary and prefers calls or handwritten letters. Wolfgang Puck Wolfgang Puck says he prefers to do work over calls. Denise Truscello/Getty Images for Drink Las Vegas The celebrity chef also favors phone calls over email when managing his restaurant empire. "I don't enjoy emails very much. I like talking to people directly. I think you understand people better that way," Puck told Business Insider earlier this year. Melanie Perkins "When I shut my laptop, I actually tune out," Perkins says. Nina Franova/Getty Images for SXSW Sydney The Canva CEO isn't against using email, but limits it to protect her personal time. "I don't have email or Slack on my phone," Perkins said on a podcast last year. "When I shut my laptop, I actually tune out." She said she remains reachable through emergency calls or pages, but otherwise tries to separate work from downtime. Read the original article on Business Insider
