events.title: ‘They’ve cut all entry-level jobs’: unlikely seaside town on frontline of AI threat
events.summary: Bournemouth became a hub for thousands of finance jobs after the 1980s big bang, but new tech risks hurting Dorset’s economy A few minutes’ drive from Bournemouth’s sandy beachfront, on the site of a former farm, lies an unlikely nerve centre of international finance. Here, miles from the glass towers of London’s Canary Wharf, more than 5,300 staff including compliance officers, analysts and software engineers help process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day for the largest US bank, JP Morgan . The sprawling five-hectare (13-acre) campus, which hosted just 650 workers when it opened in 1986, has solidified Dorset’s status as one of Britain’s largest financial hubs outside London. Now, the financial services industry accounts for 10% of the county’s turnover – the total revenue generated by all businesses in the area – with 2,500 companies, including Nationwide Building Society, the insurer LV=, and the asset manager Canaccord Wealth, collectively employing 24,000 staff, according to the Dorset Chamber of Commerce. But along with other regional finance centres outside London, from Leeds to Birmingham, and Swindon to Cardiff, it faces an existential threat from AI. Bosses are considering how the technology can help automate costly human-led jobs, putting at risk a swathe of back-office roles, such as data processors, compliance checkers and entry-level analysts. The Barclays chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, last month announced 5,000 job cuts linked to advances in AI , while another London-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, said in May it was planning to slash 7,000 roles as it doubled down on artificial intelligence. AI now poses the biggest threat to the UK’s financial workforce since the 2008 financial crisis, says Caren Evans, a national officer for the Unite union, referring to an era when banks needed multibillion-pound taxpayer bailouts and subsequently embarked on swingeing cost cuts. Unite members, who include staff at NatWest, Lloyds and Barclays , are “very very worried about AI”, Evans says. “They’re worried about losing their job, they’re worried about having future skills, they’re worried about having sustainable careers.” All that is hitting staff morale. One Barclays employee said they felt “very undervalued and insignificant”, adding: “It’s kind of hard to be enthusiastic about your work when you know, at any moment, senior executives are thinking about how to get rid of you. You’re not seen as an asset, you’re seen as a problem to be removed.” The JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, has warned of the fallout from AI, saying widespread job losses could spark “civil unrest” unless governments and business supported displaced workers. He said retraining programmes, and even state-sponsored wage support, relocation schemes and early retirement could be needed to ease the blow. In Dorset, the banking tech push has already left its mark, with bosses closing Barclays House in Poole in 2022 after 46 years of operation. “It was the original site that all the cheques in the country used to go through, to be checked,” Gareth Sherwood, the president of the Dorset Chamber of Commerce, says. “And of course, that went with digitisation.” That office block still stands empty today. Sherwood’s organisation has been coaching local business to embrace AI and increase productivity. “There’s winners and losers in all change,” he says. But “we would still encourage people to use human beings”, both to support local jobs, but also mitigate cybersecurity risks and unplanned outages. “You can’t switch a human off in the same way that you can switch an AI off,” he adds. But if cost-cutting bank bosses start to axe back office roles at pace, there would be ripple effects throughout regional economies such as Dorset. Demand for professional support from law firms and consultancies could start to dry up, and the wider ecosystem of services, such as gyms, hairdressers, restaurants and estate agents, could start to stuffer. “The collateral would be to some of the more service aspects of [the economy],” Sherwood says. “And it’s hard enough to keep young people in this area.” The Conservative councillor Lawrence Williams has served Littledown and Iford, the ward hosting JP Morgan’s campus, since 2011. He originally moved to the area in the early 1980s, shortly before the bank – then known as Chase Manhattan – took up its lodgings on former farmland. The 76-year-old regularly meets JP Morgan bosses, but says he has heard nothing of AI-related job cuts. The bank itself says the Bournemouth campus is a “centre for financial innovation”, adding: “AI will enable us to do more, and we train our people to make the most of it.” But if companies start to follow in Barclays’ and Standard Chartered’s footsteps, that “could hit quite hard”, particularly for an economy otherwise reliant on seasonal tourism, Williams says.

events.title: The Jensen Huang scandal is casting a shadow over data centers halfway across the world
events.summary: The Jensen Huang scandal could increase scrutiny of AI infrastructure companies in Southeast Asia, according to industry sources. Samsul Said/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after allegations of an affair with a Singapore-based Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the company at the center of the scandal, has been accused of funneling Nvidia chips to China. The scandal could increase scrutiny and costs for AI infrastructure operators in Southeast Asia. Jensen-Gate isn't just Nvidia's problem anymore. Data center operators across Southeast Asia might be getting caught in the fallout. In case you missed it, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a rough week. On Sunday, The New York Times published an exposé that the executive had an affair with Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing. Alice Huang worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that is the largest Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia, per Bloomberg. US authorities have investigated the company on suspicion that it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of US export restrictions . Huang resigned from his role on Thursday. Industry sources in data center financing and operations told Business Insider that Jensen-Gate could increase scrutiny on Southeast Asia's AI infrastructure companies . Jensengate could lead to increased oversight Chris Miller , the author of "Chip War" and a professor at Tufts University, said to Yahoo Finance on Monday that it was widely known that Megaspeed was "primarily building data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese customers, especially Alibaba in their case." He added that Megaspeed isn't alone, and that there are many data centers in Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore that buy advanced American chips and sell them to customers in China. He expects these relationships to face more oversight from Washington after Huang's scandal. SEA AI infrastructure operations may get slower and more expensive More scrutiny means slower and more expensive processes. Lior Prosor, the managing partner of Deep33, an NYC-headquartered venture fund that invests in AI infrastructure, told Business Insider that the Huang affair would intensify scrutiny of American tech deployments in Southeast Asia, especially which customers' hands they end up in. "That could increase financing costs and create additional hurdles for some operators," Prosor said. He said this could temporarily create a broader risk premium for Southeast Asian operators, even those with no connection to Megaspeed. Chinmoy Baruah, the CEO of Dublin-based semiconductor company ChipX, said he expects approvals for AI infrastructure projects in the region to take longer, as investors and partners will ask more detailed questions on compliance. ChipX has committed to building wafer fabrication plants in Malaysia. "That may slow some projects at the margin, particularly those with less transparent structures," Baruah told Business Insider. Michael Heinrich, the CEO of Singapore-based decentralized AI compute company 0G, said he could see fundraising for AI infrastructure get more selective over the next year. "The next round of capital will go to the operators who can prove where their chips are, who uses them, and who owns the business," Heinrich said. Bitter medicine, but better long-term health The Huang scandal won't have a lasting impact on demand for Southeast Asian AI infrastructure, but rather on the standards for it, said Baruah. He said the region's fundamentals — growing digital economies, supportive governments, improving connectivity, and rising AI adoption — remain strong. This incident, however, will make rules clearer and increase diligence among operators, chip suppliers, and regulators. "That is a positive outcome for Southeast Asia, because it strengthens the region's position as a reliable, long-term destination for global digital infrastructure investment, not a shortcut around the rules," Baruah said. Prosor from Deep33 added that AI compute is in "extraordinarily short supply, and capital will flow to wherever companies can reliably build up compute. "Southeast Asia remains an important part of that equation," he said. Southeast Asia's data center boom The Huang scandal comes as the data center industry in Southeast Asia is booming. Ember Energy, a London-headquartered energy think tank, wrote in a 2025 report that ASEAN — a bloc of 11 member states in Southeast Asia — was emerging as a "global data center hot spot" due to lower construction costs and electricity levies. Malaysia, for instance, had live data center operations totaling about 1.3 gigawatts in June, which was a tenfold increase from 2022, per a report by BloombergNEF, a think tank under Bloomberg. It has another 4.7 gigawatts planned or under construction, the report added. Indonesia had about 450 megawatts of live data-center capacity as of June, with more than four times that amount currently under construction or committed, per the BloombergNEF report. A rough week for Nvidia Huang's resignation comes after a tumultuous few days for Nvidia . Its stock took a hit after the US midterm elections on November 3, which flipped control of Congress to the Democrats, many of whom had made anti-data-center messaging a major part of their campaigns. A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell . The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. Early Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned from the role, and CFO Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community benefit deal Firmus is currently Tasmania's largest data centre proponent. ( Supplied ) Further details have been provided on Tasmania's AI data centre deal that would compel companies to pay into community benefit funds. Businesses are required to pay $3,000 per megawatt of contracted energy each year. The government says the expectations will be binding. Tasmanian data centre proponents would each run their own community benefit funds under a proposal from the state government. Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced his government's statement of expectations for data centres on Friday, which includes rules for the community funds. Once a facility is operational, proponents would be required to pay into their own funds, at a rate of $3,000 per megawatt (MW) of contracted energy each year. The requirement to pay into community funds is included in the Tasmanian government's statement of expectations. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) For Tasmania's largest AI data centre company, Firmus, its 104MW facility at St Leonards would contribute $312,000 per year. It also has a proposed 288MW centre planned for Long Reach, near Bell Bay, and a 40MW centre at Wesley Vale in the state's north-west. Last month, Premier Rockliff announced plans for a singular local community benefit fund , but did not release the cost or structure. Jeremy Rockliff (left) has since released more details about the community funds that would impact companies such as Tim Rosenfield's (centre) and Oliver Curtis' Firmus. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) At Friday's press conference, further details were announced . The premier and Industry Minister Felix Ellis spoke of a single fund governed by "local people" and "local representatives" who would allocate grants to "community groups and other eligible organisations". They did not reveal that there would be several funds or that companies themselves would control the funds. The statement of expectations outlines "transparent governance arrangements" and requires public reporting. Premier Rockliff announced plans for the fund in the days following Firmus's scrapped IPO , which unravelled due to investor concerns about the company's finances, expansion plans and social licence. He said today that the expectations document would be reviewed within six months. "In our view, [data centres] are a good investment for Tasmania and we welcome that investment," Mr Rockliff said. Six new data centre proposals for Tasmania, but companies not named Unnamed companies are looking at setting up six data centres in Tasmania, a parliamentary document reveals. Mr Ellis said proponents who did not follow the expectations "won't be able to proceed". "There are already many statutory rules that the data centre developers are required to meet in areas such as planning and environmental requirements," he said. The state government has been under pressure to step up its regulation of the burgeoning sector, following Firmus unveiling plans for multiple data centres in the state . Opponents to data centres have raised concerns about where the energy and water used by the AI data factories will come from. Proposals for AI data centres in Tasmania have been met with some local opposition. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) For the Firmus factory at St Leonards, state energy company Aurora has contracted energy supply through the initial stage, but it does not have a long-term deal. Energy Minister Nick Duigan said proponents were "required" to partner with new renewable energy projects, but they could do that "through" Hydro Tasmania. "So Hydro would go out and contract with the new renewable energy providers and act as an aggregator to provide a firmed energy product to the data centre," he said. Russell Kelly, chief executive of technology sector advocate TasICT, said the expectations "put the onus" on data centre proponents to build trust with the community. Russell Kelly says the fund will help AI data centre companies build trust. ( ABC News: Cameron Atkins ) Mr Kelly said the amount proposed for the Local Community Benefit Fund was in line with other proposals in the nation. events.title: Ukraine says the Starshield speed limit is back and Russian 'strikes have already gone through'
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, pictured here in Copenhagen, said his country's forces are once again reporting failures in Starshield. Emil Helms / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images Ukraine says it's being hit with a slowdown in its military version of Starlink — again. Zelenskyy said his staff are asking the US what happened, but so far "know very little." SpaceX denied that the service has been affected over Ukraine. Ukraine's Starlink problems are back, it said on Thursday. Troops and officials said their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, has been curbed once again to a 100-mph speed limit, severely disrupting war operations such as air defense and strikes in Russia's rear. It's the second time that Kyiv has reported a major disruption to the service, coming about three weeks after Ukraine said it suffered a 10-day slowdown under a similar speed limit. "The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour. That's 100 miles per hour," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a summit in Dublin. He added that Ukraine's interceptor drones, which it relies on to counter jet-powered loitering munitions near the front lines, couldn't maintain a connection while flying at speeds fast enough to catch their targets. "This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia. We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little," Zelenskyy said. We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory – in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine. The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour – that’s 100 miles per hour. This directly affects our ability to intercept Russian jet-powered “shahed” drones. These drones come from those areas, and because of the speed restrictions, we simply cannot catch up with them in time. Near the frontline, we cannot use our aircraft. Only drone interceptors can operate there. And without the speed we need, shooting down these “shaheds” becomes much harder. This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia. We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little. If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going. We need to be clear and never recognize Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory in any way. From an address at the 9th European Political Community Summit. (3/3) — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) November 12, 2026 A spokesperson for SpaceX denied the disruption in comments to several international media outlets, saying: "This is false. There has been no change." SpaceX and the Pentagon did not respond to comment requests sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an advisor to Zelenskyy's office on drones, wrote on his Telegram channel that communications had also been disrupted for helicopters tasked with chasing and shooting down Russian jet drones — another key pillar of its air defense. Ukraine uses hundreds of cheap interceptor drones as a cost-effective way to fight Russian Shaheds, though it also has newer designs built to counter the Kremlin's jet-powered systems. Serhii Mykhalchuk/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images "We did not rejoice for long," he said of the initial resumption of Starshield services , which happened in mid-October. Zelenskyy said in a separate post on his Telegram channel that Ukrainian forces had been "reporting significant failures" with Starshield for several days, particularly near the front lines or in Russian-occupied territories. "Unfortunately, strikes have already gotten through because interception systems cannot reach sufficient speed in time to catch them," he said. "The Ukrainian military has already checked the circumstances of this, and these are not random errors, but a system speed limit," Zelenskyy added. The Financial Times reported that several unnamed senior Ukrainian officials suspected the speed limit was related to the US putting pressure on Kyiv amid this week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi, and as US envoys flew to Russia to meet with its leader, Vladimir Putin, on Thursday. Why Starshield matters for the war Ukrainian troops and civilians alike rely heavily on Starlink for communications, but Kyiv's forces say they equip their medium-range strike drones and interceptors with terminals that link to Starshield, which is controlled by the US government. Most commercial Starlink terminals officially stop working at a maximum speed of 100 mph, meaning Ukrainian drones flying faster typically need Starshield to stay connected. When Ukraine's Starshield access was previously disrupted, it said it had tested connections outside its territory and found that the speed limit was only imposed within its borders. Zelenskyy had publicly called on SpaceX owner Elon Musk and President Donald Trump for answers about the slowdown, but both have said they were not responsible. Musk, however, had accused Ukraine of breaching Starlink's terms of service by using the service in attack drones. Ukrainian military figures, including Beskrestnov, have denied the claim. events.title: Nvidia on track for longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.6 trillion
events.summary: Nvidia shares are down 11% this week, as of Thursday's close, and are headed for their sixth straight weekly decline. That will be the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant has lost roughly $1.6 trillion in market cap since the slide began in early October. Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock toward its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 29% of its value over that stretch as of Thursday's close. That's a drop of roughly $1.6 trillion in market cap, and it fell below Apple in the process. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Thursday, bringing their loss for the week to 11%. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care. By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world. "With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote. Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout. In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets. Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term." "The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

events.title: At a major Silicon Valley AI conference, VCs and CEOs grapple with a future without Jensen Huang
events.summary: Pranav Dixit/Business Insider Jensen Huang's exit dominated conversations at the Cerebral Valley AI Summit. Founders and investors worried about losing a powerful backer of AI startups. Some said Nvidia's chip lead would endure, while rivals saw an opening. Hours after he was ousted as the CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang was still winning at the Cerebral Valley AI Summit in San Francisco on Thursday. At least in a video game. In "Cerebral Combat," an arcade game set up for attendees, the Nvidia cofounder could take down Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg with a giant GPU. Outside the game, things weren't going nearly as well for Huang. Hours after his ouster as Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang was still winning — in a video game. Pranav Dixit/Business Insider On Thursday morning, he had resigned as CEO of Nvidia, the company he founded 33 years ago and built into the world's most valuable chipmaker, following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China. Nvidia named its longtime CFO, Colette Kress , interim CEO. The news was hard to escape at the summit, where hundreds of founders, investors, and tech executives had gathered to talk about AI's future. One venture capitalist asked Business Insider's Katie Roof , who was wearing black, whether she was attending Huang's funeral. The jokes masked a genuine worry: What happens to the AI boom when one of its biggest financial backers is suddenly gone? Ali Ghodsi, CEO of Databricks, a data and AI software company backed by Nvidia, said onstage that Huang had become something of a safety net for AI startups. Whenever investors worried about a bubble, he said, Huang was there to reassure them that Nvidia would help keep the industry going. Without him, that reassurance might be harder to come by. "On the margin, I think that starts hurting a lot of startups," Ghodsi said. Nvidia's importance to the AI industry goes well beyond the chips that power much of it. Under Huang, the company became one of Silicon Valley's most influential investors, earning a reputation as the "central bank of AI" for its willingness to bankroll startups that, in many cases, also buy its chips. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Sean Gallup/Getty Images Just how deeply Nvidia is embedded in the industry became clear at the summit. Venture capital firm Bessemer Venture Partners and Newcomer, the publication that organized the conference, unveiled a list of the world's 100 most important private AI companies. Nvidia had invested in 42 of them, according to Bessemer partner Talia Goldberg. That kind of influence is hard to replace. Hemant Taneja, CEO of venture capital firm General Catalyst, compared Nvidia's importance to that of the big banks during the 2008 financial crisis. The implication was hard to miss: Nvidia had become too big to fail, and a messy leadership transition could have consequences far beyond the company. "This is not a normal company," he said onstage, "and we all need to make sure the continuity of leadership in AI for us as a nation and for the industry at large remains." Nikesh Arora, CEO of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, was less worried about Nvidia's technology than about losing Huang himself. He described the Nvidia founder as an unusually generous champion of the industry, lending his time and influence to everything from open-source AI to cybersecurity. "Is there short-term instability in the moment?" he said onstage. "Most likely, because there's a whole bunch of parts of the ecosystem which need to reexamine where their champions are." Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, a cloud platform for developers, also worried about the future of Nvidia's support for open-source AI. Under Huang, Nvidia had become a major champion of the movement. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face, a popular platform for sharing open-source AI models, for nearly $13 billion. "An Nvidia without Jensen is going to be, I think, a challenging one," Rauch said onstage. Still, he hoped the company's extensive partnerships would help preserve Huang's vision. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora Camille Cohen/Camille Cohen for Newcomer Media For founders who work closely with Nvidia, the uncertainty was more immediate. Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO of Pathway, a startup developing AI models, told Business Insider that Nvidia had been an unusually attentive partner, with employees constantly looking for opportunities to collaborate. Whether the company could preserve that culture without Huang was another matter. "I'd say we don't know yet," she said. Hassaan Raza, CEO of Tavus, a startup building AI-powered video agents, worried that any stumble at Nvidia could set back America's broader AI ambitions. Even a disappointing earnings report under new leadership, he suggested, could send shock waves through the industry. "If Nvidia misses a quarter in the next year or something, oh my gosh, it's going to be a bloodbath," Raza told Business Insider. Aravind Srinivas, CEO of AI search startup Perplexity, which counts Nvidia among its largest investors, said he had met with Nvidia executives earlier Thursday and found business proceeding as usual. Huang, he said, had built a company with technological advantages that wouldn't disappear overnight. "Even now, the best GPUs for running inference is Nvidia, and the best GPUs for running training is Nvidia, and none of that stops," Srinivas said. "It's established for years in the future." Databricks' Ghodsi, too, expected Nvidia to remain strong for at least another two or three years, thanks to the long development cycles for its chips. What happens after that was a different question. For Nvidia's competitors, meanwhile, Huang's abrupt exit presented an opening. Robert Wachen, cofounder of Etched , a startup developing specialized AI chips to challenge Nvidia, praised Huang's contributions to the industry before conceding that his departure could be good news for rivals. "Now we see there's probably going to be a big opening, which we plan to capitalize on," Wachen said onstage. There was at least some agreement that more competition would be good for AI. General Catalyst's Taneja suggested the upheaval could push startups to explore alternatives from AMD and Google rather than relying so heavily on Nvidia. Raza said that he agreed with Taneja. But he wasn't exactly celebrating. "This is not the best way to do it," he said, "but we'll be forced to do it." Have a tip? events.title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
events.summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube. Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name. Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény. The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks. Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital. The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.” The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983. While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year. At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand. The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually. Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Microsoft Outlook outage stretches on for hours Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.” Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today. “The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.” The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest. The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world. Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations. “If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said. 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Harry Kane breaks caps record as England reach Nations League knockouts
events.summary: England moved to second spot in Group A3 behind Spain, confirming their place in the Nations League last eight in March. Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking 126th England cap with a goal from the penalty spot as England beat Croatia 2-1 on Thursday to book a place in the Nations League quarterfinals. Slaven Bilic’s team were determined to avoid another embarrassment after their 7-0 mauling by England in Rijeka last month and looked much more solid from the kickoff at Wembley. list 1 of 3 Italy fight back to give Zidane first defeat as France coach list 2 of 3 Inside the circle: Senegal’s wrestlers turn tradition to Youth Olympic gold list 3 of 3 FIFA Under-17 World Cup to kick off in Qatar despite US withdrawal But goals from Morgan Rogers and captain Kane kept England second in Group A3 behind Spain, confirming their place in the Nations League last eight in March. Thomas Tuchel’s men have a chance to avenge their 3-2 defeat against the world champions in their Nations League opener when they travel to Madrid for Sunday’s clash. Spain beat Czechia 2-0 in Prague on Thursday. “After the first game when we lost here against them [Spain], we knew we left a bit out there,” Kane told ITV. “We knew we could’ve done a bit better. We said to ourselves, ‘Let’s win every game until the next one and see what happens’. It’s the perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves.” England and Croatia struggled to get out of second gear in the opening stages of their match in London. Elliot Anderson fired over in the 16th minute, and Croatia’s Josip Misic flashed a shot wide midway through the first half. Chelsea forward Rogers broke the deadlock in the 24th minute in slightly fortuitous fashion, following a neat move by the home side. Kane floated a ball to Jude Bellingham on the right of the penalty area and the Real Madrid man cushioned the ball the first time across the area towards Rogers. Manchester City’s Josko Gvardiol had a chance to clear but got in a tangle and Chelsea’s Rogers poked the ball past goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic. England started to find some rhythm as they went in search of a second goal but failed to add to their tally before half-time. The home side were again the more potent team at the beginning of the second period. But the visitors levelled against the run of play just before the hour mark after a glaring error by England defender Jarell Quansah, who misdirected a header from close range towards Jordan Pickford following a Croatia corner. The ball fell to Petar Sucic, who stabbed home. Minutes later England were back in front, with Bayer Leverkusen defender Quansah again at the heart of the action after his shirt was tugged in the penalty area. Referee Morten Krogh initially did not award a penalty, but he was sent to the monitor by the VAR and pointed to the spot. Kane made no mistake, drilling home for a record-extending 92nd England goal. Nikola Vlasic gave England a scare, firing just wide of Jordan Pickford’s goal as Croatia showed they were still alive. James Garner thought he had scored a third for England after a Bellingham cut-back, but Bellingham was in an offside position when he received the ball. Ballon d’Or winner Kane won his 126th cap when the game kicked off, taking him clear of his tie with former goalkeeper Peter Shilton. A giant banner was raised before kickoff with a picture of the 33-year-old and the words “England’s Finest”. Shilton was part of a pre-match presentation to honour the Three Lions skipper, along with Football Association patron Prince William.

events.title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation has sent ripples throughout the global technology industry, with competitors itching to take advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the chip giant Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, with rival chipmakers itching to take advantage of the uncertainty and others wondering if the downfall of one of AI's biggest cheerleaders will dampen the mood around the civilization-altering technology. Huang, who stepped down Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, was the very public face of a company that dominates the market for computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, Huang predicted Nvidia will be grappling with a $1 trillion backlog in orders for its chips by the end of the year, doubling his estimate from a year earlier. A linchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Some of Nvidia's biggest rivals, such as Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, saw their shares advance Thursday following Huang's departure as investors predicted that its customers will look to diversify their suppliers. In the end, analysts say, this might not be a bad thing. “This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand,” said Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at the global consultancy West Monroe. “Nvidia did not create that demand, and a shift in this part of the market could ultimately diversify the supply chain, create more choice for customers and strengthen the broader AI industry in the years ahead.” Nvidia carved out an early lead in tailoring its chipsets known as graphics processing units, or GPUs, from use in powering video games to helping to train powerful AI systems. Demand soared as tech companies scrambled for more chips to build and run AI systems. In annual filings, Nvidia has identified competitors including Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, Intel, Broadcom and cloud services companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft. While these other players are established and respected within the industry for their chips, they have been trying to catch up to Nvidia. Nvidia has had an advantage from the start and as soon as a competitor releases something just as good, Nvidia has put out the next better chip, said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer of International Services Inc. “Nobody’s just sitting still,” he said. While some competitors saw bumps to their share prices Thursday, “their gains are going to be smaller than Nvidia’s losses,” said Chester Spatt, a finance professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But Spatt said he also anticipates chip purchasers could also become “much more reluctant to concentrate their purchases with a single source.” The incident is also sure to prompt elected officials to seek stronger export controls on American-made chips, but that could be a boon for Chinese chipmaker Huawei , another Nvidia competitor. Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, said she suspects Chinese AI firms could accelerate efforts to secure overseas computing capacity ahead of tighter controls. “Chinese chipmakers have already rallied on Nvidia’s troubles, but China’s AI developers depend heavily on Nvidia’s ecosystem,” she said. “This could be both an opportunity and a headache for China.” While Huang is not the only face of AI — OpenAI's Sam Altman , Google's Demis Hassabis and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton are among the others — he's been an influential one. A celebrity-level industry evangelist with President Donald Trump's ear and support, he has advocated for a light touch on AI regulation and has been bullish about AI’s potential to transform society, creating faster economic growth and more scientific breakthroughs. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Microsoft Outlook outage stretches on for hours Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” said Asa Hiken, a senior analyst for research firm eMarketer. “And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.” Lee, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the resignation fallout will ripple across the AI ecosystem. “Obviously Nvidia’s technological leadership won’t disappear, but Huang had played an outsized role as its chief strategist, dealmaker and — very importantly — political advocate, with close access to both Washington and Beijing,” she said. “This happens at a critical juncture when markets are already questioning the sustainability of massive AI spending.

events.title: Coal protest to go ahead on harbour after court rejects police objections
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supreme Court rejects police objections to approve Rising Tide anti-coal protest on Newcastle Harbour The group Rising Tide has staged protests in the Port of Newcastle for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) The NSW Supreme Court has rejected a challenge from the state's police commissioner to a climate protest planned in Newcastle. The protest, organised by Rising Tide, is set to see hundreds of activists paddle out in the Port of Newcastle. The court heard the flotilla will stretch across the harbour, blocking the shipping channel for up to 40 minutes. A climate protest on Newcastle Harbour will go ahead as planned after the Supreme Court rejected an application by NSW Police to stop it. Rising Tide's Paddle for the Plant flotilla is set to see hundreds of people in kayaks take to the water tomorrow. Handing down his judgement this afternoon, Justice Edward Muston said he had to balance the interests of the public with the concerns of police. "The public interests in the facilitations of political expression through assembly outweighs the legitimate concerns which have been expressed by the commissioner," he said. Protest organisers in NSW must submit a notice of intention to hold a public assembly to the police commissioner, known as a Form 1. The NSW Police Commissioner opposed this application and asked the Supreme Court to prohibit the event due to safety concerns for those attending and other users of the harbour. Without a Form 1, protesters run the risk of being charged by police for offences including obstructing people, vehicles or vessels. Police have argued their resources have been stretched on the water and land during previous anti-coal events. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) The court heard up to 785 people on kayaks and other watercraft would enter Newcastle Harbour tomorrow morning to unfurl a 20-metre-long series of connected floating letters that will read "Coal Exports Equals Climate Chaos". They also plan to form a continuous line spanning the harbour for about 30 to 40 minutes, blocking the shipping channel, before returning to shore. On Wednesday, barrister David Hume SC, who acted for NSW Police, told the court transport officials and police predicted dire consequences. "Everyone has looked at this [event] saying it poses an unacceptable risk," Mr Hume said. The Assistant Police Commissioner echoed those calls, citing an incident last year where protesters were washed hundreds of metres down the harbour. Police watch on as protesters previously demonstrated against fossil fuels at Newcastle's port. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) "I have not seen any Rising Tide event run safely yet," Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said. The number of watercraft will be capped at 785 — more than double previous anti-coal protests in the port. Rising Tide's barrister Michael Green told the court the event would have a kayak safety team, swimming in the channel would be banned, and life jackets mandatory. He said people attending would also be briefed on hand signals they could use to raise the alarm if they get into trouble. Rising Tide's Anne Hodgson told the court it would be a family-friendly event and ruled out the prospect of civil disobedience. Ms Hodgson told the court it was hoped global media would cover the event. The world's biggest coal port in Newcastle has been a focus for groups fighting climate change. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) "Yes, as the COP31 meetings are on, we would like that," she said. COP31 is the United Nations Climate Conference — the largest international summit to negotiate and advance global cooperation on climate change. On the eve of the court action, Newcastle City councillors banned Rising Tide from protesting on community land "now and into the future", sparking fears among activists about their right to peacefully protest. events.title: Burkina Faso’s rival armed groups turn on each other as state loses ground
events.summary: JNIM and ISIL intensify their fight for control as Burkina Faso struggles to contain the wider armed conflict. Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso – Armed fighters from two rival groups have fought a series of increasingly deadly battles along Burkina Faso’s northern border with Mali, as the government struggles to reassert control over large parts of the country. The clashes between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the ISIL affiliate in Sahel Province (ISSP) have intensified since early September, with both groups competing for territory and influence across the borderlands. Their latest confrontations have produced competing claims of heavy casualties, although the figures released by the ISIL (ISIS) group remain unverified. One of the first major confrontations took place near Kacham, close to the Mali border, in early September. ISSP claimed to have killed more than 200 JNIM fighters, captured more than 30 others and seized weapons and motorcycles. The claim has not been independently verified. Heni Nsaibia, of the monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), said that, if confirmed, the reported death toll would make it the deadliest battle recorded between the two groups. The fighting escalated again on October 9 around Ganadaouri, in Burkina Faso’s northern Oudalan province. ISIL’s weekly publication, Al-Naba, subsequently claimed that more than 400 JNIM fighters had been killed. JNIM has not publicly responded to the claim, and no independent assessment has established the number of casualties. The scale of the claim came under further scrutiny when ISSP published photographs on November 1 presented as evidence of its victory, showing what it described as the aftermath of the battle. Regional news outlet i-Sahel counted at least 120 bodies in the images but said it could not independently verify whether those pictured were victims of the reported fighting. The number visible in the photos is considerably below the 400 deaths claimed by ISIL. A rivalry that is becoming increasingly costly The confrontation is part of a rivalry that has persisted since 2019, when the two groups began fighting over territory, influence and access to local populations across the Sahel. Their competition has become increasingly costly, with ACLED recording around 320 armed confrontations between them and more than 2,200 fighter deaths since the conflict began. The fighting comes as JNIM continues to make gains against government forces in Burkina Faso. The International Crisis Group says the group holds extensive areas of the country, particularly in the north, north-central region, west and east. Its influence has allowed it to challenge state authority across several regions while maintaining operations in neighbouring Mali and Niger. ACLED’s March 2026 overview documented more than 30 JNIM attacks in Burkina Faso during a February offensive against the military and state-backed Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP). The attacks resulted in the deaths of more than 120 soldiers, forest guards and militia fighters, according to the conflict monitor. The campaign illustrated the pressure facing government forces, even as JNIM had to contend with attacks from its Islamic State rival. The rivalry could offer Burkina Faso’s authorities some breathing room if JNIM is forced to divert fighters and resources to defend its positions against ISSP. But there is little reason to assume that the infighting will translate into lasting gains for the government. JNIM remains active across several countries, while ISSP’s battlefield successes could strengthen its position in areas where the two groups compete. The government faces a wider security crisis For communities caught between the armed groups and government forces, the prospect of one organisation weakening another offers little certainty of relief. Burkina Faso’s security crisis has displaced millions of people and disrupted access to farmland, markets and basic services. The scale of the humanitarian crisis remains severe. An estimated 4.5 million people in Burkina Faso need humanitarian assistance in 2026, according to United Nations humanitarian planning figures. The last consolidated official estimate of internal displacement, published in March 2023, put the number at approximately 2.1 million. That figure should not be mistaken for a newly verified 2026 count. A citizen of Niger, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity because of security concerns, said the fighting between the two groups had raised hopes that communities in the borderlands might face less pressure. “In Tillaberi, where I have family members, our people have endured too much fear. If JNIM and ISSP keep fighting each other, the danger to our communities may lessen, since their forces may weaken. People here deserve the chance to work their fields, travel safely, and raise their children without fearing attacks from either group.

events.title: What smart people in business and tech are saying about Jensen Huang's ouster
events.summary: Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO. Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images Nvidia founder Jensen Huang is out. After another report about an affair, Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Huang had resigned. This is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's departure. Nvidia is without its founder for the first time in more than 30 years. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation , ending the tenure of a leader who had overseen the chipmaker's rise to become one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang's ouster came after days of reports about his personal life. First, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia leader had a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged having an affair, and Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The Times had reported that the Nvidia founder had grown close to Alice Huang , who US officials believed had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. Then on Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had another affair with Kimberly Powell , an Nvidia executive who reported to him. By Thursday morning, one of the world's richest men and a face of the AI boom was out of a job. Clem Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue Bloomberg/Getty Images Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said, "This whole thing sucks." "I wish none of it had happened. It's a really sad day!" Delangue wrote on social media. Delangue, whose company Nvidia agreed to acquire for roughly $12.9 billion, said that he'll continue to fight for open-source AI. "I want to make one thing clear: we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever," he wrote. "This is too important to slow down now. Let's go!" Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co. Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Tech megabull Dan Ives said that Nvidia's board "had no choice." "Time to look forward for Nvidia without Jensen," Ives wrote on X. "Dark chapter for Jensen and Nvidia." Ives also pointed to his earlier statement about what he expects the stock to do without Huang at the helm, which was published before the resignation was announced. "We see the stock valuation at $225 without Jensen ($300 with Jensen as CEO)." President Donald Trump Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images President Donald Trump suggested a familiar name to take Huang's place. "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September. Lloyd Blankfein, former CEO of Goldman Sachs Bloomberg/Getty Images Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein waxed poetic about the moment. "Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean," Blankfein wrote on X. "But as de Gaulle said, 'The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.'" (While the quote is often attributed to the legendary French statesman Charles de Gaulle, at least one researcher has raised questions about its origins .) Sen. Elizabeth Warren Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is likely to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation won't end Congress' desire for answers. "Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren wrote on X. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital Shaun Maguire called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire said Huang will "leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO." "The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void," Maguire wrote in a lengthy post on X. Maguire said, "Infidelity is obviously bad," but Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money Jim Cramer said Apple's new filing was "gloves off." John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images CNBC anchor Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, said Nvidia had no choice. "It had to happen. There's way too much evidence," Cramer said on CNBC after the news became official. Cramer praised Kress who the board named as Nvidia's interim leader. "I like Colette very much," he said. "I think she's going to be terrific in trying to figure out where the pieces are. Martin Casado, A16z general partner TK. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Investor Martin Casado called Thursday a "Dark, dark day." "Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world," he wrote on X. Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management Ross Gerber has been bearish on Tesla. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Ross Gerber said Huang's departure is "certainly a low moment for us long term Nvidia investors." "Jensen has resigned which is sadly the correct action in this case. Nvidia needs to be bigger than one man," Gerber wrote on X. "AI will go on and Nvidia will continue to be the core player." Gerber compared the moment to when Steve Jobs stepped away from Apple. "I was around when Jobs died, and many thought it was the end of Apple," Gerber wrote. "It was only the beginning." Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will rebound. "The unknown is now known," Munster wrote. "This morning $NVDA will gap down ($150 floor) on the Jensen news, then rallies as the market focuses on what actually matters." Munster said Nvidia's earnings next Tuesday should confirm his view. "AI demand is still accelerating," he wrote. "Nvidia GPUs remain the clear winners." Sarah Guo, founder of Conviction Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference Investor Sarah Guo said that Huang's ouster is "a big loss." Before the news was announced, Guo described the Nvidia founder as "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." "He's bent the arc of technological progress, and the growth engine of the American economy rests on the shoulders of the company he built," Guo wrote on Thursday. Stephen Witt, author of a Huang biography Journalist Stephen Witt, who wrote "The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip," said Huang "was Nvidia." events.title: Trump says he spoke to Jensen Huang on Wednesday: ‘He’s going through hell’
events.summary: President Donald Trump said Jensen Huang talked about his family when they spoke. Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images President Donald Trump says Jensen Huang called him a day before he resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Trump said Huang was going through a hard time and spoke about his family. "What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That's what he told me," Trump said. President Donald Trump said he talked to Jensen Huang on Wednesday, a day before the Nvidia CEO resigned . In an interview with Stephen A. Smith at the White House, Trump said Huang called him and talked about the impact the affair scandal has had on his family. "I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family," Trump said. "That's what he told me." Huang resigned on Thursday. On Sunday, he admitted in a memo to staff that he had been "unfaithful" and the Nvidia board announced it was investigating whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation. The resignation also came after a New York Times report on Wednesday that said Huang had engaged in a second affair with an Nvidia executive that reported to him, Kimberly Powell . Following Huang's resignation, a Reuters report alleged a third affair, with another employee at Nvidia who was not named. In the interview on Thursday, Trump praised Huang and his work at Nvidia. When Smith asked if Huang should've stepped down, Trump said it depended on whether a woman he had an affair with was actually a Chinese spy, as US officials suspected, according to the Times. "If the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different," Trump said. He also reiterated his belief that Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple, should succeed Huang. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was named interim CEO on Thursday as the board looks for a replacement. Earlier in the week, on Monday, the president said he had talked to Huang to see how he was doing. He said the executive told him he did not know the person he had an affair with "was a spy." "And I really believe him," Trump said. The Times reported Trump also spoke to Huang on Tuesday this week and encouraged him to fight to remain as Nvidia's CEO. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. events.title: Salmon farm antibiotic use impact 'completely unfair' cray fisher says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Impact of salmon companies' use of antibiotics 'completely unfair', cray fisher says Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Kodey Rolston says "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". ( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) A Tasmanian cray fisher says the wild-caught fishing sector has been "impacted so deeply" by salmon companies' use of antibiotics. Following salmon company Tassal's use of an antibiotic, two commercial fishing areas are being closed from Sunday until February 14 to protect export markets. Premier Jeremy Rockliff says it is important "we get the balance right". A commercial fisher says the impact of salmon companies' antibiotic use in Tasmania is "completely unfair" on smaller, wild fishers. Kodey Rolston, who works as a deckhand on a cray fishing boat, said while he was a supporter of the salmon industry, "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) is closing two commercial fishing areas from Sunday until February 14. Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use. The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "therapeutic management area" (TMA). Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA. Under the state government's Aquaculture Therapeutant — Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, released last month, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed. The closures are to protect export markets as some countries have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild-caught fish. Man who burned shoebox of tax records fined for resulting bushfire Tasmanian premier apologises for 'outcome' of Christmas post AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community deal The two new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel. The company said the closure accounted for 1.6 per cent of the state's historical rock lobster catch. A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) But Mr Rolston said the closure area was "vital to the crayfishing industry". "Down south is our safe haven for abalones, for crayfish. "It's a multi, multi-generational fishing ground and it's being locked off all together because the salmon farms want to just dump as much antibiotics in the water as they can to try and save their own arse and not cooperate with other businesses," he said. "I actually don't have anything against the salmon farms. "In all honesty, I'm very much for them — they provide a lot of jobs all around the state. Tassal says the rock lobster fishery closure accounts for 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual rock lobster catch. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said the government was expecting the wild-caught fishing industry to "do all the heavy lifting". "Wild fishers have been sidelined and the interests of big salmon companies have been put first by the government," Ms Woodruff said. "They've refused to put in place any regulations to constrain the operations of salmon farming in the Channel." 'Important that all industries work together': Premier Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was important "we get the balance right". "The industry is in a transition and a very quick transition in terms of antibiotic use because of the investment that's going into breeding, for example, will mean that in future years there'll be less reliance on antibiotics if at all, and that's the space we need to get to. "We're in a transition time now and I know it's difficult … I feel for industry outside of the salmon industry very much. "It's important that all industries work together, we get the balance right." In a statement yesterday, Tassal said the closure was a "precaution to protect export market access". "Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe. "We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible.

events.title: Outlook outage expected to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Microsoft Outlook outage cost to businesses 'billions' The Microsoft outage has been ongoing for more than 12 hours. ( Reuters: David Ryder ) Experts say the Microsoft outage is likely to cost businesses billions. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner, Ashwin Pal, says small business will be hit the hardest. The financial impact is expected to last weeks. The Microsoft outage is calculated to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars, with experts warning small businesses will be the hardest hit by the technology failure. A widespread outage, which started about 3:15 am AEDT, has hit platforms including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing emails and encountering errors across the Microsoft suite of products. Workers across multiple types of businesses have reported being unable to access email or SharePoint, with some resorting to using fax machines to keep operating. Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues affecting the tech giant's apps, read our blog. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner Ashwin Pal said the cost to professional service businesses, such as lawyers or accountants, would be hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour. "It's not just the initial downtime, it's more actually about then the catch up effort because that costs money," he said. "Because now when things do normalise, you're going to have to spend money to actually catch up because of all the backlog." Ashwin Pal says Monday's backlog of work will be costly. ( Supplied ) He said the impact of the outage was amplified by the 3.9 million businesses globally that used the Microsoft suite, with many not having backup systems, resulting in huge costs to the economy. "This is what happened with CrowdStrike. So when the outage happened, because of where we are in the world in terms of time zones, we felt the impact first. "As the US and Europe come online, and they can't operate, it's going to get worse. So you're going to have a multiplier effect." Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today. He said the repercussions would be most keenly felt by small businesses, due to operating on thin margins. "You take a CBA as an example, they'll be able to absorb an impact like this a lot easier than the five-person accounting shop down the road," he said. "They were already actually working on very thin margins. All of a sudden they're actually out for three, four, five days or whatever it takes for them to recover. That could be the final straw." Owner of small Queensland business Regal Shower Screens, Tracey Tucker, said the lost day of business would cost at least $30,000, but there were numerous flow-on effects. "I'm paying my girls sitting in here in the office to do nothing," she said. "The phone rings, they can't order anything. "Then it puts undue pressure because if it's back online on Monday, everything we missed Friday, we're going to try to catch up on." Experts say the outage will hurt small business the most. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) She said the outage meant the business would struggle to meet its promoted deadlines because the glass manufacturers would also be inundated on Monday. "It's going to put pressure on everybody down the track because our girls are going to get yelled at, like, 'You just said my shower's going to be two weeks now, it's two and a half weeks', all because we can't send the order through today." Service delivery manager with telecommunication company Hubify, Chloe Mombeshora, said she had received numerous calls from less tech-savvy clients who were unsure what was happening. "They're thinking that their internet is down, they don't know what to do," she said. She added some clients had raised concerns the inability to communicate could impact their businesses' reputations. Some Outlook users were receiving notifications for emails they could not open. ( ABC News: Liana Walker ) IT support specialist James Coates said he had been inundated with requests for help but was unable to reply through his helpdesk because it used Outlook. "We actually have to call each client individually, every single personal phone number, every single Teams number, hope it gets through and update them that way because the email service is just not working on their end either," he said. He said he also could not do other work over concerns it would not be saved. Do you know more, or are you affected?

events.title: Outback cattle flown to Kazakhstan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hereford cattle from the middle of Australia flown to Kazakhstan Ben Hayes (second from right) alongside livestock agent Tim McKean, inspecting cattle with Kazakhstan buyers. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) A buyer from Kazakhstan has taken nearly 300 head of cattle from the Northern Territory after flying out to inspect them. Cattle producer Ben Hayes says Kazakhstan's government has an initiative to boost its national herd. Federal data shows Kazakhstan imported more than 1,000 head each of cattle and sheep in October. Nearly 300 head of cattle from a station near Alice Springs have been flown to Kazakhstan, in what local producers hope is the start of a new market. The distance from Alice Springs in the middle of Australia to Kazakhstan is roughly 10,000 kilometres. Ben Hayes from Undoolya Station said he got a call from his livestock agent one day with an interesting offer. "He asked if we had some heifers for this Kazakhstan job and we did," he said. "The buyer from Kazakhstan actually flew out here [with an interpreter], took a quick look and ended up taking them. "They got trucked down to Melbourne, where they stayed in quarantine for about a month and were then loaded into crates and onto the plane." Cattle from Undoolya Station ready for export to Kazakhstan. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) Mr Hayes said the animals were flown from Melbourne to Singapore and then onto Kazakhstan. "There was a weight limit on them of about 180 to 250 kilograms and they had to be preg-tested empty." He said the money paid for the animals was "on-par" with what he would normally receive in the Australian market. But he said the chance to be involved in the sale to Kazakhstan was "very special". "To know that our heifers are now becoming breeding stock for Kazakhstan is a feather in our cap, in Australia's cap," he said. ABC Landline has been told some cattle from Mt Riddock Station in the NT were also purchased for the consignment. According to data from the Federal Department of Agriculture, there were two flights of breeder cattle out of Victoria last month totalling 1,252 head. Another flight to Kazakhstan took 1,617 breeder sheep. It is understood Australia last exported cattle to Kazakhstan in 2019. It is a long way from Alice Springs to Kazakhstan. ( ABC Landline ) This is not the first time Undoolya Station has flown cattle to a distant market. In 1981, Undoolya steers were flown direct out of Alice Springs to Korea. "I was only a little fella at the time, but my father and grandfather flew steers out of Alice Springs on a Flying Tiger aircraft, straight to Korea" Mr Hayes said. "I don't know why they wanted steers, but that's what happened, Alice Springs is an international airport, it was a good opportunity." Undoolya Station is the Northern Territory's oldest pastoral lease. Established in 1872, the property has been owned by the Hayes family since 1906.
