events.title: A visit to my 85-year-old dad prompted me to move my family back to the US. I wasn't prepared for caregiving.
events.summary: Vivian Pei moved abroad to build her career and started a family. A visit to her dad prompted her move back to the US. Provided by Vivian Pei Vivian Pei left the US and spent more than 30 years building a career and starting a family abroad. She and her two teenage kids moved back after she realized her father needed help. Pei cared for him until he died last year. She's grateful for their final years together. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Vivian Pei, an American mother of two and cofounder of Snacky Mini Mart in Iowa City. After building her career abroad for over 30 years, she moved back to the US to look after her father. Her words have been edited for length and clarity. I spent more than 30 years living abroad . I never imagined I'd end up moving back to the US, especially to Iowa City, where I'd never lived before. Five years ago, I visited my 85-year-old dad and was shocked by how much he'd aged. Have you built a successful life abroad but chosen to move back home to care for or be close to aging family members ? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. He'd always been fiercely independent and had continued working at his restaurant in Wisconsin until just before the pandemic, but suddenly he seemed so much older. His house wasn't in great shape, and it was clear he needed more help than he was letting on. I'd spent decades living my own life overseas. Seeing him like that made me realize it was time to come home. Pei was happily raising her kids in Singapore. Provided by Vivian Pei I left the US as a teenager and never looked back I was born in San Francisco, but when I was 4, my dad moved our family to St. Louis to a Chinese restaurant. He worked incredibly hard and eventually helped his siblings move to the US. They opened restaurants of their own. Growing up as one of the only Asian kids at my suburban school wasn't always easy. My parents were strict, and I couldn't wait to get out and experience the world. I spent my senior year of college studying in Paris. It was my first trip abroad, and I loved it so much that I stayed for two years. It was the first place I truly felt happy. From there, I worked in Tokyo, Singapore, and London, where I earned my MBA. I spent most of my career in marketing and brand strategy. My British husband and I met in Singapore, later moved back, and spent 16 years there raising our kids . We eventually split, but continued to co-parent our children. After seeing her dad, Pei knew that she needed to change. Provided by Vivian Pei Convincing my family to move wasn't easy After seeing my dad, I couldn't shake the feeling that something needed to change. By March 2022, I'd decided I needed to move back to the US with my kids. My former husband wasn't enthusiastic about the idea, and I recognized that uprooting two teenagers from the only home they'd known was a huge decision. We had a lot of conversations before everyone eventually agreed. Now, the kids spend every other month, and sometimes summers, with their dad. I chose Iowa City because we had extended family there who could provide a support network. I arrived a few months later with my two kids and 12 large suitcases. We were essentially starting over. Caring for my dad was a whole different ballgame My dad, who'd been divorced for some time, moved in with us two weeks after we arrived. It was the first time we'd lived together since I was 16. Looking back, I probably should've given myself more time to settle before taking on his care. I was trying to help two teenagers adjust to new schools while figuring out how to buy a house, set up utilities, and navigate the American healthcare system . Then there was my dad's paperwork. He handed me piles of mail, financial documents, medical records, and insurance information. I had to find new doctors and organize his medications. I also hadn't anticipated how physically and emotionally demanding caregiving would become. My dad came from a generation that didn't complain. He'd insist everything was fine, even when he was experiencing pain. Getting him to tell me what was actually wrong was frustrating. As he started to show signs of dementia , his personality changed. He became stubborn, and managing his moods was exhausting. There were also intimate aspects of caring for him, like helping with hygiene, that I'd never imagined having to do. It sometimes felt like I had a third child. The kids got to spend some time with their grandpa when they were young, but Pei is grateful they got more time when they moved back. Provided by Viviene Pei I lost part of myself in the process Moving back was a massive culture shock. In Singapore, I had a full social life and a professional identity. Suddenly, all of that was gone. I was caught between caring for my children and caring for my father. I was holding everything together while losing myself. I was also going through menopause, which made it harder. After about six months, I knew I needed something that was just for me. I started a food business with my cousin, selling Asian-inspired snacks at farmers markets. It gave me an outlet, some independence, and the flexibility I needed while caring for my dad . I don't regret coming home, but I'd do things differently Last year, my dad passed away, and I'm grateful I made the move. My dad had spent his entire life providing for our family, rarely spending money on himself. Being able to cook and care for him felt like my chance to give something back. He also got to see his grandchildren every day, something he'd missed while we were living overseas. If I could do it again, I'd take things slower. I'd settle my children first. I'd also have more open conversations with family members about sharing the workload. I'm still living in Iowa City, although I expect to downsize once my son finishes high school. I've spent most of my life searching for somewhere that feels like home. I don't know where I'll end up next. But I'm glad I came back when I did. I got to spend those final years with my dad , and that's time I can never get back. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: World is now in ‘age of electricity’, energy agency chief says
events.summary: Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said. Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war. Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures. “We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey . “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.” Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century. Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels , mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said. The more our lives can be powered by clean energy the better, say experts, not least because, as a result of the inefficiency of fossil fuels , most of the rest of our energy is wasted as heat, so when these activities are electrified, only about half of the energy needs to be replaced. Most countries back the electrification goal, according to Birol. He has worked closely with the Turkish and Australian governments, which are jointly presiding over this year’s summit . “It will be an unmistakable signal to the markets and investors that governments see that the future of energy is in electricity,” he said. “This will make the age of electricity even earlier and cheaper. It might be one of the most consequential decisions coming from Cops in the last several years.” But even if the resolution was not adopted – some governments, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, are said to be opposed, and owing to the convention by which consensus is needed to pass decisions, a small number of countries can hold the rest to ransom – the “staggering” progress would continue, Birol said. “The reason is there are three major drivers for electrification: one is AI and datacentres; second is the electrification transportation sector; and third, the most important one in terms of volume, is air conditioning. Air conditioners are growing explosively,” he said. In the US, about 90% of households have access to air conditioning, but in India it is fewer than 20%, and in Nigeria about 5%. “With the increasing effects of climate change, and if they have more money, [people] buy air conditioners,” said Birol. “These things are happening, and electrification is not bad. It is good for energy security, because it is your own electricity [generated within a country rather than imported, as fossil fuels often are], good for the competitiveness of countries, and good for climate change.” The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential He added: “Global energy demand is growing strongly, but global electricity demand is growing three times faster than total energy demand. And it is impossible to stop it. The one and only issue is making electricity affordable for people.” Birol placed the blame for the UK’s high electricity prices firmly on gas. “There is always a debate about this in the UK, but in fact the single most important reason why UK electricity prices may be on the high side is reliance on imported gas. Gas prices went up, so did the electricity prices, full stop. And the solution is not importing more gas, but building more [renewable] electricity at home,” he said. The transformation is happening fast. “Five years ago, only 5% of all the cars sold was electric.

events.title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries
events.summary: Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines T he race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world. The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey , the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries. Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity . But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices. Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day: “I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower. “I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner. “I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes. “I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments. “We charge our car with a charging box in our garage where, like most apartment garages in Oslo, we have built a collective charging system. If everyone put their charging on at the same time it would go slow, but in practice that doesn’t happen. “I have a large battery on my EV so I charge it once every two to three weeks. Of course we pay for the electricity and a system fee, but it’s much cheaper than petrol and diesel. “In my office, we have district heating, which is quite common in Oslo in larger buildings, then we use electricity for light and computers. Lunch is made in my office in the internal canteen with electricity. At work I use Microsoft Copilot, which is a really helpful tool, but of course there are big questions there – energy demands will get too high if everyone is using AI more. “I come home and use electricity to make dinner, watch television and go to the cinema. Growing up in a small village on the western coast of Norway , we also used wood for heating as well as electricity. But it is fair to say that electricity is common part of Norwegian life and has been for a long time. “What has changed is that our transport sector is also now run on a rising amount of electricity: passenger cars, buses and also ferries. That happened quite fast. Heavy goods vehicles are also increasingly electric, so of course that changes the system and society. “Perhaps because of the war in Ukraine and more extreme weather conditions, people are becoming aware that they are quite dependent on electricity, so in recent years there has been debate on how to prepare for a crisis. In previous power cuts, some people have used their electric cars as a battery to power electric equipment. “There is also a big debate about electricity prices. In Norway we have nearly 100% renewable electricity, but even so we are connected to the European grid. So the gas prices still influence our electricity prices. And when we have dry winters, electricity prices rise because if we have less snow, the hydropower gets less water. Rising numbers of datacentres is also something consumers are starting to wonder about – what this development is going to look like and how much energy it is using.” An e-motorbike taxi driver in Kigali, Rwanda Six years ago, the Rwandan government embarked on an enthusiastic promotion of e-mobility by removing a number of taxes on e-bikes and vehicles and offering incentives for businesses operating charging stations.

events.title: UNRWA funding cuts deepen hardship for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon
events.summary: Funding cuts and Israel’s war have left Palestinians in Lebanon in increasingly dire circumstances. Beirut, Lebanon – Doumoua al-Baitan sat on the roof of a building in Beirut’s Palestinian refugee camp of Bourj el-Barajneh as the sun set. Like many Palestinian refugees in Lebanon, al-Baitan was born and raised in this camp. For decades, Palestinians in Lebanon have been supported by the UN branch focused on Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. But funding cuts have impeded UNRWA’s ability to provide crucial aid, particularly since the Trump administration’s decision in February 2025 to maintain a US funding freeze imposed the previous year. list 1 of 3 ‘Greater Israel’: Christian Zionism’s role in US policy list 2 of 3 US election results could be positive for Lebanon, Hezbollah chief says list 3 of 3 More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says Between the funding cuts and funding shortfalls, UNRWA has had to close down or reduce hours of schools, healthcare centres, and clinics in Lebanon’s Palestinian refugee camps. Palestinians told Al Jazeera that in addition to there being less work to go around and less medical support, children are being crammed into overcrowded classrooms, and the use and sale of illegal drugs has become more prevalent. “My kids cannot retain what they are taught in class,” al-Baitan said, citing overcrowding. The divorced mother of four said she has started paying $200 per month – the same price as her monthly rent – for two of her children to attend after-school lessons. Since 1950, UNRWA has supported Palestinian refugees across the Middle East. Lebanon has 12 Palestinian refugee camps, where a large proportion of the country’s approximately 230,000 Palestinians live. UNRWA’s role in the camps includes providing education, healthcare, relief and social services, camp infrastructure and improvement, microfinance, and emergency assistance. Palestinians first became refugees in Lebanon during the 1948 Nakba, when Zionist forces established the state of Israel after turning 750,000 Palestinians into refugees. Today, the majority of Palestinians in Lebanon are de facto stateless and do not have Lebanese citizenship. As a result, they are effectively banned from a number of professions in Lebanon, including medicine, law, engineering, and pharmacy, which has meant the community is one of the most vulnerable in Lebanon. And that vulnerability has only increased as UNRWA faces a severe funding shortfall. UNRWA spokesperson Fadi al-Tayyar told Al Jazeera in October that his agency needed around $70m to $80m more for 2026, forcing them to reduce service working hours by 20 percent since February. Many schools have been forced to reduce the school week from five to four days for the 2026-27 academic year. More than 35,000 pupils are in 58 schools, with 15 additional classrooms in the northern Beddawi camp, in Tripoli. Residents in Bourj el-Barajneh said that most of the schools in the camp had been shut down and that now students were being crammed into classrooms of 40 or more students at a time. According to a monthly report released by the Jafra Foundation, a nonprofit that supports vulnerable communities in Lebanon including Palestinian refugees, the funding shortfall “threatens the education, healthcare, water, and sanitation services provided by UNRWA and exacerbates the pressures on millions of Palestinian refugees in its five areas of operation: the Gaza Strip, the West Bank (including East Jerusalem), Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria”. UNRWA’s June 2026 emergency report found that out of 26 primary healthcare centres and clinics, only 15 were operational. Eleven had shut down. While the precarity has had an impact on the Palestinian community in Lebanon at large, some refugees also suffer from compounding difficulties. There are between 3,000 and 5,000 Palestinian refugees who are undocumented. There are also an estimated 19,000 Palestinian refugees from Syria living in Lebanon, many of whom fled Lebanon’s eastern neighbour during the country’s 13-year war. A policy change in Lebanon in May 2024, however, halted residency renewals for many Palestinians from Syria, leading to increased exposure to detention, more difficulty in finding legal employment, and registering for education or civil issues. Locals and experts also said the funding shortcomings have led to a proliferation of issues related to drugs and violence in the camps. “There is a very tired economic situation and there is no work,” Fadi Abu Halawa, the security officer at the Jafra Foundation in Beirut, told Al Jazeera. He added that Jafra’s monthly report showed an increase in crime and drug use and distribution in the camps. “Of course, all of this is 100 percent due to the economy,” he said. People in the camps have responded to the funding cuts, lack of work, and subpar services by organising sit-ins. Shatila camp, one of the largest in Beirut, has organised one for Friday.

events.title: Haze-linked First Resources, Bumitama post higher profits for Q3
events.summary: First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter. First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in Q3 underlying net profit to US$122.7 million, helped by higher palm oil sales and stronger output after buying Austindo Nusantara Jaya. Bumitama’s Q3 net profit rose 1.9% to 614.1 billion rupiah, as better plantation and mill productivity lifted production, though dry weather hurt shipments. Both firms said biodiesel demand and higher energy prices may support palm oil, but they also stressed zero-burning policies and cooperation with authorities over the haze. SINGAPORE – Two palm oil companies linked to the transboundary haze in October reported higher profits for the third quarter ended Sept 30, in separate business updates published on the morning of Nov 13. Palm oil producer First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million (S$158 million) for the third quarter of 2026, from US$87.5 million in the year-ago period. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palms, it said. Sales were up 24.9% at US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation rose 26.6% to US$207.4 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from US$163.8 million a year ago. For the nine months ended Sept 30, sales grew 36.5% year on year to US$1.6 billion, driven by higher sales volumes. A net inventory drawdown of 28,000 tonnes over the nine-month period, compared with a build-up of 80,000 tonnes in the corresponding period in 2025, also supported higher sales volumes. The group’s stronger production output in the first nine months of 2026 was also attributable in part to the full nine-month contribution from Austindo Nusantara Jaya, an Indonesian agribusiness company acquired in May 2025. However, profits were partially offset by foreign currency translation losses resulting from the depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah against the US dollar. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. In addition, elevated crude oil prices arising from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East are expected to support biodiesel economics and crude palm oil demand. Performance supported by productivity improvements Meanwhile, Bumitama reported a 1.9% increase in its net profit to 614.1 billion rupiah (S$43 million) for the quarter ended Sept 30, compared with 602.9 billion rupiah in the previous corresponding period. For the nine-month period, net profit rose 30.6% to 2.4 trillion rupiah, up from 1.9 trillion rupiah in the year-ago period. Revenue increased 9.7% to 4.2 trillion rupiah in the third quarter, up from 3.9 trillion rupiah a year ago. For the nine-month period, revenue was up 20% at 16.3 trillion rupiah. Bumitama said its performance was supported by productivity improvements in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. In July, internal production of fresh fruit bunches reached 383,203 tonnes, accounting for almost 40% of the quarter’s production. Quarterly production of crude palm oil increased 14% year on year to 368,323 tonnes. However, exceptionally dry weather conditions in its Kalimantan estates during the third quarter put additional pressure on logistics infrastructure and disrupted shipments, said Bumitama. Consequently, third-quarter revenue declined compared with the second quarter. The prolonged dry season also heightened the risk of land and forest fires across parts of Kalimantan. Fires affected certain areas within or adjoining the group’s concessions, including community-managed, conservation and unplanted land, the group noted. Bumitama said that elevated energy prices and Indonesia’s biodiesel programme coupled with a relatively constrained palm oil supply growth could provide a “supportive backdrop” for palm oil fundamentals heading into 2027. However, market conditions remain subject to uncertainty. These include changes in global energy prices, supply-and-demand dynamics, and the potential effects of prolonged dry weather on future production, it added. Both First Resources and Bumitama reiterated their commitment to upholding a zero-burning policy, and cooperating with the Indonesian and Singapore authorities in relation to the haze.

events.title: Iranophobia: Netanyahu’s bid to transform fear into political survival
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Despite knowing war with Iran was manufactured for Netanyahu’s survival, many would still rally behind it As the right-wing coalition government that oversaw the genocide in Gaza, launched attacks across the region, and eroded civil liberties at home appears to lose its grip on power by the day, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s increasingly frantic efforts to derail the political transition suggest a growing desperation to stay in office. Among those efforts appears to be an attempt to reignite the war with Iran. Netanyahu has reportedly ordered the Israeli military to prepare for war ahead of a potential attack on Iran, in defiance of the opposition’s calls for restraint. list 1 of 4 Netanyahu fights to stay relevant as Israel’s opposition closes in list 2 of 4 Is Washington rethinking its relationship with Israel? list 3 of 4 Iran warns of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack list 4 of 4 Netanyahu’s legacy: Personality politics reshapes Israeli democracy The reports follow revelations that Netanyahu had been phoning US President Donald Trump almost daily to press for renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli media have also reported repeated confrontations between Netanyahu and military chief Eyal Zamir, who has resisted proposals for military action against Iran, warning that they could trigger a wider conflict. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a viable government, but that is not a foregone conclusion. Netanyahu has been pushing for a national unity government that would include himself and his Likud party, or waiting for Eisenkot to fail, leading to another election. “Netanyahu is desperate,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli political analyst at King’s College London, said. “He knows – and you can see it from his behaviour – that it is likely that he is politically done, and only a national unity government could save him.” “A little war could compel Eisenkot & Co,” he said, referring to the opposition bloc and its leader, Gadi Eisenkot, “to form such a government in a time of crisis.” Many in the opposition, including Eisenkot himself, have accused Netanyahu of attempting to drag the country into a potentially devastating war for his own political survival, or of deliberately stalling the coalition-building process in the hope of running down the clock and forcing another election. Yet while critics see Netanyahu’s attempts to reignite war with Iran as a cynical bid to retain power, analysts have suggested that even his fiercest opponents could rally behind him if he does launch an attack. “It’s paradoxical,” said Haggai Ram, a professor at Ben-Gurion University and author of the book Iranophobia, which details Israel’s longstanding hostility to Tehran. “Everyone knows it would be contrived, but the hysteria over Iran cuts through everything. If Netanyahu succeeds, and manages to start a war with Iran, of course the opposition would fall in behind him, and the public would expect them to. They’d recognise the cynicism for what it was, but this is Iran. This is the great enemy.” “For the former military members of the opposition, confronting Iran was what they spent their entire lives training for. For the public, after years of being told of the Iranian threat, many already see the war as inevitable,” he said. Israel’s decades-long cold war with Iran has been a constant throughout much of the Israeli population’s lifetime. For decades, Israelis have lived with the threat of attacks from Iran’s regional allies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, whose rhetoric threatening Israel’s destruction has been widely reported in Israeli media. That fear has been reinforced by repeated warnings from Israeli leaders, dating back to at least the 1990s, that Tehran was on the brink of acquiring a nuclear weapon and would likely use it against Israel. Tensions came to a head as Israel launched multiple wars across the region following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023. A 12-day exchange of strikes with Iran in June 2025 was followed by a joint attack with the US launched in February, which has disrupted some of the world’s critical waterways, thrown financial markets into turmoil, and affected household expenditure across much of the world. Nevertheless, another war with Iran may offer Netanyahu a route out of the political bind he finds himself in, political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University suggested. As things stand, a majority of the public oppose him and his coalition, and, in Bar-Tal’s framing, he is “fighting for his life”, with multiple active criminal cases against him. Although Bar-Tal doubted that Trump, Israel’s principal ally and military backer, would allow Netanyahu to derail US negotiations with Iran, he believed that Israelis would still “support such a war, and this is a good card for him to play [to create the] turmoil” needed to extricate himself from his current predicament.

events.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
events.summary: Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though. The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.  The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though. Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet. Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he cofounded in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing. In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.  The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.  Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks. Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: From ocean legend to undersea reef: Why has the SS United States been sunk?
events.summary: The ship had been inactive for years despite various owners attempting to save and restore it. The historic SS United States ocean liner has taken its final trip, this time to the bottom of the ocean, as it becomes part of an artificial underwater reef . The nearly 1,000-foot (302m)-long vessel, the fastest ocean liner in the world, was sunk on Wednesday after its hull was hollowed out to ensure it remains on the ocean floor, in a process also known as scuttling. Over five hours, the ship gradually filled with water and, in its final moments, tilted to its side and sank to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico off the coast of Destin, Florida. The vessel will now feature as part of the world’s largest artificial reef, which is expected to become a popular diving destination. Here’s what we know about the vessel: Built between 1950 and 1951, the ship was larger than the Titanic, which was 882 feet nine inches (269.1 meters) long. The SS United States was known for its speed, strength and luxury. Officially launched in 1952, the vessel made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its first trip, crossing the Atlantic in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 35.59 knots (almost 66km/h). The ocean liner’s record has yet to be broken by another passenger liner. During 17 years of operation, the SS US carried thousands of passengers, including former Presidents John F Kennedy, Bill Clinton, Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower. Hollywood stars Marilyn Monroe, Elizabeth Taylor and Marlon Brando also graced the ship, as did surrealist painter Salvador Dali and jazz musician Duke Ellington. With the advent of air travel, the ship’s career came to an end in 1969. The ship had been inactive for years and remained docked in Philadelphia as various owners attempted to save and restore it. However, the costs of maintaining the vessel mounted. In 2021, Philadelphia port authorities raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700, which the nonprofit SS United States Conservatory could no longer afford. In 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa County bought the ship for $1m, with plans to transform it into the world’s largest artificial reef. According to the county’s website, the ship underwent a yearlong process to ensure it would be environmentally safe to sink as an artificial reef, and the county said it followed all standards set by regulatory agencies. “Artificial reefs prepared in this way are a benefit to the marine ecosystem, not the other way around. They create habitat that did not previously exist and foster the development of a diverse environment that can thrive for the overall health of the environment that benefits marine life, our fishing industry and tourism as a whole,” a statement from the county says. The forming of the world’s largest artificial reef is expected to attract wreck divers to the site, creating more tourism opportunities for Florida. Why are ships sunk to become reefs? There are an estimated three million shipwrecks lying on sea and ocean floors around the world, according to a 2007 report from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation. Many are reclaimed naturally by marine life and are used by coral, eels and snappers as homes. While some ships are sunk through disaster, others are deliberately sunk to begin reef deployment and attract fish. Preparation for the sinking of ships is extensive, as harmful substances including paint, wiring and fuel must be removed before they can safely become part of marine life. Eventually, a sunken ship’s facade will be unrecognisable, with marine life such as fish, barnacles, and crustaceans all inhabiting or using the vessel. What else has been sunk to make reefs? Besides other decommissioned ships which have been deliberately sunk, oil rigs, radio towers and train boxcars have also been used to make artificial reefs on which fish and other marine life can thrive. More than 600 oil rigs and gas platforms previously installed on the US outer continental shelf were used as part of a 1984 US programme called “Rigs to Reefs” in the Gulf of Mexico. Other materials have also been used to make artificial reefs, including log huts, household goods such as fridges and shopping trolleys, and even retired New York City subway cars. Last year, one of the world’s largest artificial reefs was installed around the base of a single wind turbine off the Sussex coast in England. It is made up of 75,000 specifically designed, low-carbon, concrete reef cubes, each with a central chamber and an outer honeycomb texture to encourage marine life to use them. The cubes were also designed to help the wind farm withstand erosion by acting as a barrier against sea currents and wave energy, slowing sediment that could scour the base. In Australia, the Queensland Government established its eighth artificial reef in Moreton Bay Marine Park in 2018, using concrete blocks.

events.title: US Senator Chris Van Hollen seeks to lead Democrats: Who is he?
events.summary: Van Hollen is the son of former US diplomats known for his antiwar position and for championing progressive causes. United States Senator Chris Van Hollen has declared that he is running for Senate majority leader as Democrats prepare to take charge of the US Congress in January, following a Democratic landslide in this month’s midterm elections. Van Hollen said in a post on X late on Thursday that Americans had “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption”. list 1 of 3 US lawmakers urge Trump team to free American student held by Israel list 2 of 3 US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank list 3 of 3 Mississippi elects first black senator in nearly 150 years “To deliver, we need new leadership,” he wrote, adding that “this isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call. He is a Democratic senator from Maryland who has been in Congress since 2003, rising to prominence for his opposition during the second term of US President Donald Trump. Van Hollen was born in 1959 in Karachi, Pakistan. His father was a Foreign Service officer who later served as the US deputy assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern and South Asian affairs. His mother worked at the CIA and the US Department of State. Why is he running for Senate majority leader? Van Hollen has had mounting calls to enter the race for Senate majority leader amid growing opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s continued tenure, over criticism of his handling of the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency. US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan has said he will not support Schumer as the majority leader in the Senate and welcomed Van Hollen’s decision to run. In a post on X, El-Sayed said: “I called on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed said. In April 2025, Van Hollen drew attention when he travelled to El Salvador to meet a Maryland resident mistakenly deported by the Trump administration, in a case which ultimately saw Kilmar Abrego Garcia returned to the US. In September, Van Hollen forced a vote on a resolution that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention. The resolution failed 47-53, with senators voting largely along party lines. In August 2025, Van Hollen accompanied US Senator Jeff Merkley to the Rafah crossing at Egypt’s border with Gaza as Israel continued to prevent humanitarian aid delivery to Palestinians in the enclave. Van Hollen has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Israel and has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “ chronic liar “. He told Al Jazeera earlier this year that the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”. Van Hollen has been one of the foremost advocates for ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and violations in the occupied West Bank. He has consistently pushed for strict accountability for Israeli actions and for restricting US military assistance to Israel.

events.title: ST Engineering Q3 revenue rises 9% to $3.4 billion, declares interim dividend of 5 cents per share
events.summary: Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion. SINGAPORE – ST Engineering’s revenue for the third quarter ended September rose 9% year on year to $3.4 billion, from $3.1 billion in the previous corresponding period, the group said on Nov 13. The technology and engineering company declared a third-quarter interim dividend of five cents per share, up from four cents a year earlier. Its Q1 and Q2 dividends were four cents and five cents per share, respectively, bringing the total for the first three quarters to 14 cents per share. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased 10% to $10 billion, from $9.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. Excluding LeeBoy, its US-based construction equipment business divested on Sept 4, 2025, revenue grew 13% on a rebased basis. Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion, up 7% year on year. Excluding LeeBoy, revenue from the segment grew 13%. Q3 revenue rose 8% to $1.4 billion, or 12% on a rebased basis. The increase was led by marine and digital systems and cybersecurity businesses. The segment secured $5.5 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, including $1.8 billion in Q3. These included a five-year contract to supply 40mm ammunition to the British Ministry of Defence, projects involving defence command-and-control systems in Singapore, and maintenance and support services for the US Navy’s fleet. Meanwhile, commercial aerospace revenue rose 12% to about $4.1 billion in the first nine months, supported by higher contributions from engine maintenance, repair and overhaul work and nacelles, a container for aircraft parts. Revenue for Q3 increased 7% to $1.4 billion. The segment secured $4.2 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, of which $1.4 billion was won in Q3. The latest wins included its first Airbus A220 airframe heavy maintenance contract with an Asia-Pacific operator and airframe maintenance agreements with Asia-Pacific airline customers. Revenue from urban solutions and satellite communications increased 15% year on year to about $1.7 billion in the first nine months. Q3 revenue also rose 15% to $600 million, with higher contributions from both businesses. The segment secured $3.5 billion in new contracts in the nine-month period, including $2.4 billion in Q3. Wins included turnkey rail services for the Taoyuan MRT Brown Line and Green Line Extension in Taiwan, integrated smart security management solutions contracts in Singapore and tolling infrastructure modernisation work for the Tampa-Hillsborough Expressway Authority in the US. Across the group, contract wins totalled $13.2 billion in the first nine months, including $5.6 billion in the third quarter. The nine-month figure excluded $1.7 billion in New Jersey Turnpike Authority order book recognition. The group’s order book stood at a record $37.7 billion as at September, up from $33.2 billion as at end-2025. About $3.1 billion is expected to be delivered in the remainder of 2026. ST Engineering also reported a record-low operating expenses-to-revenue ratio of 9% for the first nine months, compared with 10.2% for the whole of 2025. The 2025 figure excluded a one-off impairment loss of iDirect group. Separately, ST Engineering said it is exploring long-term opportunities in the nuclear energy sector, drawing on its capabilities in complex, safe and mission-critical environments and partnering organisations with complementary expertise. Its current collaborations include those with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, Sembcorp Utilities and Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Areas of activity include factory-fabricated structural modules, such as protective steel structures, and advanced materials for fusion reactors, including tungsten coatings for reactor’s inner walls. The group also sees opportunities to apply its capabilities in digital twin technology and artificial intelligence, advanced materials and manufacturing, and large-scale systems integration.

events.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
events.summary: Joon Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, have been retained by Nvidia to investigate allegations that then-CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang resigned Thursday after reports he had an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected spy for China, and a second affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Kim has a long track record as a federal prosecutor and lawyer in private practice. His investigations have included ones into former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and the FDIC. Joon Kim , the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia to investigate former CEO Jensen Huang , and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases. Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John "The Teflon Don" Gotti's son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo , the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp . and other high-profile people and companies. The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer , which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to "conduct a thorough and independent investigation" of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him. That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe. Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim. Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job. "I think he's the ideal person for this role," said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related. "I think they're going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead," Edward Kim said. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University. After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit. The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included "racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism," the office has previously said. Kim's trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti's nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries. "He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate," said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends. "He's incredibly smart," Conniff said. "I think he's known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned." Kim in 2006 returned to Cleary Gottlieb as a partner in the firm's litigation and enforcement group but then went back to the SDNY in 2013. During his second stint there, he served as deputy U.S. attorney, and then served as acting U.S. attorney from 2017 to 2018. events.title: A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
events.summary: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. March 2023 Megaspeed, a datacenter firm, is spun out from a Chinese video game company Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. November 2023 Megaspeed is sold to a Singaporean shell company and becomes an Nvidia cloud partner Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. June 2024 Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are seen together in Taipei, Taiwan Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. 2024 to 2025 Megaspeed receives several hundred shipments of Nvidia AI chips The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. September 2025 The US Department of Commerce begins investigating Megaspeed The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. January 2025 Jensen Huang meets Donald Trump for the first time Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. April 2025 Jensen Huang attends a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. May 2025 Jensen Huang is again seen with Alice Huang The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. October 2025 Trump is reportedly briefed on the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. December 2025 Trump approves the sale of more advanced Nvidia chips to China Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. May 2026 Marco Rubio reportedly drafts a memo about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy.

events.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December. Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X. "The American people deserve answers," he added. Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony. Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December. How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 15 hours ago The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 14 hours ago Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China. A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee. Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? Published 16 hours ago Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

US authorities provided only “limited assistance” in the matter, despite Singapore asking for help. The Ministry outlined its activities in a statement published late on Thursday, Singapore time. The document reveals that Singapore’s Police Force (SPF) and Customs agency commenced an investigation into Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, in February 2025. “The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences,” the Ministry wrote, adding that the exec “was not investigated for espionage.” Singaporean authorities wanted to know if servers bought by local companies, but exported to Malaysia without ever touching Singaporean soil, might have ended up in a third country. It is not unusual for Singapore-based companies to acquire goods that never reach the island, because it promotes itself as the ideal spot from which to run an operation that trades across Asia. Singapore does so because it is tiny – the whole nation is the same size as the five boroughs of New York City. That small size means Singapore restricts the number of datacenters that can operate on its soil. Those limits are a big reason why Malaysia’s Johor region, which is under 20kms from the border with Singapore and a joint special economic zone, has become a major datacenter province. Singapore needs deals like that to thrive but works hard to ensure its hospitality is not abused. Which is why it felt Megaspeed’s activities worthy of investigation. US authorities were interested too. On 24 June 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security, which regulates sensitive goods subject to export controls, visited Megaspeed in Singapore to check the hardware it bought arrived at its intended destination. Ms. Huang attended that event and later met the SPF for an interview. That meeting ended with the SPF impounding her passport, so it could keep her in Singapore while the investigation continued. As the matter progressed, the SPF suspected perennially troubled server-maker Supermicro had a role in this situation. Readers may recall that the US Department of Justice indicted two Supermicro execs for conspiring to ship servers to China in contravention of US law. Supermicro investigated the matter and parted ways with three staff who acted improperly. The company has denied ever selling to Megaspeed. Singaporean authorities say they received only “limited cooperation” from Supermicro, so in July 2025 the office of the nation’s Attorney General asked US authorities for help. “Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” the statement reveals. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.” In February 2026, the SPF “concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.” But the police did decide that Ms. Huang provided inaccurate information “to downplay her role in Megaspeed.

events.title: Mount Isa's $145 million critical minerals pitch one step closer
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mount Isa critical minerals hub gets early government backing Federal and state governments have agreed to fund a feasibility study into a new research facility in Mount Isa. ( ABC News: Harriet Tatham ) A business case for a $145 million critical mineral research hub in Mount Isa has secured funding for a feasibility study. The centre will provide early analysis and testing for prospective mines trying to scale operations in the region. The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund trials, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council. Mount Isa's push to reinvent its regional economy with a new mineral research hub has secured state and federal backing for a feasibility study. Mount Isa City Council and the University of Queensland released a business case earlier this month for a $145 million critical minerals research centre. The facility would allow mining companies to analyse rock samples from local mineral deposits to see what minerals were present and if they would be viable to mine. The $145 million centre is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs. ( Supplied: Mount Isa City Council ) In July 2025, Mount Isa's underground copper mine closure saw nearly 500 workers sacked in the 19,000-strong community, forcing the council to search for economic alternatives. While Mount Isa's economy has been affected, exploration and investment across the wider North West Minerals Province has boomed, with about 85 critical minerals projects underway. Sustainable Minerals Institute director at the University of Queensland Rick Valenta said the proposed hub would allow industry to scale operations quickly. Rick Valenta (right) says the facility will help mines understand what minerals are in deposits and how they could be mined. ( ABC Rural: Eric Barker ) "The reason you can't just find a deposit and put it into production in a year is because you've got to answer … 'What's the content of the metal that you're after? And … how do we get the metals out of that rock?'" Professor Valenta said. "[At the moment], those rocks would be going elsewhere in Queensland … Australia or the world … [and] that involves a cost and a delay. "This centre is aimed at providing a local solution to that sort of thing." The proposed research centre would be situated between the George Fisher Mine and Mount Isa Airport. ( Supplied: Mount Isa City Councill ) Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she hoped the research hub would help future-proof the city by giving mining companies a dedicated site to research problems locally. "[Currently] minerals are just going to be ripped up and shipped," she said. "What we want to do is add the value and do as much processing as we can … to help us secure the future for our communities." Peta MacRae hopes the project will centralise some of the regions' mining investment into the town's economy. ( ABC News: Abbey Halter ) The proposed hub is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs and would be located near the Mount Isa Airport. On Friday morning, Federal Assistant Minister for Resources Anthony Chisholm confirmed funding would be released to consider the proposal. "We want to make the most of these opportunities … and ensure that Mount Isa remains a great place to live and work and attract people at the same time," he said. "We know that there is enormous potential, but it's about proving that and then also ensuring that we can attract the industry investment." Anthony Chisholm says the cenrre is about proving Mt Isa's potential and attracting industry investment. ( ABC News: Tim Little ) The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund a feasibility study, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council. If successful, the hub would operate in conjunction with similar facilities in Mackay and Townsville. Initial testing and analysis would start at Mount Isa's centre, before small-scale piloting took place in Mackay followed by large-scale trials in Townsville.

events.title: Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
events.summary: IRGC claims Bahrain radar strike is a response to attacks on Iranian telecom tower in southern Hormozgan province. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday. list 1 of 3 Iran’s chief negotiator tells Al Jazeera ‘ball in US court’ list 2 of 3 Hegseth entourage reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier list 3 of 3 Iran warns of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. “Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said. The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation. There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama. Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. The Fifth Fleet headquarters, at the Naval Support Activity base in the capital, Manama, is the main command centre for US naval operations in the Middle East. It was hit in the opening hours of the war on February 28, and satellite images analysed by Al Jazeera showed direct hits on several radar domes and damage to buildings across the base. The US has reportedly reduced its troop numbers at bases in the region and ordered some diplomatic staff to leave, according to news outlets, as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran, US Central Command said it “regularly” moves personnel and assets to “optimise mission readiness”. First Bahrain attack since September According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country. The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran , according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes. A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the war. Analysts say several US bases in the region have been almost rendered unusable. US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary. In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court “. Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports. The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

events.title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
events.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Why it matters: Van Hollen's bid gives grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure Senate Democrats before they cast secret ballots in the Dec. 1 leadership election. The attempt to oust Schumer (D-N.Y.) underscores that deep divisions are plaguing the Democratic Party despite its overwhelming midterm success . Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003. Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999. Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday. "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader." In a statement of his own, Schumer said: "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader." Zoom in: Van Hollen acknowledged he's the "underdog" in the race but claimed Thursday on MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side. "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from party leadership. Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader. The other side: Schumer has far more public backers at this stage than Van Hollen. That includes Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio) and Democratic Sens. John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sheldon Whitehouse (Rhode Island). Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and has been updated.
