events.title: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
events.summary: Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs , including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees. Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker. Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm. Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported. “Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.” But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal . Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions. However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”. Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse. “Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy. Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” , will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor. The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more. Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries. In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games. She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.

events.title: US firm Advent seeks to sell Singapore tutor chain Learning Lab again, sources say
events.summary: Advent invested in The Learning Lab in 2014, but there has been no publicly available information on how much stake it holds. Advent International is trying to sell Singapore tutor chain The Learning Lab again, its second attempt since 2021, sources say, with a planned price of US$400 million to US$500 million. Some sale proceeds will repay a S$265 million private credit facility from KKR, HPS Investment Partners and Nomura, which matures in 2027. The deal comes as private education investment in Asia fell 87% to US$240 million in 2025, with AI worries and many firms still trying to exit investments. SINGAPORE – US buyout firm Advent International has put up Singapore’s tutor-chain The Learning Lab for sale, marking its second attempt since 2021 to unload the asset, in part to repay debt, according to people familiar with the matter. Advent has hired an adviser to kick-start the sale process and plans to offer the company for about US$400 million to US$500 million (S$514.6 million to S$643.3 million), said the people who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. Some of the proceeds will be used to settle a S$265 million private credit facility jointly provided by KKR & Co, HPS Investment Partners and Nomura Holdings in 2023 and which will mature in 2027 , they said. Representatives for Advent, KKR and Nomura declined to comment. HPS did not respond to a request for comment. Private money has been pouring into schools in Asia in recent years as investors seek to profit from growing demand for quality education. Financiers such as Apollo Global Management and KKR have bought stakes and lent to school chains, hoping that a growing number of rich people in the region would fuel expansion. But private equity and venture capital investment in education services in Asia slumped 87% to US$240 million in 2025 , according to S&P Global, citing more rigorous deal selection and the potential impact of artificial intelligence on the sector. Another key challenge is the backlog of private equity firms seeking to exit companies they have bought into. Advent invested in The Learning Lab in 2014, but there has been no publicly available information on how much stake it holds. People with knowledge of the matter said Advent fully owns the learning company. The Learning Lab provides education for pre-school, primary, secondary and junior college students in Singapore, according to its website. It also has online services for other Asian markets including Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia. In Singapore, the company charges about S$702 a month for its junior college programmes. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATSB releases preliminary report into Bob Bramley's NT plane crash Bob Bramley was flying to pick up passengers for a return trip when his plane crashed. ( Supplied ) The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has released its preliminary report on the August crash of pilot Bob Bramley. Bramley is believed to have died when his plane dived into the water off Groote Eylandt, in the Northern Territory. Fishermen witnessed young Tasmanian pilot Bob Bramley's plane crash in waters off the Northern Territory in August "at very high speed", a report has revealed. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) today released its preliminary report into the crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria on August 25 this year, which is believed to have killed 23-year-old Bramley. Northern Territory Police conducted extensive marine and air searches at the time, which recovered parts of the plane, but Bramley has never been found. At the time, 23-year-old Bob Bramley was working as a charter company pilot. ( Supplied. ) As a teenager, he became a passionate advocate for suicide prevention, and sought to raise awareness by becoming the youngest person to circumnavigate Australia solo by plane. Friends and family expressed their shock and sadness in the wake of the crash, remembering Bramley as a "beacon of hope", and for his love of flying. The ATSB report detailed the circumstances of the August crash, but noted the investigation is continuing and that a final report will be published at its conclusion. Fishers found plane parts in sea after crash The report, which refers to "the pilot" but does not identify Bramley, details his movements on the morning of August 25, as he prepared to fly between the small communities of Gove and Numbulwar in the Northern Territory. At the time, Bramley had been working as a pilot for aviation operator Air Frontier for more than a year, and had been the company's senior base pilot for the Arnhem region since April. The report noted that after fuelling the plane and lodging a flight plan, the Beechcraft 58 Baron plane departed from the Gove Airport at about 11am, with only the pilot on board. "The flight plan for the return to Gove indicated four passengers were to be on board," the report noted. The ATSB's map of Bob Bramley's final flight on August 25, 2026. ( ATSB/Google Earth ) About half an hour later, at 11:27am, fishermen in a boat south-west of Isle Woodah in the west of the Gulf of Carpentaria watched the plane pass overhead. "They expected the aircraft to pull up; however, it did not change trajectory, and it impacted the water at very high speed. "The witnesses motored to the impact point and found a fuel/oil slick on the water surface along with many small floating fragments of shattered airframe." NT Police image of wreckage underwater at the crash site. ( NT Police ) No audio recording of cockpit before crash The report noted that the Baron was not fitted with, and was not required to have, a flight data recorder or a cockpit voice recorder. The ATSB said the flight wasn't detected by radar, and data tracking the flight was recorded by Bramley's iPad, which it was transmitting to the online platform OzRunways. The final data point was transmitted at 11:24am, about 23 kilometres north of the crash site. Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and take-off, and phone records indicated "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. The report noted Bramley's qualifications to operate the Baron aircraft, that he held a valid medical certificate and that he had completed a multi-engine instrument proficiency check the previous month. Bramley had more than 1,138 hours total flight time, more than 300 of which were in the Baron. The Baron itself was initially built in 1978 and had been serviced most recently in June in Darwin. The report noted no significant weather activity was observed on the day, consistent with the witnesses and other pilots flying in the area. The report noted Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and takeoff, and "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. ( Supplied: Lachlan Bennett ) Large parts of plane, including engine, found in sea floor In August, NT Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the search for Bramley and the crash site had been particularly difficult, adding that "tiger sharks and crocs" had complicated efforts. NT Police confirmed today that human remains had not been found. Police divers had to contend with sharks and crocodiles during search efforts.

events.title: Spanish court suspends far-right group over alleged hate crimes
events.summary: Judge orders office shut and accounts blocked after 14 arrests and the seizure of more than 20 firearms. A Spanish judge has suspended the activities of the ultra-right group Nucleo Nacional as part of an investigation into alleged hate crimes and illegal association. The court in the northern city of Gijon announced the ruling on Thursday, ordering the group’s office shut and its social media content and bank accounts blocked. list 1 of 3 ‘It’s just too expensive’: Housing and wages at the heart of Spain’s strike list 2 of 3 Photos: Protesters clash with police after housing cost rallies in Spain list 3 of 3 Spain approves housing reforms after nationwide strike over costs The move follows the arrest last week of 14 of its members on suspicion of inciting hatred against vulnerable groups and people with opposing ideologies. The decision comes ahead of Spain’s general election on November 29 and a day after the first nationwide general strike in 14 years. In a video posted on X, an unnamed Nucleo Nacional representative wearing a black shirt with the group’s logo said the movement was a victim of “persecution and political repression”. “They won’t beat us,” the post said. Nucleo Nacional describes itself as a political movement. On its website, which has now been blocked and suspended by court order, it says it seeks a “national awakening”. Spanish authorities have scrutinised the group over its anti-immigration rhetoric, particularly after thousands of migrants crossed in July into Ceuta, Spain’s North African enclave. Police also searched the group’s headquarters in Madrid and other locations. They said they seized more than 20 firearms, some of them unlicensed, along with large quantities of ammunition and other illegal weapons. The court said key members of the organisation had already been placed under precautionary measures, including a ban on leaving Spain and a requirement to report weekly to a court. Reuters also reported last month that Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group in Madrid on October 3, after tens of thousands marched across the country over the housing crisis. The Spanish government said far-right activists, some performing Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped in the Puerta del Sol square.

events.title: Government back to the drawing board on backpacker crackdown
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government reconsidering backpacker, UK working holiday visa overhaul The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The government is reconsidering its controversial overhaul of the working holiday visa scheme. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says he is also looking at ways to reduce the number of British backpackers coming to Australia. Business leaders are urging the government to provide certainty to industries that rely on backpackers to fill jobs. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has all but confirmed the government is going back to the drawing board on its proposed backpacker crackdown, as it grapples with the twin issues of a surge in UK working holiday-makers and pressure to rein in overall migration. On Friday, Mr Burke said Australia must "find a way" to reduce the number of UK backpackers arriving and staying in the country under a free trade deal introduced in 2023, which allows British citizens to live in Australia for up to three years without specific work requirements. "We can find a way to bring that back to something more sensible and in the national interest, without jeopardising the other parts of the free trade agreement," he said. In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled out imposing regional work requirements on backpackers from the UK, which apply to other working holiday-makers seeking to extend their visas beyond 12 months. The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of British backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data. "The conversations with the United Kingdom continue," Mr Burke said. The government had also proposed introducing a ballot system for non-British backpackers seeking to extend their stay into a second or third year, to dramatically reduce visa numbers. The Australian newspaper reported the government was now considering delaying the rollout of the ballot system until early next year, after farming, tourism and hospitality groups warned the changes could cripple their industries. The report suggests the government is considering lifting the cap on third-year visas from the proposed 5,000 to 20,000 (down from the current 31,000) and imposing longer regional work requirements on visa-holders. Mr Burke said the government was continuing to engage with industry stakeholders, but the "parameters" around reducing the overall number of working holiday-makers were unchanged. "The total number of working holiday or backpacker numbers that I've announced at the National Press Club, I cannot shift from," he said. He described potential changes to the implementation as "tweaks" that would allow businesses to "get the best possible use out of people, while they are here". "I am completely open to that," he said. Industry urges government to make quick decision Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said there had been "extensive discussions" between the government and affected industries about the backpacker issue. He warned the original proposal risked disrupting businesses outside major cities, particularly in regional areas that relied on working holiday-makers to fill jobs. "And those regional areas really need those people to be coming out there and to be undertaking that work, supporting work in those areas," he said. Andrew McKellar says the government must move quickly to grant businesses certainty. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Mr McKellar said business groups wanted the government to "make a decision", warning the "clock is ticking" for businesses seeking certainty ahead of summer. "Let's ensure that those people who are already here can continue with their plans … and that there's a fresh set of rules for anyone else who's coming in," he said. Backpackers are not migrants, advocate says Agricultural advocacy group WA Farmers president Steve McGuire welcomes a "walking back" of the visa changes. Steve Mcguire says backpackers should not be treated the same as migrants. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) "What we're seeing with these changes is they're [the government] indicating they're listening," Mr McGuire said. "It's relief for the moment but there's still more work to be done. "It means those staying their second year have a lot more incentive to do six months regional." WAFarmers wants the Commonwealth to separate working holiday visa numbers from overseas migration quotas. "Our argument is they shouldn't even be in that number, they should be taken out," Mr McGuire said.

events.title: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
events.summary: Cerebras reported better-than-expected revenue for the third quarter and issued strong guidance. The AI chipmaker said it recently signed a deal with hyperscaler Microsoft. Cerebras' stock price has lost almost half its value since the company's IPO in May. Cerebras Systems reported better-than-expected results and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft . The stock soared 17% in extended trading. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus: Earnings per share: 12 cents adjusted vs. loss of 14 cents expected Core revenue: $230.9 million vs. $214.7 million expected Cerebras' core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement . "I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units. events.title: Chris Van Hollen launches bid to lead Democrats in US Senate
events.summary: Van Hollen’s leadership drive follows Democratic sweeps in elections and challenges veteran leader Schumer. US Senator Chris Van Hollen has said he is running for Senate majority leader as Democrats gear up to take charge of the US Congress in January following a Democratic landslide in this month’s midterm elections. Van Hollen said in a post on X late on Thursday that Americans had “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption”. “To deliver, we need new leadership,” he said, adding that “this isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call”. Van Hollen has faced mounting calls to enter the race for Senate majority leader amid growing opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ‘s continued tenure after he faced criticism over his handling of the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency. Responding to Van Hollen’s decision, Senator Chuck Schumer wrote on X “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader”, he said. Schumer said he looked “forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people”. US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan, who said he would not support Schumer as the majority leader in the Senate, welcomed Van Hollen’s decision to run. In a post on X, El-Sayed said: “I called on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.” “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed said. On Thursday, Democratic Party leaders gathered in Denver, Colorado, for a two-day conference on the future of the party, following the sweeping victories in the midterms. Some progressives at the conference have argued that it is time to change the direction and the leadership of the Democratic Party. “[Chuck] Schumer has spent nearly 50 years in elected office,” said Washington, DC-based political commentator and strategist James Butler, adding that while he respected the US senator’s service, “it is time for veteran Democrats to make space for younger, more energetic members”. Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Middle Eastern partners. Van Hollen, the son of a US diplomat, has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “ chronic liar “, previously telling Al Jazeera the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”. He also attempted to push forward legislation in Congress that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention. This week, Van Hollen and 10 Senate colleagues urged congressional leaders to remove provisions from the annual defence policy bill that would expand weapons development and intelligence sharing with Israel.

events.title: Stocks recover from Nvidia whiplash, dollar climbs with US yields
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy. Stocks in Asia steadied after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned over affair claims, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, shaking the AI sector and chip supply chain. Investors lifted US Treasury yields and the dollar as they priced in a bigger Fed rate hike in December, while the yen stayed near 160 per dollar and risked intervention. Markets also tracked wider fallout from the AI slump, with Nvidia shares and related stocks falling, while rivals may gain and senators sought testimony on the company’s recent troubles. SINGAPORE – Stocks in Asia were on steadier footing on Nov 13 after a turbulent week dominated by revelations of extramarital affairs involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang that culminated in his resignation, in a blow to the global AI boom he helped advance. US Treasury yields climbed, with the two-year yield hitting a one-month high, lifting the dollar as investors weighed the prospect of an outsized 50 basis point rate hike by the US Federal Reserve in December. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of the affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, which plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves through the AI industry. His exit could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader artificial intelligence industry and supply chain, given Huang’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market as well as his close ties with US President Donald Trump. “His departure leaves a vacuum that will be difficult to fill... We do not assume existing commitments change, but new deals could take longer or require more compensation as investors look for reassurance about Nvidia’s role,” analysts at JPMorgan said in a note. “The bigger implications are for the rest of the AI trade, particularly GPU (graphics processing unit) financing and infrastructure deals in which Nvidia would presumably be involved as a supplier, investor or provider of contractual support.” Nvidia shares fell 3% in extended trading, while those of its customers, including South Korea’s Naver, extended declines on Nov 13 , with Naver down 2.75%. Jon Zauderer, Citi’s head of specialist sales, said competitors such as AMD, Arista and Broadcom could benefit from the Nvidia fallout. “If you think about the uncertainty that’s created about a potential management change, investors are going to look for alternatives,” he said. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 0.26%, reversing some of its 1.3% fall from the previous session. South Korea’s Kospi rose 2.35%, while Japan’s Nikkei added 1.4%. The recovery in global equities also follows last week’s market meltdown sparked by US Republicans’ electoral drubbing, which stoked fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure build-out that has helped send stocks to record highs in 2026 . Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures rose more than 0.2% each, while EURO STOXX 50 futures fell 0.37%. US Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott sent letters on Nov 12 to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Huang, asking them to testify over the recent developments at Nvidia. Concerns over the AI outlook also spilt into metals, with London copper prices hitting a four-month low in the previous session on fears of weaker demand, while shares of Australian-listed miner Capstone Copper Corp fell more than 5% on Nov 13 . The two-year US Treasury yield peaked at 4.8920% in the early Asian session, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose to a three-week high of 5.1433%. Investors now see a 14.5% chance of a jumbo 50-basis-point Fed hike in December, up from zero a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool. “Right now, the US Fed has three hikes priced in for effectively the next 12 months... The (most recent) CPI (consumer price index) print obviously was a bit hotter than expected. If those kinds of prints continue to happen, we can definitely see the Fed hiking three more times. It’s very within the realms of possibility,” said Manusha Samaraweera, fixed income investment director at Capital Group. The increasingly hawkish Fed expectations in turn boosted the dollar, which was on track for a weekly gain of 0.9%, its biggest in more than a month. The strength in the greenback, meanwhile, weighed on the yen, which languished close to the key 160 per dollar level on Nov 13 , leaving traders on alert for any intervention from Tokyo. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Nov 12 it bought 79.4 billion yen (S$638.9 million) in the spot market on July 31, selling euros from the Exchange Stabilization Fund as part of a joint US-Japan intervention this summer to shore up the yen.

events.title: Visa holders are delaying purchases and tuning out the news amid immigration uncertainty
events.summary: Immigration uncertainty is influencing some visa holders' decisions about jobs, major purchases, and their futures in the US. Namas Bhojani/Bloomberg via Getty Images Government and corporate immigration policy changes have raised concerns among tech visa holders. Some worry that fewer employers will sponsor foreign workers, making future job searches harder. Workers described how immigration uncertainty is affecting their careers and long-term plans. When Ashok Kumar lost his job in 2019, the H-1B visa holder had 60 days to find a new employer willing to sponsor him. He pulled it off, but he's worried his next job search could be even harder. This week, Business Insider reported that IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in its consulting division. The company cited evolving skill availability and client needs as reasons for the move. Kumar, a tech lead at a large corporation, said he's concerned that more companies could follow IBM's lead. He's among several tech visa holders who told Business Insider that immigration policy uncertainty and concerns about job security are influencing their career decisions and long-term plans. Some worry about their ability to stay in the US or find new jobs, while others remain focused on the opportunities available to them. IBM's decision comes amid other developments affecting foreign tech workers. In October, the Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and six major IT services companies from the Permanent Labor Certification program, a key step in the employment-based green card process. The move prevents the companies from submitting new applications or moving forward with pending ones. The administration said the move was aimed at stopping companies from misusing the program to favor foreign workers over American workers. The administration has also sought to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas , though federal courts have blocked the measure. Kumar's employer wasn't among the companies suspended from the PERM program, but the news added to his concerns about the future of immigration sponsorship. He said friends he discussed it with shared similar concerns. "Everyone was worried about their future," he said Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . 'You can do everything right' One Microsoft employee is preparing for her final attempt at the H-1B visa lottery, but she's already worried about what comes next. The worker said she initially ignored Instagram reels that friends sent her about the October PERM suspension. When she finally watched one, she was shocked to learn that Microsoft was among the companies affected. Even if she's selected in the lottery, she worries that the PERM suspension could create another obstacle to securing a green card and staying in the US long-term. "You can do everything right, build a career at a company like Microsoft, and still not feel secure about your future here," she said. Microsoft has disputed the administration's allegations that it misused the visa system. For some foreign tech workers, the uncertainty extends beyond their careers. One tech worker on an F-1 STEM OPT visa said he's delayed buying a car because he doesn't know how long he'll be able to remain in the US. He also raised the possibility of moving to another country, such as Canada or the UK. "My friends are indeed panicking and getting restless," he said. Different reactions to immigration uncertainty Not every foreign tech worker is equally concerned about their immigration future. Some pointed to the fact that the PERM suspension currently affects only a handful of companies. One Big Tech visa holder said he's not too concerned because he doesn't have long-term immigration plans in the US. Others have tried to tune out immigration news altogether. "It's exhausting to follow everything so I'm staying away from all of it," one tech visa holder said. For Aman Goyal, a product manager on an H-1B visa, the uncertainty hasn't outweighed the opportunities he sees in the US. Goyal, who came to the US in 2023, considered looking for work abroad after being laid off last year but ultimately landed a new role based in the Seattle area. He said visa challenges remain a concern as he considers his long-term future in the country, but he wants to make the most of his time in the US. "I'm definitely interested in continuing to be here, meeting and building my network as much as possible, as well as learning about the next phases of AI as much as possible," he said. events.title: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why
events.summary: The super-rich are increasingly piling into alternative investments, diversifying portfolios once dominated by traditional assets. The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets and geopolitical uncertainty. The world's wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification. From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers. JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm's regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients. "So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category," Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore. The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said. "We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to," said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier. Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth . Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found. Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added. Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges. Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets. Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods. Citi's 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility. Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga. The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. "This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets," Woods said. Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity. Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security. Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts. Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS. Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors' alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth's Aganga. Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier's Woods.

events.title: Who guards the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier? Hegseth just honored the sentinel who scolded him and his group at Arlington.
events.summary: A sentinel with the Army's 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as "The Old Guard," guards the Tomb of the Unknown at Arlington National Cemetery. Elizabeth Fraser/US Army Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth honored a soldier who reprimanded him and his entourage at Arlington National Cemetery. The soldier is a member of the elite Army unit guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Tomb sentinels undergo a rigorous selection and training process. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded an Army soldier a medal on Thursday, one day after the soldier publicly reprimanded the Pentagon chief and his entourage for boisterous behavior near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery. Spc. Thomas Iglesias received the Joint Service Commendation Medal for his conduct during Wednesday's Veterans Day observance. "We love soldiers. We love standards." Hegseth wrote in an accompanying social media post. "Well done, Specialist." These developments have spotlighted the specially selected soldiers from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, known as The Old Guard, who have guarded the nation's most sacred military memorial since 1948. On Wednesday, Hegseth, his wife, and several senior aides were posing for photographs near the memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony attended by President Donald Trump. As the group departed, laughter from a member of Hegseth's party could be heard. "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," Iglesias shouted, stopping his patrol to address the group. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell subsequently said the soldier had "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum." Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth presented the Joint Service Commendation Medal to Army Spc. Thomas Iglesias on Nov. 12, 2026. SSgt. Madelyn Keech/US Air Force Who guards the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier? The soldiers who guard the tomb, known as sentinels, are volunteers who undergo a demanding selection and training process to earn one of the Army's rarest military badges, the Tomb Guard Identification Badge. Business Insider previously documented the rigorous training and evaluations soldiers must complete to qualify for the role. Over 735 soldiers have earned the badge since the Army started tracking sentinel numbers. Sentinels must be at least 5 feet 8 inches tall. Just eight women have held the job. Sentinels are on duty at the memorial regardless of weather. Each follows a tightly choreographed ceremonial routine. According to Arlington National Cemetery , each sentinel marches 21 steps, pauses for 21 seconds, and repeats the sequence. The number symbolizes the 21-gun salute, the military's highest ceremonial honor. The tomb contains the remains of unidentified American service members from World War I, World War II, and the Korean War. The soldiers work on a three-team rotation schedule, working 24 hours at a time, and wearing wet gloves to improve the grip on their 1950s-era M14 rifle. Guards are swapped out every 30 minutes in the summer and each hour during winter. But when the cemetery is closed, postings last for two hours. They are also responsible for preserving the dignity of the memorial and ensuring visitors observe its strict standards of respect. In a 2022 Army news release , one sentinel said it's normal to correct misbehaving visitors two or three times a day. "It's usually just them being oblivious," the sentinel said. "They're talking and not realizing how loud they're being, or laughing or making jokes amongst their group. It detracts from the other people that are trying to pay their respect." events.title: The US has been holding secretive talks with a regime it accused of genocide
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Donald Trump's quest for rare earths reopens US talks with once-isolated Myanmar regime Min Aung Hlaing, pictured in Malaysia, has been trying to rehabilitate Myanmar's image. ( Reuters: Azneal Ishak/Pool ) The United States has reopened direct talks with Myanmar, raising alarm among advocates and analysts. It marks a reversal of efforts to isolate the military junta after it took power in a 2021 coup. Analysts believe the US's desire to access Myanmar's rare earths could influence diplomacy. As US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Asian leaders in the Philippines next week for the 49th ASEAN Summit, his administration is holding secretive talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, the same regime the US has accused of genocide. Five years ago, Washington imposed sanctions on Myanmar's military leadership and downgraded diplomatic ties following a 2021 coup that ousted an elected government . This year, however, senior Trump administration officials have travelled to Tokyo and Myanmar's capital, Naypyidaw, for talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing. The goals of the diplomacy include countering China's influence in the region and potentially gaining access to Myanmar's "bountiful rare earth resources", according to a US State Department document . But the outreach has raised concerns among human rights advocates that Washington's pursuit of strategic interests could help rehabilitate a military leadership accused of widespread atrocities. Debbie Stothard believes pressure on Myanmar's government should not be weakened, with attacks on civilians ongoing. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "It's pretty shocking and almost illogical that the US would engage in secret talks with a sham president elected by a sham election," said Debbie Stothard, chair of the International Network for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. "The military junta views engagement at this level as something that's encouraging and positive for them. "They see this process as legitimising them, and that is very bad news indeed for civilians on the ground and for regional security." The diplomatic opening followed the detention of an American businessman at Yangon airport on June 11 by Myanmar authorities. Adam Castillo, 40, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained for three months after being accused of financial impropriety, allegations he denied. Adam Castillo was detained in Myanmar earlier this year. ( Supplied ) A former US Marine, Mr Castillo was reportedly lobbying Washington to lift sanctions against Myanmar in exchange for negotiating American access to the country's vast rare earth deposits. He also ran one of Myanmar's largest security companies. Mr Castillo's detention provided an opening for Washington to establish direct contact with the military leadership, said Hunter Marston, director of the Lowy Institute's Southeast Asia Program. "A delegation of US representatives travelled to Naypyidaw to secure the release … that was the supposed setting or context for the US delegation to visit Myanmar," Dr Marston said. "But it also paved the way for more substantive discussions about changing US policy and engaging with the Myanmar military regime. "It seems like his detention was essentially hostage diplomacy, and the release was used tactically to secure talks with Washington. "I think that played right into the hands of the Myanmar regime, but I think it also served as a useful pretext for Washington to engage in discreet talks with the military." Analysts believe the discussions surrounding Mr Castillo's release may have opened the door to broader negotiations over access to Myanmar's rare earth minerals, potentially in return for a normalisation of relations. Since his release in September, meetings between senior US officials, led by Michael Vance, the Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, and Myanmar's military-backed government have continued. The latest took place in Tokyo in October. Rare earths are essential to manufacturing a wide range of modern technologies, from computer screens and electric vehicles to solar panels and advanced weapons systems. "Whoever supplies today has the upper hand in the race for artificial intelligence," he said.

events.title: Genting Singapore shares fall as high rollers play less, resort revamp continues
events.summary: Genting Singapore expects the renovation works at Resorts World Sentosa to improve its hotel offerings and broaden the property’s appeal over the longer term. Genting Singapore’s profit fell 42% to S$54.7 million and revenue dropped 13% to S$566.1 million, as high rollers played less at Resorts World Sentosa. Casino revenue fell 22% to S$315 million, hit by weaker premium gambling and a lower share of wagers kept in September, though Genting said this matched regional trends. RWS is still being upgraded through 2027, with marketing, events and new Weave openings aimed at drawing premium visitors and boosting long-term appeal. SINGAPORE – Shares of Genting Singapore were down by more than 6% at 57 cents at noon on Nov 13, after the company reported another quarter of shrinking profits, as high rollers played less at Resorts World Sentosa (RWS) and ongoing renovations at the resort crimped visitor footfall and spending. Net profit fell 42% year on year to $54.7 million for the three months ended Sept 30, while revenue fell 13% to $566.1 million, Genting Singapore said in a business update on Nov 12. Both net profit and revenue for the July to September quarter were also lower than in the previous quarter from April to June. Casino revenue fell 22% to $315 million for the quarter under review compared with a year ago, as lower activity among premium gamblers and a lower-than-usual share of wagers retained by the casino in September further dented revenue. However, Genting said this was in line with trends in key regional markets. The group said adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for the quarter, a measure of operating performance, would have been about $36 million higher than the reported $161.8 million if the casino had kept its usual share of premium wagers. Outside the casino, non-gaming revenue rose 1% year on year to $250.9 million for the quarter, despite fewer hotel rooms being available. This was up 29% from the previous quarter, although Genting did not elaborate on what drove the increase. The resort operator is banking on the year-end holiday season to draw visitors, even as upgrades to its hotels, gaming areas and other guest spaces limit how much of the resort it can operate through 2027. As part of efforts to attract premium customers, the resort is stepping up its marketing and using events and new openings at Weave, its retail and dining precinct, to give guests more reasons to visit. At the same time, RWS is revamping its gaming areas, lounges, restaurants and other guest spaces. It expects the upgrades to improve its hotel offerings and broaden the resort’s appeal over the longer term.

events.title: No love for Lambo: Luxury car dealer EuroSports reports losses, seeks funding to support business
events.summary: Lamborghini is expected to introduce a new version of its Temerario sports car (pictured on April 22) by the end of EuroSports’ financial year in March 2027. EuroSports Global’s losses widened as car sales fell, with revenue down more than 30% to $7.83 million. It blamed weak demand, high luxury car fees and economic uncertainty. The dealer hopes new Lamborghini models, including the Urus SE, will lift orders. It also expects the Temerario to arrive by March 2027. Its Scorpio Electric unit has won European and Singapore approval for the Lambda Scorpii motorcycle. EuroSports is seeking funding, as losses and short-term debts raise concern over its ability to keep operating. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s Lamborghini dealer EuroSports Global is looking to new luxury models to draw buyers after a tough quarter of falling sales, even as it seeks fresh funding to support its car business and plans to mass-produce a home-grown electric motorcycle. The group on Nov 12 said its net loss had widened to $1.24 million in the quarter ended Sept 30, from $752,000 a year earlier. Revenue fell by more than 30% to $7.83 million. For the first half of its financial year, the group’s net loss widened by 57% to $2.29 million as revenue fell 21.7% to $15.1 million, weighed down by falling car sales and thinner margins on cars sold. EuroSports is the distributor for Lamborghini and Touring Superleggera in Singapore, with some models selling for more than $2 million. However, hefty additional registration fees for luxury vehicles and rising certificate of entitlement premiums have crimped demand for high-end supercars here. EuroSports is also expecting economic and geopolitical uncertainty to make buyers more cautious in the months ahead. But the group said new models could help attract more orders, and expects to start delivering two new versions of Lamborghini’s Urus SE sport utility vehicle in the October-to-December quarter, although prices for this model may be lower. Lamborghini is also expected to introduce a new version of its Temerario sports car by March 2027, following the recent launch of its Revuelto SV. EuroSports’ electric motorcycle business has a longer timeline. The Lambda Scorpii, developed by its subsidiary Scorpio Electric, became the first electric motorcycle designed from scratch in Singapore to secure European vehicle type approval in 2025, the group said. The approval certifies that the motorcycle meets European Union safety, environmental and technical standards. The motorcycle has also secured approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority on June 12, and Scorpio Electric registered the first unit for use on Singapore roads on July 13. It is also setting up sales and servicing networks in the Asia-Pacific and Europe, with plans to build a network of distributors and dealers across 10 to 15 cities. EuroSports expects mass production and deliveries to begin in 2028, and is in the process of securing additional funding to support the commercialisation of this business. The company has spent heavily on research and development for the Lambda Scorpii, which has placed pressure on its financials over the years. The group disclosed in its financial statements that its losses, cash outflow and short-term obligations raised a material uncertainty over its ability to continue operating. In the first half, it burned through $1.18 million in cash to run its operations. As at Sept 30, what it owed in the short term exceeded its short-term assets – which included cash, cars and spare parts held for sale, and money that customers owe the company – by $6.54 million. Still, the board said it expects the car distribution business to generate enough cash to cover operating expenses over the next 12 months. It is in talks with financial institutions and potential investors for additional funding to support operations over at least that period.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Open weight model can now say things Chinese authorities don't like OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them 10 hours ago Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads 13 hours ago Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit 1 day ago Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python 1 day ago Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory 2 days ago An American AI lab has re-educated Qwen3.8-27B, a popular open-weight large language model from Alibaba, so the software forgets its Chinese ancestry. Nous Research, an Austin, Texas-based AI lab, has subjected the model to re-education through training, not to be confused with China's " Re-education Through Labor " system. With the help of a post-training process, Qwen3.8-27B has been reborn under the name Arete "to reinforce Western values on a Chinese-trained model." What qualifies as a "Western value" remains open to interpretation. "Open-weight Chinese models are among the strongest available, but they ship with state-aligned behavior baked into the weights," Nous Research wrote in a blog post . Your correspondent tested this with a variant model, Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-6bit, locally. Asked about events during 1989 in Tiananmen Square, the model either refused to discuss the topic or provided euphemistic response. What's perhaps more surprising is that Anthropic claims operators affiliated with Alibaba's Qwen lab used outputs from its Claude models to train competing AI models via distillation . Nous Research, maker of the Hermes Agent , cites that sort of censorship as a risk for users of AI models trained in China. The concern comes amid broader scrutiny of Chinese influence in the tech industry, heightened by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation following controversy involving a woman US intelligence has accused of spying for China. Nous says the risk posed by Chinese-made AI models go beyond promoting Beijing's worldview. Some Middle Kingdom models have been found to produce more vulnerable code under certain conditions, according to a study by Booz Allen Hamilton, which does a lot of business with the US government. Hirundo, a vendor which says it is building "the first Machine Unlearning Platform to ensure that AI models only know what they should," makes the same argument . The company also notes that its efforts to apply "unlearning" to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B saw a dramatic drop in output that reflects Communist Party of China's preferred censorship, propaganda messaging, or bias. 89.8 percent of the model's output reflected those values before unlearning reduced the incidence to 2.8 percent. Nous Research did not achieve such dramatic results, but did see an overall reduction in viewpoints deemed to be propaganda. "On our evaluation, Arete-27B raised its fact score from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5 and cut answers containing propaganda from 22 percent to 1 percent, in line with the Western models we tested," the company said. To handle Arete's unlearning, Nous Research says it briefly considered Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra , "but had found evidence that it too had a checkered record on China-related topics." "We don't know definitively, but theorize that the bias imparted to Nemotron came from working with Chinese open models during the training process," the company said. "We have experienced similar contamination, because the vast majority of high quality open models are Chinese, and only open models have terms of use that permit this kind of tinkering and experimentation." In the end, the biz tapped Inkling , an open weight model from US-based Thinking Machines Lab, to act as the teaching model. Nous Research says its model re-education efforts show that the propaganda layer is shallow and, with 50 million tokens worth of supervised learning, is relatively easy to remove.

events.title: Builder fined $150k after mother and baby injured in wall fall
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Builder fined $150k after mother and baby injured in concrete wall collapse Topic: Housing Construction Industry The concrete wall fell onto the rear part of the neighbouring house. ( ABC News: Marco Catalano ) A construction company has been fined after a 30-tonne concrete wall fell on a neighbouring property. A mother and her baby sustained minor injuries. Smart Builty Pty Ltd has been convicted and fined $150,000. A construction company has been fined $150,000 after a 30-tonne section of a concrete wall fell on to a house in Adelaide's inner south, injuring a mother and her baby. According to a ruling handed down by the South Australian Employment Court, the concrete wall was not properly secured and fell onto the rear of a neighbouring property at Wayville on November 28, 2023, during severe weather. It fell onto the back 60 centimetres of the home and most of its outdoor living area. The ruling said the principal contractor at the site, Smart Built Pty Ltd, was constructing a three-storey residential development which included 10-metre high precast concrete wall panels. It said the panels had been supported by temporary "propping" but the company had requested its removal about two weeks earlier to allow for better access to parts of the construction site. "No inspection of the precast panels or their permanent structural support was undertaken by any engineer prior to removal of the temporary propping," the ruling said. The ruling noted that victim impact statements had described the "profound impact the offending" on the mother and her baby, who both suffered minor injuries. The mother required stitches to her knee, while her baby "sustained superficial cuts only", but the court said those injuries could have been more serious. "Other section[s] of the inadequately supported wall loomed over the rest of the … family's home," the ruling said. On the day the wall fell, flooding and storm damage were reported around Adelaide, including at Wayville. ( Supplied: Spence Denny ) The court said the cost of structural damage to the home amounted to $85,413.82 and a further $19,211 damage to its contents. "The defendant [Smart Built Pty Ltd] paid $10,000 to the neighbours affected by the collapse to compensate them for the inconvenience of ongoing building works," the ruling said. It said the defendant had helped with practical steps to facilitate repairs, which were being arranged through the family's insurer. The ruling said the removal of the propping meant the wall was not "connected to other significant structural elements". "The design drawings clearly state … that the precast panels are to remain propped until the wall bracing is installed," the ruling stated. The court said it accepted "the offending did not involve deliberate or reckless conduct" but that the "poorly controlled risk of harm … was of death or extremely serious injury to multiple people". "I conclude the offending involved mid-range objective seriousness rather than a lower level," the ruling said. "I accept the defendant's evidence of its subsequently changed safety systems … I also accept the defendant's current intention is to not use precast panels again." The court imposed a conviction and fined Smart Built Pty Ltd $150,000.

events.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
events.summary: Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016. The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November. Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire". The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset". While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election. Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this. The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU. Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes. Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc. Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Published 1 day ago UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Published 5 days ago Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion? Published 13 hours ago Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit. Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line. "But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line." Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too". He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016." Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration". Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards". On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill." The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU". Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy. The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK". events.title: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
events.summary: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation , according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. “We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset . The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned . In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: Singtel H1 net profit falls 55% to S$1.54 billion on lack of divestment gains; underlying profit up 10%
events.summary: The group’s operating revenue rose 6% to $7.29 billion in H1, from $6.91 billion in the previous year. Singtel’s H1 net profit fell 55% to S$1.54 billion after last year’s S$2.21 billion divestment gains were not repeated. Underlying net profit rose 10% to S$1.49 billion, helped by NCS, Digital InfraCo, Optus, Airtel and AIS. Revenue rose 6% to S$7.29 billion. Singtel lifted its interim dividend to S$0.09 and raised full-year OpCo Ebit guidance. SINGAPORE – Telecommunications giant Singtel on Nov 13 posted a 55% decline in net profit to $1.54 billion for the first half-year ended September, from $3.4 billion in the year-ago period. This was mainly due to the absence of $2.21 billion in net exceptional gains recorded a year earlier from the partial sale of its stake in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Excluding exceptional items, underlying net profit rose 10% to S$1.49 billion, from S$1.35 billion a year earlier. The increase was driven by stronger performances at NCS, Digital InfraCo and Optus, as well as higher contributions from regional associates Airtel and AIS. In constant currency terms, revenue would have increased 1.4%, while underlying net profit would have grown 16%, Singtel said. The board approved an interim dividend of $0.09 per share, comprising a core dividend of $0.071 and a value realisation dividend of $0.019. This is 10% higher than the $0.082 per share declared a year earlier. The group also raised its full-year operating company earnings before interest and tax (OpCo Ebit) growth guidance to between mid and high single digits, from its previous forecast of mid-single-digit growth. Singtel group chief executive Yuen Kuan Moon said the stronger operating performance reflected double-digit Ebit growth at NCS, Digital InfraCo and Optus, alongside robust contributions from regional associates. “We are raising our full-year guidance on the back of this results momentum,” he said.

events.title: Applied Materials forecasts quarterly revenue above estimates on strong AI chip demand
events.summary: Applied Materials is benefiting from increased spending by chipmakers racing to meet the extraordinary AI-led demand for chips and memory. Applied Materials expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of about US$11.10 billion, above Wall Street’s US$10.89 billion estimate, as AI chip demand keeps spending high. Fourth-quarter Semiconductor Systems revenue rose 64% to US$8 billion, and adjusted profit was US$4.16 a share, beating forecasts. Chief executive Gary Dickerson said 2027 could be “another record year”, with wafer fab equipment demand set to rise more than 30% and customers wanting tools sooner. Applied Materials forecast fiscal first quarter revenue above Wall Street expectations on Nov 12 , betting that strong demand for advanced AI chips will continue to fuel spending on its semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The company, which supplies equipment for key wafer fabrication processes, is benefiting from increased spending by chipmakers racing to meet the extraordinary artificial intelligence-led demand for chips and memory. “The actual metrics of the market show that demand is still very strong,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. Applied’s results show chipmakers and foundries are “buying as much equipment as they possibly can”, he added. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s Semiconductor Systems revenue jumped to US$8 billion (S$10.2 billion) in the fourth quarter, up about 64% from a year earlier. The company is one of Apple’s partners for its American Manufacturing Program, which includes work at Applied’s Austin, Texas, facility to boost US production of chipmaking equipment. “We expect 2027 to be another record year for the market and Applied,” chief executive Gary Dickerson said on a post-earnings call. He said wafer fab equipment demand should rise more than 30% and customers are asking for tools sooner, not later. China accounted for 25% of fourth quarter revenue, down from 29% a year earlier, though sales there rose about 35% to US$2.64 billion. The company forecast quarterly revenue of around US$11.1 billion, plus or minus US$500 million, compared with the average of analysts’ estimates of US$10.89 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company reported fourth quarter adjusted profit of US$4.16 per share, beating analysts’ average estimate of US$4.05. REUTERS
