events.title: Nvidia abruptly changed how it reported revenue in Singapore last year, adding to questions about its relationship with Megaspeed
events.summary: A sudden change in how Nvidia reported some of its financial results last year is getting renewed attention, raising questions about its relationship with Megaspeed, a major Nvidia client at the time and now at the center of chip smuggling allegations. The financial change under scrutiny involves Nvidia’s accounting for revenue from Singapore, where Megaspeed is based. Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of the semiconductor chip giant on Thursday, following stunning revelations of his affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), a woman suspected of being an operative for China. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will lead the company in the interim, Nvidia announced on Thursday. Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Asia, has been suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced chips to China , in violation of U.S. export laws. Megaspeed, and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric, moved at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China, tech news site The Information has reported . Singapore authorities said on Thursday that they investigated Megaspeed and its former executive Alice Huang beginning in February 2025 and did not find sufficient evidence of espionage. However, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country. The U.S. is also investigating Megaspeed for export control violations. Jensen Huang has previously said there is no evidence of Nvidia chips being smuggled to China, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing . In June 2025, Nvidia added Megaspeed to its internal block list , prohibiting sales to the company, according to the Wall Street Journal . Around the same time, Nvidia stopped reporting revenue from Singapore, one of the five geographic areas Nvidia had previously listed in its breakdown of global revenues (they were U.S., Singapore, Taiwan, China, and “Other”). In the fiscal quarter ending in July 2025, Nvidia reported $10.2 billion in revenue from Singapore, 22% of the company’s total revenue, and an 81% increase in year-over-year revenue from the country. In the next quarter’s earnings report, for the three months ending in October 2025, Singapore had disappeared from Nvidia’s geographic revenue breakdown, which now listed only four markets: U.S., Taiwan, China, and Other. According to the October 2025 earnings report, Nvidia was now separating out markets based on “location of the customers’ headquarters” instead of “customer billing location.” The change was made even though Nvidia’s previous earnings reports had clearly stated that “customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere.” Nvidia did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment, including an inquiry if the change in how it reported its earnings was at all connected to it adding Megaspeed to its block list. Making sense of the unlisted Singapore revenue Shiva Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, told Fortune correlation is not causation, and it is impossible to say with just public information whether concerns around Megaspeed’s export control adherence or Alice Huang’s alleged espionage caused Nvidia to change how it reported revenue. However, he noted, Nvidia’s changes in the filings will no doubt become part of the Department of Justice or Department of Commerce’s investigations into Nvidia’s export control compliance. “The timing is curious,” Rajgopal said. “Even if it is not curious, people are going to raise questions given all this information now.” Auditors will likely look at what Nvidia knew about where the Megaspeed chips were ending up, how Nvidia checked and documented customer end-use, and if Huang’s affair was related to Nvidia’s business with Megaspeed. But they will also look at whether investors were given an accurate picture of the risks associated with potential smuggling in China and Southeast Asia. Rajgopal made it clear that as CFO, Kress’ role in how finances were disclosed publicly, will certainly be scrutinized, but based on public filings alone, there does not appear to be evidence at this time showing Kress was aware of whether an earnings reporting change could have potentially been related to Megaspeed. “I wouldn’t say Kress must have known,” Rajgopal said. “These are just financial statements. Nothing is illegal. It’s disclosed.” Rajgopal argued Kress’s biggest challenge has little to do with the company’s past or immediate finances. Finance executives who take interim chief executive roles in tech companies rarely stay because they lack the buy-in of the tech community, he said. Nvidia’s priorities will soon shift from sustaining its financial momentum today to working to recreate or build upon the forward vision Huang gave the company, which is a decidedly different role than a finance head. “A CFO running a tech company is not a good idea,” Rajgopal said, “especially something that’s so deeply tech-heavy.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over poorly timed floor vote fumbles
events.summary: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office. The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye. "I think everyone's frustrated with how that all went down, I'm not going to lie to you about that," said Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.). "People are pissed," a senior House Democrat told Axios. The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies. "I think everyone's explained what the situations were — somebody was recovering from surgery. There are certain things that are unavoidable," said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.). Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios. Others said the speakership election offers a window into how Jeffries' approach to the speakership might play out over the coming year. Jeffries has always taken a more hands-off approach than his predecessor, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), preferring to let issues and fights among members resolve themselves.

events.title: Senate Dems can look forward to unlikely MAGA allies
events.summary: Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party . Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power. Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top. Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress. Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom. He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have tag-teamed on numerous tech and AI safety bills, including a joint statement on Nvidia this week. Hawley is also a major critic of AI. Schmitt worked with Warren in 2024 and 2025 to challenge Big Tech's dominance of Pentagon AI contracts, and with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in July to crack down on search engine monopolies. What to watch: While there will be fewer this Congress, Democrats will also have a club of more moderate Republicans they can try to pick up too. Murkowski, along with Sens. John Curtis (R-Utah) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), will be top targets.

events.title: Nvidia fallout fuels questions about Lutnick’s staying power
events.summary: The News Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has kept his job through scrutiny over his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; his cryptocurrency firm, Tether; and his former financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald. The Nvidia fallout may be the toughest test yet of his staying power. A growing GOP contingent is pointing the finger at Lutnick for not cracking down hard enough on Megaspeed, the AI chip firm with ties to an alleged Chinese spy with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair, and for what they see as the Commerce Department’s broader failure to restrict AI chip exports to China. In the wake of reporting that other administration officials had urged the Commerce secretary to move faster, Republicans on and off Capitol Hill are accusing Lutnick of defying President Donald Trump by not imposing curbs on the firm — and even positing his job could be at risk. “We’re hearing … Trump has directed three times that [Megaspeed be blacklisted],” Rep. John Moolenaar, the top Republican on the House Select Committee on China, told Semafor. “If that’s true … then clearly, it seems that those questions need to be answered.” But so far the balance of GOP officials are coming to Lutnick’s defense, suggesting the commerce secretary won’t be going anywhere soon. The president himself is so far standing by Lutnick despite the bipartisan backlash, reinforcing his willingness to go easier on China as he pursues a trade detente with Beijing. “What I would say to everybody: Just settle down,” Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. “We don’t need to shoot Howard today.” “There’s lots and lots and lots of stuff here that’s going to come out. Should it come out? Absolutely,” Justice continued. “Should we get on some witch hunt running through the wilderness? … I don’t do that.” Congress will get more answers soon: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that Lutnick will testify before the chamber’s Commerce Committee. And House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., said that Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following revelations of another affair with a colleague, will appear before his panel . Even Lutnick’s critics think he’ll eventually pull himself out of trouble, even as longstanding interagency tension threatens to boil over. “When you saw [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent blowing up at Lutnick in the Situation Room, you can rest assured the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year,” Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and Bessent ally, told Semafor. “Now the issue becomes: Does Lutnick start inventing excuses to save himself?” A Commerce Department spokesperson said that “Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship,” adding that both “are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda.” The Nvidia news landed just in time for Democrats, who are finalizing their oversight plans for the next Congress. Already, lawmakers have laid the groundwork to investigate Lutnick’s involvement with Cantor Fitzgerald , Tether , and Epstein . The detractors No GOP lawmaker has called explicitly for Lutnick’s firing. But they haven’t hesitated to blame him for many of the recent revelations about Nvidia — including the fact that Huang accompanied Trump to China earlier this year despite the since-revealed existence of a State Department memo outlining his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy. “How on Earth do you put somebody on Air Force One [when you have] been informed there was a suspected improper relationship beforehand? How is that protecting the president?” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president; to me, that’s a disqualifying moment for Lutnick.” Compared to Epstein, “this, to me, is next-level,” he added. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., rebuked Commerce for not shedding more light on the circumstances, particularly when it comes to the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed. “If I were the secretary, I’d call a press conference and explain what happened,” Kennedy said. “This is as serious as an aneurysm.” Even some of the Trump administration’s staunchest allies have weighed in, accusing Lutnick of defying the president by failing to rein in Megaspeed. “Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen,” China hawk Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News. He urged Lutnick to testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The defenders Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor that “you’ve got to get the facts” before drawing any conclusions, adding that Lutnick has “always responded to my questions, so that’s all I can ask.” Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., also cast doubt on whether Lutnick really was at fault. “In a lot of cases, where they simply blame someone, I want to know what the rules are that he’s trying to comply with,” Rounds told Semafor. “Is there something that we’ve done, in terms of policy, that might have either delayed his ability or something else? I don’t know, and I’d rather get the facts before I make a decision as to guilt.” The AI industry sees little problem with Lutnick’s conduct either way. “Commerce’s job is to expand the economy, domestic and foreign, pretty much at all costs,” National Artificial Intelligence Association CEO Caleb Max said. “So if you zoom out, I don’t think it looks nefarious; I think it looks natural.” The View From the white house Far more crucially, the White House’s public posture on the debacle indicates that Trump is not particularly concerned about the fallout, let alone Lutnick’s role in it. “Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” a White House official said. “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” The White House pointed Semafor to the president’s comments earlier this week, when he told reporters that he didn’t think he’d bring up the subject during his upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Notable The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule to block China’s remote access to AI chips, The Information reported . White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out of his role, Reuters reported .

events.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
events.summary: The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r) Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person? Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw. From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place. But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing". So how much AI enhancement is too much? Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye. But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place. "The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different." For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison. AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI. But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time. "It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for." All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down. Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible. It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly. According to a recent survey , external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was. Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months. He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential. But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time. "I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person." He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated. Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove. In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter. In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down. Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing. "If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says. In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property". "It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold." Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology. But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

events.title: Advocates warn FIFO standards are slipping on mine sites
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts FIFO worker advocates warn 'bare minimum standards' not being enforced FIFO workers face long shifts away from family, with accommodation playing a crucial role in their wellbeing. ( ABC News: Cody Fenner ) Researchers say minimum accommodation standards are dropping on mine sites around the country. As a result, FIFO workers are more likely to experience psychosocial hazards like isolation and harassment. A code of practice for worker's accommodation is set to be endorsed by the WA government next year. With six years' experience as a WA fly-in fly-out (FIFO) worker, Vicky Pellowe still remembers the creeping sense of loneliness at the end of a 12-hour shift. "If you have had any kind of challenge or if there's anything going on at home, you are very much isolated with your own thoughts in your room," she said. "It needs to be comfortable, clean and connected." Mining camps are often built up with demountable "dongas". ( ABC: Jessica Shackleton ) As the Australian resources sector has exploded with year-on-year production records, advocates warn basic accommodation standards on remote mine sites are slipping. Ms Pellowe says the options range anywhere from extravagant camps to motel-style overflow to "donga" demountables. Ms Pellowe, executive director of the FIFO Family Project, represents one of 50 organisations that submitted to the WA government about a draft code of practice for workers' accommodation. Vicky Pellowe heads the FIFO Family Project, an advocacy group she founded after working in the mining industry. ( Supplied ) The code outlined best practice for amenities, including deadbolts on doors, better lighting in outdoor areas, king-single beds and reliable Internet connections. Triggered in part by revelations of widespread sexual harassment on site , it closed for feedback in June. The Department of Local Government, Industry Relations, and Safety says the code will receive final endorsement next year. Once the code of practice is in place, mining companies will not be legally bound to follow it, but it could be admissible in court if a hazard has not been properly managed. Ms Pellowe said there remained critical gaps when it came to connecting workers with their loved ones back home. She called for a mandated 24/7 contact point for families to raise welfare concerns. "They can be a real part of the safety net if they're included in these conversations about psychosocial wellbeing of workers," she said. Over-reliance on 'wellbeing washing' Architectural sociologist Jack Tooley, who also entered a submission, said mining companies had failed to connect the challenges to their bottom line. In a study published last month by journal Safety Science , Dr Tooley identified a reluctance to grant access to outside researchers, a lack of trust in survey data and an over-reliance on "wellbeing washing" like swimming pools. Mid-tier operator Mineral Resources built luxury-style Mungala Resort for its Pilbara workers in 2021. ( Supplied: MinRes ) Dr Tooley attributed 60 per cent of the psychosocial issues faced by mine workers to the built environment around them. Modelling by Dr Tooley's consultancy found simple improvements that lifted a worker's experience to a "neutral standard" — things like a better bed or noise-cancelling acoustics — could generate about $1.6 billion in annual revenue. Some advocates say the disparity is growing larger between rudimentary camps and resort-style accommodation. ( Supplied: Courtney Mason ) In 2025, Mineral Resources grabbed headlines by opening its $140 million Mungala Resort at Ken's Bore mine in the Pilbara, which boasts a pool and accommodation built for couples. The mid-tier miner has spruiked the 45-square-metre accommodation as three times the size of traditional FIFO rooms. Erin Turner delivers mental health training at Queensland mine sites and says growing workforces mean FIFO workers often feel shunted from room to room. "What that means is that people can't have their photos, they can't have certain homelike things that they would usually have," she said. Ms Turner said "creature comforts" were important to navigate the isolation and recover from long hours. Researchers from Edith Cowan University found employees in WA's Pilbara region were scared to speak up about the issues. They approached 20 for in-depth interviews across FIFO and residential rosters. Senior lecturer Heidi Vivian argued a wave of industrial action at BHP's iron ore and port operations earlier in the year was a reaction, having spoken with union-affiliated workers.

events.title: Photos show flowers outside Nvidia’s headquarters following Jensen Huang’s resignation
events.summary: Flowers were placed outside Nvidia HQ in Santa Clara, Calif. Haven Daley/AP Flowers were photographed outside Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. A man was also spotted leaving behind a candle. Following the resignation, Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. RIP, Nvidia under Jensen Huang . Several bouquets of flowers and at least one candle were photographed outside Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Thursday after Huang resigned as CEO. The founder and longtime chief executive resigned Thursday morning in the midst of a scandal involving one confirmed extramarital affair and two reported others , and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence operation. Flowers and a candle were left outside Nvidia's headquarters. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images On Thursday, several bundles of flowers sat against the Nvidia company sign in front of the company's headquarters. A man was also photographed adding a white candle in a glass jar in front of the sign. A man places a candle in front of an Nvidia sign outside the company's headquarters on Thursday. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images The apparent tributes to the tech executive highlight just how influential Huang had become as he helped Nvidia grow into one of the world's most valuable companies and a leader in the AI boom. Huang and his signature leather jacket had become largely synonymous with Nvidia, and he was one of the most visible figures in the AI revolution. Jensen Huang remains an influential figure in the tech world. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Nvidia's future without Huang remains uncertain. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was announced as interim CEO while the company searches for a replacement. As of Thursday, the stock was down 13% since Friday's market close, before Huang's admission of infidelity and the board's investigation were announced. Following Huang's resignation, leaders in the business and tech world weighed in on what his absence will mean for Nvidia. A woman walks past the apparent tribute to Jensen Huang. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images On Thursday, workers carrying Nvidia's signature green badges and backpacks seemed to be going to work as normal amid the shake-up. events.title: Cisco lifts annual revenue forecast on strong AI networking demand
events.summary: Cisco expects fiscal 2027 revenue in the range of US$74.8 billion (S$96.2 billion) to US$75.8 billion, compared with its previous forecast of US$72.2 billion to US73.4 billion. Cisco beat first-quarter estimates and raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to US$74.8 billion-US$75.8 billion, as demand for AI networking gear stays strong. Chief executive Chuck Robbins said: “We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle,” and Cisco lifted AI infrastructure revenue guidance from hyperscalers to US$9 billion. The firm is also building software for AI agents and cybersecurity, but investors still watch gross margin pressure from higher memory and component costs. Cisco beat Wall Street estimates for first quarter results and raised its annual revenue forecast on Nov 12, as the network gear maker bets on sustained strong demand from companies building out their AI infrastructure. The company has doubled down on its artificial intelligence efforts through strategic investments as Big Tech’s massive spending moves beyond artificial intelligence processors to the switches and routers required to connect large data centre systems. “We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking super-cycle,” chief executive Chuck Robbins said in a statement. The company raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to US$9 billion from US$7.5 billion. The segment generated revenue of US$4 billion a year earlier. Investors have been worried about a possible slowdown in data centre build-out following Democrats’ sweeping win in the US midterms , as well as rising borrowing costs and their impact on the debt-fuelled construction. Cisco reported first-quarter revenue of US$18.5 billion, compared with analysts’ average estimate of US$18.14 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company reported an adjusted profit of US$1.40 per share for the quarter ended Oct 24, above estimates of US$1.33. Cisco is also building software tools that businesses can use to build their own ​armies of bots, known as AI agents, to protect their IT ‌infrastructure against cybersecurity threats. They have risen about 32% so far in 2026 through the Nov 12 close. Cisco’s gross margin has been a worry for investors, as a shortage of memory chips has pushed up component costs for hardware makers while suppliers prioritise chips for AI data centre customers. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” said Bob O’Donnell, president and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. Cisco’s raised annual forecast and results above estimates are what the market wants to see from a company tied to AI infrastructure, he added. The company reported first quarter adjusted gross margin of 65.6%, in line with estimates, but down from 68.1% a year earlier. REUTERS

events.title: Anthropic’s IPO is about six times oversubscribed, say sources
events.summary: The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as US$64.4 billion (S$83 billion) in the IPO and US$26 billion in a private placement. Anthropic’s IPO is about six times oversubscribed, as strong demand builds for what could be the biggest listing ever. The firm aims to raise up to US$64.4 billion in the IPO and US$26 billion privately, with Nvidia set to buy about US$10 billion of shares. Anthropic is using investor events and a US$1.4 trillion valuation target, while its revenue run rate rose to US$81 billion by Oct 31. Anthropic’s initial public offering has drawn about six times the orders for the shares available, according to sources familiar with the matter, as interest increases for potentially the biggest first time share sale ever. The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as US$64.4 billion (S$83 billion) in the IPO and US$26 billion in a private placement, its filings show. Taken together, the offering would be bigger than SpaceX’s IPO, making it the biggest listing of all time. Bankers have told prospective investors that existing backers will be prioritised by Anthropic, and some would-be buyers will receive smaller allocations than they expect, some of the sources said. Details of the IPO including the demand for shares could change, said the sources, who asked not to be identified as the information is not public. A representative for Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The surge of interest in Anthropic shares contrasts with investors pulling back support for Nvidia Corp. after chief executive Jensen Huang was ousted from his post after reports of several affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. The chipmaker has agreed to buy about US$10 billion worth of shares in Anthropic as part of a US$26 billion private placement concurrent with its IPO, the artificial intelligence model firm’s filings show. Anthropic counts Nvidia as a strategic partner, and has committed tens of billions of dollars to deals securing access to its most advanced chips. Anthropic is looking to bolster demand for the IPO with a campaign of events for prospective investors, including a live-streamed event with its CEO Dario Amodei and JPMorgan Chase & Co CEO Jamie Dimon on Nov 13 , a source familiar with the matter has said. The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.4 trillion, below where some investors expected the company to settle, Bloomberg News reported. Some companies set terms conservatively when they begin formally marketing their IPO, in the expectation that strong demand will push up the final figure and set them up for robust trading in their debuts. Anthropic’s filing on Nov 10 supported the case for AI spending as sales continued to increase. The company reported a revenue run rate of US$81 billion as at Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, the filing showed. Anthropic had a US$65 billion run rate figure at the end of July, Bloomberg News reported. Anthropic defines the metric as annualising consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and subscription-based fees for a single month. Some investors are offering a portion of their Anthropic IPO allocation to other prospective backers, letting them collect additional fees and reduce their risk before trading begins, while others with pre-IPO stakes are marketing them to buyers via special purpose vehicles. Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley are leading Anthropic’s IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filing shows. The stock is expected to trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. BLOOMBERG

events.title: DOJ takes aim at $1.2B in Binance loot as FBI disrupts North Korean scam
events.summary: The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft. The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months. It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks. 900+ faces stolen The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers. Here’s how the attack works. First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible. “You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles. “They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday. The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite. Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.” ‘You’re on mute’ as a social engineering vector The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix. Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff. “The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.” Binance heist update The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group. Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.” Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

events.title: ‘A dark day’: Jensen Huang’s sex drive threatens to pop the AI bubble, and the industry isn’t sure what’s next
events.summary: Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Beatrice Nolan. In today’s issue: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns . Nvidia CFO Colette Kress and its first-ever board chair Harvey Jones are now in charge. Anthropic’s IPO demand was poised to exceed expectations —before the Nvidia bombshell . United Airlines blocks agents from booking flights. Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco . We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li , now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng , now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO N ikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase , and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research. Plus, we’ve got Nick Fox from Google. We’ve got Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao . We’ve got Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman , Vanta’s Christina Cacioppo , Unconventional AI’s N aveen Rao, Brex’s Pedro Franceschi , Maven Clinic’s Kate Ryder , Box’s Aaron Levie , Atlassian’s Mike Cannon-Brookes , New Work Foundation’s Clara Shih , Twilio’s Khozema Shipchandler , Rubrik’s Bipul Sinha , Harvey’s Winston Weinberg , Dynamic Creatures’ Marc Theermann , SendCutSend’s Jim Belosic, Apptronik’s Jeff Cardenas , Accenture Song’s Ndidiamaka Oteh , and Senra Systems’ Jordan Black . It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on December 7th and 8th . You can apply to attend here . Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO may be the biggest story in AI we’ve seen since the launch of ChatGPT almost exactly four years ago. Not only because it’s a stunning, swift downfall, but also because it’s the end of the first major phase of AI development as we’ve known it. At Fortune , we’ve been following the story closely over the past two days. You can check out our coverage by following the links in the “Fortune on AI” section of this newsletter. It turns out, one man might just be able to single-handedly pop the AI bubble by not keeping it in his pants, with not one but three affairs—at least that we know about so far. But in all seriousness, this is a sad story. It’s a visceral betrayal for Huang’s family, his wife of 41 years, Lori, and their two children, both of whom work at Nvidia. Huang has disappointed just about everybody in his orbit, from shareholders to customers, to people who held him up as a role model. Martin Casado, an investor at the prominent firm a16z called today a “dark, dark day,” and a “horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world.” “It’s very sad by every dimension,” Penny Herscher, a longtime executive in the semiconductor industry, told me today. “It’s sad for his family, for the employees, for the customers. Jensen’s a remarkable person, and it’s sad to see such a remarkable person in this horrible situation—self-inflicted, but horrible.” “I am extremely sad today as I see Nvidia without Jensen Huang,” one Nvidia employee posted . Several others have made similar public remarks. My hunch is Nvidia will prevail, given the immense amount of money and geopolitical stability hanging on the health of its GPU business. But there will likely be a period of uncertainty, both in the boardroom and in Washington. America’s position at the top of the AI industry hangs in the balance, and stricter regulation may be more likely, especially given the Democratic Party’s sweeping midterms wins. As Jeremy Kahn wrote in Tuesday’s edition of Eye on AI, Huang had been a leading voice opposing both U.S. export controls on AI technology and government regulations on open models, and now that community has lost their main champion. “This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!” posted Clement Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, the open source repository Nvidia acquired for nearly $13 billion in September. “But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!” There is much more to the story yet to unfold. Huang has agreed to appear before Congress. More investigations are likely to ensue. Meanwhile, rumors are swirling that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei may have orchestrated Huang’s downfall. Amodei has warned that open models can serve as uncontrolled weapons that bad actors can harness to incur serious societal harm, and is in favor of industry-wide slowdowns. I’m not quick to believe that theory, mostly because there is not yet any proof, but also Anthropic had every incentive to wait until after its IPO if it was going to take down Huang. The dark cloud his ousting has cast over the AI industry threatens Anthropic’s valuation as investors enter arguably the greatest period of instability we’ve seen yet in AI. “My expectation is a 10–15% valuation haircut, potentially approaching 20% if Nvidia’s leadership crisis raises doubts about its $10 billion anchor commitment,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult, tells Fortune . “Anthropic’s underlying business hasn’t changed overnight, but investor confidence has. I expect the anchor to hold, but investors will demand a greater margin of safety. The larger question is whether this marks the beginning of a broader repricing of AI risk.” The big unknown is how the stock market will react. Nvidia shares are trading down 4% at the bell today, a modest dip. As far as silver linings go, there will be a few winners to come out of Huang’s downfall. Nervous Nvidia customers could place bigger orders with other chipmakers, such as Google, Amazon , AMD , and Broadcom . Another winner could be Nvidia’s next CEO, who stands to score the role of a lifetime, and perhaps propel the company into a new and even more successful era. That search is already underway. But given the allegations against Huang at this time, particularly that he may be complicit in funneling chips to China via Megaspeed, the shell company helmed by his paramour Alice Huang—there could always be more executives involved. The biggest story in AI since ChatGPT is far from over. With that, here’s more AI news. Emily Forlini emily.forlini@fortune.com @emilyforlini This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Binance finishes covering US$6.3 billion of stolen customer tokens
events.summary: The crypto exchange said it had restored all crypto-assets lost as at Nov 12. Binance said it has covered all US$6.3 billion of stolen customer tokens after the Oct 29 hack, which the US and analysts blamed on North Korea. The exchange used profits and emergency funds to restore most tokens fast, but some obscure assets took longer to buy back and replace. The hack showed major crypto security risks, with thieves using thousands of wallets, 65,000 transactions and laundering networks to hide the stolen funds. Binance said it has covered all US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) in crypto assets pilfered from customers, marking a capstone to the largest cybertheft in history. The Oct 29 incident , which the US government and analysts have blamed on North Korea, involved not just common cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, but more obscure tokens that took Binance more time to find and purchase. As at Nov 12, the crypto exchange had restored all of them, according to a social media post. “To our users and community: thank you for your patience and understanding,” Binance said in its post on social media platform X. Binance spent a mixture of its profits and other emergency funds to quickly restore most of the stolen tokens in a matter of days, but said a remaining 10% would require more effort. It pledged throughout the process to completely cover lost funds. Hackers used a maze of tools to launder the cryptocurrencies stolen from Binance, including transferring the tokens through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins. The thieves used meme-coins to launder a slice of the proceeds, allowing them to pass through about US$430,000 of the stolen crypto. The automated nature of the transactions was also notable. Within a week of the hack, the laundering effort used more than 20,000 wallets and executed at least 65,000 transactions, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic. That equates to roughly one new wallet being used every 30 seconds and one transaction completed every 10 seconds. Blockchain security firm Chainalysis also recently highlighted the role of Chinese money-laundering networks in cashing out the funds. The enormous cyberheist of the world’s largest crypto exchange came at a time when the digital asset industry is pushing ever more into mainstream finance. It also highlighted the prevalence of cybersecurity challenges – especially since a key vulnerability appears to have been an engineer who was phished through a phoney job offer. Crypto exchanges Bitget and Bybit, as well as companies that helped keep tokens safe with physical hardware, such as Coinkite and Ledger, have all also experienced major incidents recently. events.title: Cramer says Jensen Huang betrayed Nvidia shareholders. How to pick up the pieces
events.summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer criticized former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday for putting the chipmaker's future at risk. "Did he betray you, the shareholders?" Cramer asked. "Yes. End of story." Huang resigned Thursday morning following reports of an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Hours later, Reuters reported that he had an "intimate relationship" with a second employee. These revelations came days after Huang admitted to an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing company whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO of Nvidia. Cramer said Huang's departure was necessary to protect Nvidia from further fallout. While questions remain about what comes next for the AI chipmaker, Cramer argued that Nvidia's future extends beyond the executive who helped build it into one of the world's most valuable companies. "There won't be a better Nvidia, just a different one [without Huang]," Cramer said, envisioning a company that is better organized and more disciplined about its investments. Under Huang, Nvidia built an extensive equity investment portfolio that included a $5 billion investment in Intel in 2025 and a $2 billion investment in AI cloud provider CoreWeave earlier this year. The investments, and many others, were part of Huang's strategy to strengthen Nvidia's position across the AI industry. During the CNBC Investing Club's Morning Meeting livestream Thursday, Cramer recalled urging Kress to reduce the company's stakes in Intel and CoreWeave, only to be told that Huang preferred to maintain them. Cramer suggested that new leadership could take a more disciplined approach to capital allocation, potentially cashing in on some of those investments and returning the proceeds to shareholders through even bigger stock buybacks. Cramer expressed confidence in Kress, praising her deep understanding of Nvidia's operations and financials. He argued that the longtime finance chief is well positioned to provide stability as the company navigates the investigations surrounding Huang, which stretch from the boardroom to Washington, D.C. Nvidia didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment on Cramer's remarks. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not respond to CNBC's request for comment. Going forward, Nvidia's underlying business remains strong, Cramer said, pointing to its substantial cash reserves and expectations for a robust earnings report Tuesday evening. But he cautioned that even strong quarterly results might not be enough to reassure investors during this time of lingering uncertainty. Investigations into Huang's conduct and possible violations of U.S. chip export restrictions could result in sanctions that hurt Nvidia's international business. Meanwhile, competitors, including Advanced Micro Devices , are making progress with their own AI chips, potentially threatening Nvidia's market dominance. AMD shares surged almost 6% on Thursday, extending their winning streak to five straight sessions. Those risks have prompted Cramer to take a more cautious approach to Nvidia stock , particularly after the substantial gains shares have delivered over the years for Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio of 32 stocks managed by the Club. On Tuesday, as Huang's future at Nvidia looked more and more in doubt, the Club downgraded Nvidia to a hold-equivalent rating. "Don't ever turn a successful investment into an unsuccessful trade," he said, urging longtime shareholders sitting on big gains to consider taking some profits. "You don't want to give up all of your gains if the stock falls further. It fell further today after many of the analysts jumped ship and downgraded the stock from buy to hold. There could be more ahead." At the same time, Cramer cautioned against giving up on Nvidia altogether, pointing to the company's extensive engineering expertise and multiyear product roadmap as reasons to believe it can continue competing at the forefront of AI without Huang. The "Mad Money" host also drew parallels to Apple's leadership transition from Steve Jobs to Tim Cook , suggesting that Nvidia could benefit from a similarly capable successor who brings a different management style without sacrificing the company's technological edge. events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO: The outside contenders to succeed Jensen Huang
events.summary: The biggest guessing game in business has begun: Who can fill Jensen Huang’s shoes? Colette Kress, chief financial officer at Nvidia since 2013, was appointed interim CEO of the company on Thursday. Kress will also continue in her CFO role as the board conducts its search for Jensen Huang’s permanent successor. “Colette is very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told Fortune . But Simmons, who has worked in executive recruiting for almost 30 years, thinks Nvidia’s board will seek a technologist as Huang’s permanent successor, potentially from outside the company. If Nvidia goes with an external candidate for the CEO job, Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at The Futurum Group, is putting his money on Arm CEO Rene Haas. “He spent seven years at Nvidia and understands Jensen’s culture; and what makes him interesting is that Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs run on Arm architecture,” Boloor wrote in an X post . “So while he missed [the] rise of NVLink, Mellanox and rack-scale AI he understands [the] CPU side of Nvidia’s platform better than almost anyone else on the outside.” Sam Sugarman, a venture capital and private equity investor who co-founded and leads the VC/PE Secondaries practice at Concordia Capital, also placed Haas on his list of external candidates . Haas would bring a combination of Nvidia experience and public-company leadership, having steered Arm through its 2023 IPO and expanded its business beyond processor licensing. His background spans engineering, product strategy and sales. But his familiarity with Nvidia dates to an earlier era: he left in 2013. The board will have to assess whether running Arm has prepared him for Nvidia’s much larger, more complex business. Sugarman also pointed to AMD CEO Lisa Su as a potential successor to Huang. Su (who ironically happens to be a distant cousin of Huang’s) would bring a combination of semiconductor engineering credentials and a proven record of running a major chipmaker. She has led AMD since 2014, overseeing a turnaround that made it a formidable competitor in processors and a challenger to Nvidia in AI chips. That experience could appeal to a board. But recruiting her would mean persuading a sitting CEO to leave the company she rebuilt. Meanwhile, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told Fortune that he sees Tim Cook , the former CEO of Apple ; Tom Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud; and Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks , “as the top three external candidates for Nvidia’s CEO role.” Cook would bring experience with a challenge few executives have faced: succeeding a technology company’s defining leader. Cook took over from Steve Jobs and spent 15 years running Apple before becoming executive chairman in September. Cook’s mastery of supply chains and logistics would be a good fit at Nvidia, and the fact that Apple has developed its own processors in-house over the past decade means Cook has some direct experience in the chips business. His continuing work on Apple’s international relationships would also be relevant to a company navigating geopolitical pressures. But his continuing responsibilities at Apple as chairman could complicate the prospect of recruiting him. That said, Cook has the support of one high-profile observer: President Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday that Cook should replace Huang. Kurian would offer a connection to Nvidia’s AI infrastructure business. Before taking over Google Cloud in 2019, Kurian spent 22 years at Oracle , ultimately becoming president of product development. At Google Cloud, he has also worked closely with Nvidia through the companies’ AI infrastructure partnership. The question is how readily that experience would translate to leading the chipmaker itself. Arora would bring the experience of a sitting public-company chief executive with a career spanning enterprise technology, global sales and investment. Before joining the cybersecurity company in 2018, Arora was president and COO of SoftBank and held senior commercial roles at Google, including chief business officer. His appeal as a candidate could depend on whether Nvidia wants a strategist who can build around its technical leaders. There may be pros and cons for each potential candidate, but the board’s choice will ultimately determine Nvidia’s fate. “There’s such a small pool to fish in when you think about people capable of stepping into this,” Simmons said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Analysis: Nvidia’s leadership crisis tests the chipmaker’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday follow revelations that he had extramarital affairs. Nvidia has made substantial financial commitments to AI infrastructure companies, including cloud-service purchases and project guarantees. The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are examining how leverage and interconnected financing could amplify an AI downturn. Financial experts distinguish potential losses for technology investors from the more serious risk of losses spreading through banks and credit markets. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector. A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion. But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said. "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against. And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts. In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy. "I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit. Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years.

events.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
events.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers. Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business. Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess. Ian Buck Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia. He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development. Chris Malachowsky Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page . "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads. Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership. Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position. René Haas Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports . He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes . Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products. Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition. Tim Cook President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia. Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse. Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation. Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO. Johny Srouji Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg has identified Srouji , Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor. Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. Nikesh Arora Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks , has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name. Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity. He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography . Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development. Lisa Su AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry. Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, and she was just named " CEO of the Year " by Yahoo! Finance. Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried says Su might relish competing with a weakened Nvidia rather than taking over for Huang. Thomas Kurian Thomas Kurian speaks onstage during Oracle's OpenWorld conference in San Francisco in 2017. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud could also be considered . Kurian oversees cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience with major customers and technology essential to Nvidia's business. Yes, but: His resume does not feature chip design experience. Pat Gelsinger Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger holds up a processor while speaking onstage at the Computex technology conference in Taipei in 2024. Photo: Annabelle Chih/Bloomberg via Getty Images The former Intel CEO boasts decades of semiconductor engineering and leadership experience at one of Nvidia's longtime competitors. events.title: Microsoft struggling to fix massive cloud outage that's taken down email and Intune
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters ‘Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief’ Microsoft's massive M365 outage stretches past 12 hours as its fixes keep failing 51 minutes ago Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era 16 hours ago Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update 19 hours ago Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss 1 day ago Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit 1 day ago Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed. The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too. On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.” The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.” According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.” “We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote. But those efforts may not be working. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted. Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.” But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration. This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ® UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they " initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic." So not usefully healthy at all, then. "We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised.
