events.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
events.summary: In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks. Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations. “Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.” The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip. One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027. The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law. DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center. According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery. Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything. TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment. On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg. In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays. Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash. Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.” Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey.

events.title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
events.summary: Cisco reported fiscal first-quarter earnings that topped estimates. The computer networking company is trying to become a bigger player in AI after missing out on the early years of the boom. The stock is up 35% this year, trouncing the Nasdaq, which is up about 9%. Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: EPS: $1.40 adjusted vs. $1.33 expected Revenue: $18.5 billion vs. $18.1 billion expected. Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago. Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch. Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement . For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

events.title: Nvidia stock closes down over 4% after CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation
events.summary: Nvidia’s stock plunged after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation here. Nvidia shares declined 4.34% Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker. The stock hovered under $4 trillion in market cap for most of the day, but climbed slightly heading into the close to finish above the number. The 4% fall pared steeper losses earlier in the day of as much as 14%. Nvidia has closed above the $4 trillion market cap benchmark since July 2025. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair . The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed , according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. Alice Huang is also tied to Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, and may have owned stakes in Chinese businesses benefitting Huawei while simultaneously doing business with Nvidia, CNBC's Eamon Javers exclusively reported Thursday. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times. Huang also had an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee, Reuters reported Thursday. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month. Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia's stock by half from $400 to $200. Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday that Huang's alleged affair with a direct report means it is "much tougher for the board to leave him in position." Huang was central to Nvidia's rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the "visionary" to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO. "Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they're in the position that they're in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago," Rasgon said. "Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don't intuitively know who that person would be." Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang's resignation , adding further pressure to the CEO and the company. Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia's lack of a succession plan makes the stock "uninvestable." "Nvidia doesn't have that person in place, and so it's going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations," Reyle told CNBC's "Access Middle East." "Or they're going to have to move on from him, and that's just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn't make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable." events.title: Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors
events.summary: Nvidia stock dropped sharply during early trading Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. Reports also said he had a separate extramarital relationship with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, the chipmaker's vice president of healthcare. Many popular ETFs have a roughly 6% to 8% stake in Nvidia. Nvidia stock plunged in early trading on Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO . Huang co-founded the chipmaker 33 years ago and built it into a behemoth at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Since Nvidia is among the largest publicly traded companies by market capitalization, its stock is, by default, a substantial holding in several popular mutual funds and exchange-traded funds. Many investors therefore hold the chipmaker's stock in their portfolios — and may worry about their exposure. But mutual fund and ETF investors' exposure to Nvidia stock is likely relatively low, data shows — and any big swings in its stock price are likely to have a fairly muted impact on investor portfolios, financial advisors said. "This is just a very contemporary, sensational case of risk," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "But that is part and parcel to stock investing." More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Roth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisor Nvidia's stock fell more than 10% early Thursday on news of Huang's resignation. Huang stepped down following his admission to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China, and after reports that he had a separate extramarital relationship with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at Nvidia. Reuters also reported Thursday that Huang had an "intimate relationship" with a second Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. The stock has since pared some of those losses, and was down more than 5% as of roughly 2:50 p.m. EST. However, investors "shouldn't worry" about their exposure, Chao said. For example, if Nvidia were 5% of an overall fund's holdings and the stock dropped 10%, the fund's value would decline 0.5%, assuming all else was equal, Chao said. "It's not a big deal," he said. "Most people are just reacting to the sensational aspect of this [news]." A flash poll of members of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios. Three are increasing their stake, and six do not own the chipmaker. None of the respondents are decreasing their ownership. The online poll, conducted from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, was sent to 122 firms and 27 responded. Let's look at some of the most popular stock ETFs for some specific examples of why investors likely have limited exposure. Nvidia stock is the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO ). The fund, as the name suggests, tracks the performance of the S&P 500 U.S. stock index and had a market capitalization of $1.7 trillion as of Sept. 30, according to the most recent Vanguard data. On that date, Nvidia stock accounted for about 8.4% of the entire portfolio. Assuming that weighting carried forward to today, a 5% decline in Nvidia's stock would only cause the fund to lose about 0.42% of its value, all else equal, according to an analysis by Experiential Wealth for CNBC. A 10% decline would lead the fund to drop by 0.84%, according to the analysis. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ) is an ETF that tracks the performance of the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index. The fund held about $473.8 billion as of Nov. 10, according to Invesco data . Nvidia was its second-largest holding, at 6.8% of the overall portfolio. Apple was No. 1, at about 8.4%. Based on that weighting, the fund would lose just 0.34% of its value if Nvidia's stock lost 5%, all else equal, according to the Experiential Wealth analysis. A 10% Nvidia loss would equate to a 0.68% loss for the overall fund. 3. Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF Nvidia stock was the largest holding in the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ( VTI ). The fund had $1.8 trillion as of Oct. 31, according to Vanguard. Nvidia stock accounted for about 7.13% of the fund, as of Sept. 30 .

events.title: ‘That Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago’: What Jensen Huang’s exit means for neoclouds
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia hits the AI industry’s most indebted borrowers hardest, according to one investor who backs AI infrastructure. Nvidia said Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. His exit follows his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, and following a board investigation into the affair. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO , and the board named Harvey Jones its first chair. While Nvidia’s leadership switch-up is sending shockwaves across every industry that relies on its chips to those who simply have stock or their 401Ks resting in company, some say the companies that are most at risk are the so-called neoclouds that rely on Nvidia’s chips. How Nvidia props up the neoclouds Nvidia designs the chips that most AI models are trained on, and Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures them, and that’s a problem. So says Joe Kaiser, who started Switchyard Partners at the beginning of this year after serving as CEO of Mercato Partners, which managed about $1.5 billion. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius buy those chips by the hundreds of thousands, fill data centers with them and rent the computing power to AI labs and other companies, competing with Amazon , Google and Microsoft . But Nvidia does more than sell to them. It invests in them: the company held about $329 million in Nebius shares, for example, at the end of June. Nvidia also guarantees their business. In July, Nvidia began offering to rent back unused GPU capacity from neocloud partners at a fixed rate, a floor meant to make banks more willing to lend. The company later joined a $500 billion financing platform with six institutional partners, of which Nvidia may backstop up to $125 billion. That backstop, Kaiser said, posed an issue for what lenders are pricing. “The chip isn’t what puts them at risk, but it’s the financial backstop that allows CoreWeave or Nebius to go get those hundreds of millions of dollars of debt from Blackstone and Brookfield ,” Kaiser told Fortune . “Why is Blackstone willing to back a CoreWeave project? It’s because they know that there’s an Nvidia backstop, a written backstop, behind it, and so it lowers the risk, and then obviously lowers the interest rate.” CoreWeave carried $35 billion in debt at the end of June, and lenders had grown wary of businesses that depend wholly on AI demand, well before Huang left. “If the capital providers now say that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Kaiser said. “At the end of the day, this is a heavy-asset, infrastructure-based industry.” The winners and losers OpenAI and SoftBank’s SB Energy may be the biggest beneficiaries of Nvidia’s backstops, with CoreWeave and Nebius close behind. Kaiser referenced how Nvidia has been in talks over a reported $250 billion backstop to help OpenAI lease an Ohio data center campus that SB Energy is developing. Following Huang’s resignation, Neocloud stocks fell Thursday: CoreWeave dropped about 9%, giving back part of a 25% rally the day before. Nebius fell 16% , though it also issued weak full-year guidance the same day. Nvidia itself lost about $450 billion in market value in the days after Huang admitted the affair, before Thursday’s drop. Kaiser doesn’t expect Nvidia to lose its grip on AI training for at least two or three years, because customers built on its CUDA software will find it “really hard” to switch. The fight is over inference, the work of running models once they’re trained, which Kaiser said now takes up more AI compute than training. There, buyers are weighing Nvidia’s general-purpose chips against cheaper ones built for specific jobs: Qualcomm for robotics, Cerebras, Etched, Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium. “If Nvidia no longer has Jensen as its rainmaker, did that just tip the scale towards using specialized chips?” Kaiser said. “The bigger play is actually for the specialty chip makers,” he said, but said AMD and Broadcom will inevitably gain an opening. Google and Amazon could win twice: by pitching their own chips to labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, and by lending their balance sheets. “The Googles and others can step into that Nvidia backstop arrangement,” he said. TSMC should come through fine, Kaiser said. He estimated about two-thirds of its capacity goes to Nvidia, but said it could shift that to other customers “in pretty short order.” Following Intel Kaiser said Huang ran Nvidia on a “hub-and-spoke” model. “The stories are true about Jensen having 60-plus direct reports,” he said, which now leaves “this leadership vacuum and vision vacuum.” He referenced Intel after Andy Grove stepped down as CEO in 1998. “Andy Grove and Jensen both have just this iron-fist approach to management, very disciplined approach,” he said. Intel kept growing revenue after Grove left, he said, but the company lost margin and “didn’t adapt as well” as chip demand moved toward new uses. “Intel is the roadmap here to what might be ahead for Nvidia.” Kaiser also tied Huang’s exit to last week’s midterms, where data centers became a campaign issue. Calling Huang the industry’s “true spokesperson” for data centers, and with that spokesperson now gone, he said, the case for giant single-site data centers weakens further. “This is just more push for distributed edge compute,” he said, “away from these mega monolithic data centers.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ian Buck built Nvidia's secret weapon. Jensen Huang's departure makes it even more essential to the company's future.
events.summary: Ian Buck has spent his career building CUDA, Nvidia's most important software. Bloomberg/ Getty Images Ian Buck is a lesser-known force behind Nvidia's technological moat and market share. Jensen Huang's resignation elevates Buck's role as a steward of the company's original vision. How Nvidia maintains its moat and what's next for the company, in part, lies with Buck. Editor's note: This story was originally published in June of 2025, but has been updated to reflect Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Users on the prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket are giving Nvidia's Ian Buck the highest odds of permanently succeeding Huang. As Nvidia enters its post-Jensen Huang era, one of the people best positioned to shape its future is the engineer who helped build its moat. Ian Buck has spent more than two decades at Nvidia and created CUDA, the once-obscure software platform that has since become the foundation of the AI boom. The 48-year-old's contribution to Nvidia is hard-coded into the company's history. He's been working alongside Huang since 2004, when he started building the company's breakthrough software, CUDA. Back then, the team had two people and two libraries. Today, CUDA supports more than 900 libraries and artificial intelligence models. Each library corresponds to an industry using Nvidia technology. Especially in light of Huang's departure, Buck's influence is just beginning. CUDA is the platform from which Nvidia jumped to, at one point, 90% market share in AI computing. CUDA is how the company defends its moat. It's the heft of Buck's contribution that has led industry analysts and onlookers to repeatedly cite Buck in discussions of a possible successor to Huang, even long before one was needed. CUDA started with two libraries. It now has more than 500. AP Photo/Nic Coury One architecture to rule them all Dion Harris, Nvidia's senior director of high-performance computing and AI factory solutions, sometimes forgets that he's in the room with the Dr. Ian Buck. Then it hits him that his boss, and friend, is a computing legend. Since Buck's undergrad days at Princeton in the late 1990s, he had been focused on graphics — a particularly punishing field within computer science with no obvious connection to AI at the time. "Computer graphics was such a dweebie field," said Stephen Witt, the author of " The Thinking Machine, " which details Nvidia's rise from obscurity to the world's most valuable company. "There was a stigma to working in computer graphics — you were maybe some kind of man-child if this was your focus," Witt said. While pursuing his Ph.D. at Stanford, Buck connected multiple graphics processing units to push them to their limits. He had interned at Nvidia before pursuing his Ph.D., so he was familiar with the GPU. Initially, he used it for graphics like everyone else. Buck has said that he and his cohort would use the chips to play video games such as "Quake" and "Doom," but eventually, he started asking himself what else his gaming setup could do. He became fixated on proving that you could use GPUs for anything and everything. He received funding from Nvidia and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, among others, to develop tools to turn a GPU into a general-purpose supercomputing machine. When the company saw Brook—Buck's attempt at a programming language that applied the power of GPUs beyond graphics, Nvidia hired him. He wasn't alone. John Nickolls, a hardware expert and then director of architecture for GPU computing, was also instrumental in building CUDA. Buck may have been forever paired with Nickolls if the latter had not died from cancer in 2011. "Both Nickolls and Buck had this obsession with making computers go faster in the way that a Formula 1 mechanic would have an obsession with making the race car go faster," Witt told BI. (The author said Huang expressed frustration that Nickolls doesn't get the recognition he deserves since his passing.) Buck, Nickolls, and a small team of experts built a framework that allowed developers to use an existing coding language, C, to harness the GPU's ability to run immense calculations simultaneously rather than one at a time and apply it to any field. The result was CUDA, a vehicle to bring parallel computing to the masses. The rise of CUDA as an essential element in the world of AI wasn't inevitable. Huang insisted on making every chip compatible with the software, even though hardly anyone was using it, despite it being free. In fact, Nvidia lost millions of dollars for more than a decade because of CUDA. The rest is lore. When ChatGPT launched, Nvidia was already powering the AI computing revolution that is now the focus of trillions in infrastructure spending , much of which eventually goes to Nvidia. King of the nerds Buck's smarts do have limits. He joked to an eager audience at GTC in 2025 that quantum chromodynamics, a field of particle physics, just won't stick in his brain. But he thrives in Nvidia's notoriously rigorous environment. Under Huang, the Santa Clara, California, company has maintained an intense culture that eschews one-on-one meetings and makes missteps and disagreements public. It might sound terrifying, but for those with the brains to keep up, the directness and the rigor are ideal. For this report, Business Insider spoke with four people who have either worked directly with Buck at Stanford, Nvidia, or both. Those who know Buck personally describe him as gregarious and easygoing but capable of intensity when goals are on the line. He's focused on results rather than theory. In his public remarks, at panels and in interviews on behalf of Nvidia, Buck volleys from rapid, technical lines of thought to slower, simple descriptions in layman's terms. At a GTC press conference, he detailed the latest development in convolutional neural networks and then described proteins as "complicated 3D squigglies in your body." He describes the tiny, sensitive interconnects between parts of an Nvidia chipset like the Geek Squad explaining the back of a TV from memory — it's all in his head. Harris said storytelling ability is particularly important in the upper ranks at Nvidia. Since the company essentially had a promising technology waiting for a market for years, Huang saw being early as a business strategy. He branded it "going after zero billion-dollar markets." The potential of AI, "AI factories," and the infrastructure spending that goes with them is a story Nvidia can't stop telling. Buck's shilling skills have improved over the years. But even in 15-year-old footage, he's most animated when explaining the inner workings of Nvidia's technology. "A lot of developers are amazing, but they say, 'Leave me alone. I'm going to write my code in the mountains somewhere," Paul Bloch, president of Nvidia partner DDN , told BI. Nvidia's leaders aren't like that, he said. events.title: ‘A high probability’: Congress pushes tighter export controls following Nvidia scandal
events.summary: The News Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year. In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidia’s now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. That’s raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that there’s a “high probability” that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China. Three measures were included in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation, known as the NDAA, however both Thune and Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., acknowledged there is no deal yet to include them in the final version of the bill currently under negotiation between both chambers. “I give it a better than even chance,” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Semafor of the possibility of strengthening export controls, which are handled by the Commerce Department. “I understand people have affairs but if you’re going to do it, try not to have an affair with a Chinese spy.” What’s on the table There are three main bills that could be included in the NDAA and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass all three of them “to cut off China’s access to advanced American technology before it’s too late.” The Chip Security Act aims to prevent illicit smuggling of advanced AI chips to foreign adversaries, partly by verifying their location once they’ve been shipped out. The MATCH Act closes loopholes around chipmaking equipment and export rules in allied countries. And the AI Overwatch Act would make it so chip sales are treated more like foreign arms sales and give Congress oversight of how Commerce approves or disapproves a license to sell chips to a “country of concern,” including China. Johnson told reporters Thursday that there’s “a developing consensus in Congress” around more chip restrictions, calling it “an important position to take, especially in light of recent developments.” And Democrats like Jeffries have signaled their support for putting the AI-related provisions into the NDAA, as have some Republicans. “I think the NDAA does provide us an opportunity to put guardrails around AI” or export restrictions, said Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said he’d otherwise defer to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the incoming House Armed Services chair. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., argued the Nvidia debacle “reinforces” the need for Congress to include more export controls in the defense bill, adding that there’s “strong demand” to do so even as there’s no final agreement on what it will entail. “Which plan takes priority in the final product, I don’t know yet. I think there’s several different strategies to be vetted yet,” Rounds said. Why this year is different During last year’s NDAA fight, the GAIN AI Act from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act, made it into the Senate version of the NDAA but got dropped from the House version after pressure from Nvidia, the broader semiconductor industry, and the White House (including then-AI adviser David Sacks). Congress did include some investment controls, but senators in both parties wanted to do more. This year, the bills are much further through the process, buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal and gaining momentum among GOP leaders, one Senate Democratic aide told Semafor. Anthropic has publicly supported all three bills, and OpenAI has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals. Nvidia hasn’t stood alone in its opposition to the bills — the broader tech industry has also lobbied against them, with the Information Technology Industry Council arguing they would “undermine the American tech stack.” But Congress will feel more emboldened to act than ever giving the security risks exposed by the controversy. Still, the defense bill, one of the few pieces of legislation that passes on an annual basis, could be imperiled by Democratic efforts to add provisions to sunset the war in Iran. Many in the party are pushing to use the must-pass legislation or a December government funding deadline as leverage over President Donald Trump, which could poison Republican support for the bills. “We have leverage. Take when the appropriations bills run out. I want the war in Iran stopped. I think we should put provisions into that bill, into the NDAA for that matter to stop it,” said Smith, the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair. Democrats face tough decisions about how hard to push for those provisions now and risking a government shutdown or the failure of the defense bill, especially when they could put the legislation together on their own terms next year when they take control of the House and Senate. Room for Disagreement Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said Congress has already done “a lot before more than people probably realize” on restricting chip exports to China and that they need to think before they do more. There’s also worry about going too far and inducing more Chinese manufacturing of chips by denying China technology. “This is a balance. Until someone comes up with a better construct, we need to put very strong export controls on the most powerful computer chips. That seems like a no-brainer to me,” said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. “Then the question is, how robust in terms of processing power can those chips be that we sent to them? … I don’t think it’s formulaic.” Burgess, Nicholas, and Ashley’s view Scandals move Congress and boy is this a scandal. And it comes at the perfect time for supporters of stricter chip curbs on China. events.title: Meet Lisa Su, Jensen Huang's cousin, who's CEO of Nvidia rival AMD
events.summary: Lisa Su, CEO of Advanced Micro Devices. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP AMD's CEO, Lisa Su, grew up in Queens and obtained three degrees from MIT. She's also the cousin of Jensen Huang, former CEO of rival Nvidia, who resigned on Thursday. Here is a look at her career rise, personal life, and challenges over the years. Editor's note: This story was originally published in October of 2025 and has been updated to reflect Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Lisa Su is the engineer behind one of the most dramatic corporate turnarounds in the tech industry. The Taiwanese American CEO is widely credited with transforming AMD from a struggling semiconductor firm on the brink of collapse into a global powerhouse competing head-to-head with Intel and Nvidia. When Su joined AMD in 2012, the company's market value was under $2 billion. Within a decade of her leadership, AMD's innovations in high-performance computing and graphics, especially the Ryzen CPUs and EPYC server processors, catapulted the company's value to over $950 billion as of Thursday. Su's leadership has not been without challenges. AMD's two largest competitors, Nvidia and Intel, are now working together in a strategic collaboration. Under the second Trump administration, export regulations related to China, one of AMD's largest markets, are also constantly changing. On Thursday, AMD's biggest rival Nvidia announced that its CEO Jensen Huang , who is also Su's cousin, is resigning. As Nvidia searches for a new CEO, some industry observers have floated Su as a possible outside candidate. AMD's stock was up 5% on Thursday. Here's a look at the timeline of Su's career, from her early life in New York City to her role as one of the most influential women in tech and innovation: Early life, family Tony Shi Photography/Getty Images Lisa Tzwu-Fang Su was born in Tainan, Taiwan, in 1969, to Su Chun-hwai and Sandy Lo. Her family immigrated to the US when she was around 3 because her father, a statistician, was pursuing his graduate studies at the University of Texas in Austin. At that time, her mother was an accountant. The family eventually settled down in Queens, New York City. As a child, Su liked to take apart and rebuild remote-controlled cars and other gadgets, which sparked her interest in engineering. She eventually attended The Bronx High School of Science and graduated in 1986. Education Neoclassical architecture columns and stairs to the entrance of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts. MIT was informally called Boston Tech. Sergi Reboredo/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Su attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Boston for many years and focused on electrical engineering. She eventually completed her bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees all at MIT throughout the 1990s. Su's doctoral work on MOSFETs — tiny electronic switches inside computer chips — helped cement her future in some of the world's best-known semiconductor companies. Semiconductor research IBM also had similar rounds of layoffs in 2024. Hollie Adams/REUTERS After leaving academia, Su worked in engineering, research, and managerial roles at Texas Instruments, IBM, and Freescale Semiconductor. As the lead scientist at the IBM Semiconductor R&D Center, she contributed to the development of copper interconnects in chips, replacing aluminum ones. Her later role as senior vice president and general manager at Freescale, where she prepared the company for its IPO, gave Su the experience she needed to take on roles beyond research. Joining AMD Liz Hafalia/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images Su joined AMD in 2012 as the general manager of Global Business Units. AMD's market cap that year was a little less than $2 billion. At that time, most of AMD's revenue came from traditional chips for PCs. However, the PC market was shrinking in the early 2010s while demand for smartphones and tablets was booming. AMD began adopting a "semi-custom" approach, modifying its core technologies to meet individual customer needs. This approach helped secure contracts to design and manufacture chips for Sony's PlayStation 4 and Microsoft's Xbox One , which reduced reliance on the PC market. In October 2014, Su was promoted to become President and CEO of AMD . Su is related to her competitor REUTERS/Ann Wang Su and Huang, former CEO of Nvidia , are actually related. They are first cousins, once removed , with Huang being the elder. Su's maternal grandfather is the eldest brother of Huang's mother. Despite both immigrating to the US from Taiwan as children, they did not grow up together and had never met until well into their respective careers. On Thursday, Nvidia said Huang had resigned from his role. It follows an extramarital affair scandal and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has also previously joked about his rivalry with Su. At an all-hands meeting last year, he recalled how his parents had sent him and his brother to live with an uncle related to Su in the US before they enrolled in a Kentucky reform school, where he was assigned to clean bathrooms. He blamed the ordeal on Su's side of the family, saying they'd been "out for blood" since he was nine "When we give a presentation, the whole market goes up," he joked. "When she gives a presentation, my stock price goes down." The big AMD turnaround Liz Hafalia/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images In 2014, AMD had a large but scattered portfolio of chips for PCs, embedded systems, graphics, and low-power mobile, but the lack of focus was causing the company to lose market share to Nvidia and Intel. In a change of direction for the company, Su decided to discard the market of low-power chips with small margins to focus on producing high-end chips for the cloud, data centers , and consoles. The development of the Ryzen chips helped revive its market share among consumer products, while the simultaneous launch of the EPYC processor chips helped carve out its share among data centers and servers. Companies with high demand for cloud services, such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google Cloud , have all been adopting EPYC chips. In 2018, AMD also launched the world's first 7-nanometer data center GPUs, namely the Radeon Instinct MI50 and MI60. By 2020, AMD's market cap had reached over $110 billion. An early viral moment Screenshot via YouTube Before Su started gracing magazine covers, she went viral in a clip from the 2018 Chinese Grand Prix, where Formula 1 commentator Martin Brundle yelled, "Excuse me, Ma'am, do you speak English?" at the CEO, who was sponsoring the event. "I'm with AMD," Su said, a response that immediately gained her the internet reputation of being humble. events.title: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test
events.summary: Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere. Now, Mississippi faces a new question: Was Scott Colom's victory a once-in-a-generation breakthrough, or the beginning of an era of Black political power? Driving the news: Colom's defeat of incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith broke a barrier that had stood since Reconstruction. Mississippi was the first state to send Black senators to Congress, before violence and disenfranchisement stripped Black residents of their political power. In Colom's race, Democrats gained ground in 75 of the state's 82 counties, Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, told Axios. "It wasn't just a fluke of super high turnout in one particular region," he said. "Scott Colom's victory can signal that maybe Mississippi is ready to govern differently." The big picture: During the Great Migration , roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South to escape discrimination and seek better opportunities. Many Black Mississippians built political power in Northern cities such as Chicago, said Keneshia Grant, a Great Migration expert at Howard University. For many, the question became, "should we go and try for a better life in these other places ... or should we stay and fight where we are?" Grant said. "It was about economic opportunity, but I also think it was about terrorism too," Cassandra Overton Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, told Axios, pointing to the lynchings that drove families away. Welchlin left Mississippi for graduate school and considered staying away. "I did not want to come back to Mississippi because it is hard here," she told Axios. Mentors encouraged her to return. She did, eventually becoming a voting rights organizer. Zoom in: "What Colom did is he really jazzed up his base. He didn't run from them," King said. "His campaign style and that strategy can certainly serve as a model" for future campaigns. Welchlin pointed to years of "nickeling and diming, doing organizing work to make sure that people had what they need to turn out the vote." Between the lines: Colom rode a Democratic wave and discontent with the Trump administration's economic policies, but those conditions may be difficult to recreate, said Andra Gillespie, who studies Black voter behavior at Emory University. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi's population, while most white voters favor Republicans. Unlike Georgia, Mississippi lacks the same diverse potential Democratic coalition. "[T]he conditions that we see this year are probably not going to be the new normal," Gillespie says. "It'd be way too early to diagnose that there's a realignment happening." Welchlin also cautioned that one historic victory doesn't mean Mississippi's racial barriers have disappeared. "We understand here in Mississippi that racism ain't over, ... Racism is still very much embedded in everything from our policies to our elections." What we're watching: Mississippi holds elections for governor, other statewide offices and state legislators in November 2027, testing whether Colom's coalition can hold. "For the first time in forever, Mississippi Democrats will go into an election with momentum," King said. The bottom line: Welchlin hopes Colom's victory changes how Black Mississippians view their futures: "I believe ... this election has given people hope that maybe I can stay here and be that change." events.title: Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women
events.summary: The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress , the new interim CEO of Nvidia —but her predecessor, Jensen Huang , failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic. Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry. We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod. As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts. He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive. Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure. As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy. Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls. events.summary: The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote in the post. The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump said Thursday as he directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. "We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, a key choke point in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. The announcement came just over a week after Republicans suffered huge losses in the midterm election. Vance and other Republicans have pinned those losses on the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel started in late February. In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump repeatedly suggested the U.S. could resume launching military strikes, which have largely subsided as a tense stalemate has taken hold in the region. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Vance, who has led diplomatic efforts with Iran in prior months, was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official. Stock futures declined following Trump's post. The unpopular Iran war, which Trump and others in his administration said would be won in a matter of weeks, is now in its ninth month with no clear end in sight. The conflict has driven up global energy prices, creating a ripple effect through the economy and exacerbating concerns about inflation and affordability that were paramount to voters in the midterms. Corruption emerged as another top issue that broke in Democrats' favor in the election. Trump's post Thursday morning attempts to flip the script, blaming Democratic-run areas for allowing corruption and crime to proliferate. "I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," Trump wrote. "The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters. Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month," the president wrote. "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity." "CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!" he added.

events.title: AI industry execs brace for future without leading hype man, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
events.summary: Tech industry insiders awoke Thursday morning with an unfamiliar, and somewhat alarming notion to contemplate: life without Jensen Huang. Huang’s abrupt resignation as CEO leaves one of the world’s most valuable companies without the leader who has steered it for the past 33 years; the person who almost singlehandedly transformed Nvidia from a small maker of video game graphics chips into the driving force of the AI boom.  “NVIDIA’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” Stephanie Balaouras, Forrester’s VP, group research director, told Fortune .  The importance of Nvidia, and of Huang, to the AI industry extends well beyond the company’s own P&L statement. In addition to being the leading maker of the GPU chips powering AI services like ChatGPT and Claude, Nvidia has become the AI industry’s “central bank” financing scores of other companies. And then there’s Huang’s unique standing as AI’s senior statesman and cheerleader on everything from AI regulation to industrial policy. Whether the AI industry turns out to have lost its most famous champion with the ignominious exit of Huang and his famous black leather coat, or a more crucial, Jenga-like piece may be the most important economic question to be answered in the coming weeks and months. “Obviously Nvidia is more than Jensen Huang, but he kind of championed a whole range of investments,” a VC investor focused on early-stage companies told Fortune . “There is a question around whether the pace of investment in AI and the size of the amounts of capital going into companies can be continued. Because by any stretch of the imagination, it’s been quite extreme,” the investor said. In the immediate aftermath of the news, the stock market appears to be keeping its composure. While shares of Nvidia were down 6.3% in midday trading on Thursday, and certain AI-linked stocks took a hit, the broader market reaction was relatively muted, with the Nasdaq down only 95 points.  But with spending on AI and data centers so important to the broader U.S. economy, the extent of the potential fallout from the Nvidia shakeup is difficult to overstate. Looming largest on the horizon is Anthropic’s widely anticipated initial public offering , scheduled to occur next week. The Anthropic IPO (along with OpenAI’s IPO expected in 2027) represent make-or-break moments for the AI industry—closely watched events that will serve as proxies for the health, and momentum, of the AI business. If nothing else, one startup founder told Fortune , the Nvidia drama raises the stakes for Anthropic’s upcoming IPO: “If the Anthropic IPO doesn’t go well and if the OpenAI IPO [down the line] doesn’t go well, there’s a question of: Is there a path to profitability for any players in the AI space?” Antropic is seeking to raise upwards of $60 billion in the offering slated for November 18, giving the five-year old AI company a valuation that could exceed $1.4 trillion when it makes its expected Wall Street debut next week.  Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, argued that investors will recognize the strength in Anthropic’s business, regardless of the Nvidia shakeup. “From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong and as good a position as it was before this news came out,” Alomar said. “I’m not sure it’ll have a massive impact on them. Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need,” he said.  Last stop for the money train? Anthropic’s business prospects are closely intertwined with those of the cloud providers, which provide the data centers and compute capacity to train and run AI models like Claude. (According to Anthropic’s S-1 filing, it has roughly $900 billion in compute spending commitments over the next several decades.) While the tech giants like Alphabet , Amazon , and Microsoft have the wherewithal to ride out whatever turbulence is caused by the changes at Nvidia, the situation may be trickier for the smaller “neo-cloud” companies —many financed by Nvidia—that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the computing power. Huang has championed these neo-cloud companies because it was good for business and the company’s influence, Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock. “He’d rather have 300 small customers who are dependent on him than three massive ones who you can’t negotiate with,” he said. With Nvidia CFO Coleen Kress now serving as interim CEO, the company’s attitude towards neo-clouds could shift. According to a report in The Information on Thursday, Kress has occasionally pushed back against Huang’s deals in the AI ecosystem, including a deal to backstop $250 billion in credit for an OpenAI datacenter project. The “Nvidia money train” that has kept parts of the market that propped up could come to an end, said one venture capital partner invested in numerous AI startups. “ The idea that they could count on Nvidia for future financing is unlikely.” Shares of CoreWeave one of the leading neocloud providers were down 7.5% on Thursday, while Nebius Group, another neo-cloud company which gave a lighter-than-expected sales forecast during its quarterly earnings on Thursday, were down 18%.  Investors are likely to look harder at the numbers Huang used to justify the complex web of investments. Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, expects investors and policymakers alike may start re-examining “Jensen math.” Incoming: regulation U.S. policy towards data centers could also come in for harsher treatment, particularly after last week’s midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly registered their opposition to having the facilities built in their communities.  Huang gave much of the industry credibility, even amid the backlash to datacenters. He was well-liked and not seen as a polarizing political figure, said Goldberg, of Seaport Research. But with Huang gone, the data center industry becomes “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” he said Goldberg.  Similarly, lawmakers advocating stricter regulation of AI technology, both the large language models as well as the chips that power the models, now have a much stronger hand. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI. But his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has destroyed his credibility on the regulatory issues.  “This guarantees new export controls,” Ed Mills, policy analyst at investment firm Raymond James, said of the spy scandal that contributed to Huang’s downfall. “It was extremely likely before the scandal and this is the accelerant to push it over the finish line.” Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are currently attached to the defense

events.title: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been a singular figure in the development of the AI industry, which suddenly has to survive without him. Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the company that powered the AI boom, doing so with no second-in-command. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's "Fast Money." Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. To expand his customer base, Huang designated compute capacity to a number of so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , putting equity into the companies and helping them build big businesses around renting out GPUs. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process.

events.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Jensen Huang: in the spotlight and out of a job. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.” Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies . She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair . And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026. The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked. Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose. Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .” As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors. The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems ,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership. The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience. Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history. In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge. According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu ,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs. The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu. A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi. Wikimedia Commons Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery. Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly. A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms ,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature. It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo. The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor. The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap .” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War . Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu . The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s. Bernard Boursicot and Shi Pei Pu in the dock during an espionage trial in Paris in May 1986. Laurent Maous/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang , a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office. Why Jensen Huang is strategically important Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power. Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development . Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers. From Beijing’s perspective , advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition. This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang. However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation. events.title: United Airlines won’t let AI agents book your flight. Expert says you shouldn't let a bot do that for you, anyway
events.summary: Spend Betting on sports online? Here are the rules you shouldn't take lightly Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Work AI resumes, cover letters are out: The new rules of finding a job right now Become Debt-Free This is ‘one of the worst’ credit card habits—41% of cardholders do it Life Celebrity divorce attorney: Ask 5 'essential' money questions by the third date—'spot red flags before your heart is in too deep' United Airlines said Wednesday it would be restricting artificial intelligence bots from its digital platforms, warning that allowing third-party AI assistants to access account credentials could expose sensitive personal information, lead to unintended purchases or other unauthorized account activity. The move is similar to Amazon's recent blocking of Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its site. Still, AI agents can complete a wide range of tasks on your behalf. Instead of just asking Muse what the weather will be tomorrow, you can tell it to suggest an outfit based on tomorrow's weather forecast and book you a rideshare if it's going to rain, for example. Or, rather than just creating an itinerary for your next vacation, you can connect a payment option and have your Dot — OpenAI's agent offering — book flights, hotels and excursions for you. You can even have an AI agent buy and sell stocks through investing platforms like Robinhood. Relying on an AI agent for any of these tasks may come with mixed results depending on which agent you use, what data you allow it to access and the complexity of the task you've asked it to carry out. Because broadly, agentic AI is still in its infancy, you may not want to let an agent make decisions "anytime [your] health, wealth, or privacy are involved," says Shomit Ghose, adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco School of Management, and lecturer at the University of California, Berkeley College of Engineering. "You can have agents do interesting things for you, like categorize your spending, or flag unusual charges, or model what-if scenarios," he says. "Those are good things, but bad things would be moving money, making trades, filing forms. All those things should stay manual at this point." AI-enthusiast traders may need some convincing, though. Here's what you should consider before outsourcing your whole to-do list to an AI agent. Though AI agents' capabilities are improving, they still operate in a fairly literal sense, which can create problems, Ghose says. If you tell your agent to book you the cheapest flight, for example, it may book you a flight at 3 a.m. or one with three layovers, unless you give the agent specific guardrails. "The bot only knows your context," Ghose says. "It cannot infer, as we humans are able to do, because of instinct and culture and education." Further, bots can still get it wrong even with a seemingly clear and direct command. They "treat all data as being equal," Ghose adds. So if it finds information on the web that is either inaccurate or subjective, it could give you misleading guidance or fail to meet your standards for the given task. For example, if you tell your agent to book you a reservation at a good barbecue restaurant, it may get you a table at a place that claims to be "the best barbecue in the world" on its website. But the restaurant may be in an inconvenient location or have poor reviews elsewhere on the web. Your command may need to be more specific, like asking your agent to check reviews on Google Reviews or Yelp. 'Ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?' Depending on what task you've assigned the bot, the outcome could be rather innocuous. But when individuals consider letting bots make purchases for them, make changes to their investment portfolios or and the like, the result could be more consequential. "In the end, you want to ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?" Ghose says. If you're booking a vacation, for example, it's reasonable to ask an AI agent to help make a decision on your destination based on the weather, your budget and other factors. But actually booking the flights and hotels "should still come back to me," Ghose says. He wants to maintain final say over major financial decisions. Doing so may even save you money. In Booking Holdings ' third-quarter earnings report, the Connecticut-based travel technology company reported 20% higher spending among customers who used AI assistants versus those who didn't to book accommodations on Agoda, one of its travel platforms. It's unclear whether those customers were led to pricier options or did, in fact, seek more expensive amenities. The company doesn't cite a single factor for the finding. AI agents are also making their way into the healthcare sector, which can pose risks for users too quick to rely on the agents' advice, Ghose says.

"A nasty inflation surprise in the latest Consumer Price Index data released this week has led to heightened expectations of interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.

events.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
events.summary: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”
