AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Lego fans demand answers as outage approaches a week with no confirmed cause C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute now Microsoft's massive M365 outage stretches past 12 hours as its fixes keep failing 51 minutes ago Developer cleverly shrank 2,600 lines of C into a six-line script but still ending up losing sleep 1 hour ago Singapore says US authorities, and Supermicro, hardly helped investigation of Jensen Huang’s Chinese friend 3 hours ago Alibaba's Qwen3.8 re-educated with a more Western worldview 6 hours ago Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online.

events.title: US Marines are training to break up and move their command posts to survive a Pacific war
events.summary: Future wars could require command nodes to be widely dispersed and highly mobile if targeted by an enemy. US Marine Corps photo by Sgt. Jonathan Beauchamp US Marines practiced working with dispersed and mobile command and control in the Pacific. The concept builds on lessons that command nodes need to be spread out, concealed, and easy to relocate. Russia's war in Ukraine is showing the vulnerabilities of fixed high-value targets. US Marines have been rehearsing how to spread out and relocate their command and control in the vast Indo-Pacific region, while still maintaining the ability to make battlefield decisions quickly. Modern conflicts have shown that large, centralized command posts are vulnerable to enemy detection and attack. The US and other Western militaries are learning that their command-and-control networks  will need to be dispersed, concealed, and capable of being moved quickly to survive. Earlier this month, Marines with the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, completed a five-day exercise in Hawaii that tested how quickly they could establish and maintain command and control from dispersed positions, according to a Marine Corps release. During the training, the Marines set up independent command nodes and conducted "aggressive displacement drills" that required them to relocate quickly via ground vehicles and MV-22B Osprey aircraft. These nodes oversaw missions including littoral combat, reconnaissance and counter-reconnaissance, countering air and surface threats, and coordinating with partner forces. "Between physically moving, managing rapid battle handovers, and coordinating simultaneous activities across our units, this was a great rep at validating our ability to disperse and still maintain the fight," said Marine Corps Chief Warrant Officer 2 Cameron Carver, the senior watch officer during the exercise. The Marines and other armed services have been practicing this dispersed force posture in preparation for a potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific. In such a war, an adversary could leverage sensors and faster kill chains to detect critical command posts and target them with missiles and drones. If these nodes are fixed and overly centralized, these attacks could severely harm commanders' ability to make  battlefield decisions . The US and other Western militaries are learning from Ukraine and other developments in modern warfare just how vulnerable large, fixed targets can be. US Marine Corps photo by Sgt. Jonathan Beauchamp The US Army has designed its new Next Generation Command and Control system, or NGC2, with that threat in mind. In tests, soldiers have experimented with command posts that can be packed into vehicles and moved in 30 minutes or less, while concealing them from detection both in the environment and the electromagnetic spectrum. Soldiers told Business Insider at an exercise earlier this year that the transition to dispersed command nodes was initially jarring. These nodes were designed to not only maintain connection with one another across distances but also to continue gathering information and making decisions during setup or on the move. Some command nodes also had built-in redundancy. For example, if one was acquiring targeting data for a certain location and was discovered by an enemy, another node could pick up where it had left off. During the recent Marine Corps training exercise, when command-and-control nodes had to stop what they were doing and relocate, there was a handoff to other command posts to make sure operations continued without pause, the service said. Carver said in the Marine Corps release that the recent training exercise "brought our staff out of predictable headquarters settings and required our planners to operate in distributed environments." And the shift from fixed operations toward dispersal and mobility for increased survivability is one that extends beyond command and control. US officials have said in recent years that large air bases are vulnerable targets to drones and missiles, requiring dispersal and concealment. In the Indo-Pacific, US forces have also tested operating aircraft in austere locations, like taking off from rugged fields. The Air Force regularly conducts this kind of training, while the Marines run through expeditionary basing practices. While the US military is rehearsing these concepts in training, the war in Ukraine is showing what it looks like for real. Both Ukrainian and NATO officials have said that mobility, redundancy, and survivability in command and control are becoming essential to the fight as Russian forces target high-value command centers. events.title: Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis
events.summary: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead. And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas. A marred reputation One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea. It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer. Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom. After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful . One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country. The consequences of controversy When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself. Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat. Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries. Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. Regardless, with Nvidia’s reputation marred and its future shrouded in uncertainty, once loyal customers may be more willing to explore alternative providers. There are certainly plenty to choose from. Amid a surge in custom AI chips from the likes of Broadcom, Marvel, and others, Nvidia’s main advantage wasn’t so much technological as it was simply considered a safe bet. AMD is the most obvious winner here. As we reported earlier this year , the House of Zen’s GPU tech has already surpassed Nvidia’s, at least on paper. What’s more, the company has a long and unblemished relationship serving the US government. AMD’s chips now power two of the Department of Energy’s three largest and most sensitive supercomputers. Meanwhile, hyperscalers with sufficient cashflow – think Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta – may seek to insulate themselves from Huang’s fallout by investing more heavily in homegrown silicon and offering it to customers. Then there's the threat from the man himself. Huang's ambitions and influence are such that he's unlikely to fade into obscurity. He may disappear from the spotlight while things blow over, but it’s a pretty sure bet that he’ll pop up at a new company eventually, and will still have enough sway to poach some of Nvidia’s top engineers. ®

events.title: SA gives green light for gas to help power future data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA government gives green light for gas to help power future data centres The proposed data centre at Bundey in SA's Mid North would require up to 800 megawatts of electricity to operate. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) South Australia's energy minister says he is "absolutely fine" for gas-generated power to be used to help supply energy to proposed AI data centres across the state. The SA Greens leader says it is a "total backflip" by the state government. Plans are underway for at least four major data centres in SA. The South Australian government has been accused of doing a "backflip" by allowing gas-generated power to be used to supply energy for proposed AI data centres. Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis has told the ABC that he was "absolutely fine" with gas being used to help run the new large-scale centres that are proposed in various regional locations around the state. "We support the idea of gas use to firm data centres the same way we support the idea of gas firming our renewable energy right now," Mr Koutsantonis said. The government's own Data Centre Strategy, released just under five months ago, focused on the promotion of the state's renewable energy sector. That strategy document stated: "South Australia can produce the clean energy needed, at scale and on time, to power the artificial intelligence revolution". But Mr Koutsantonis said that data centres needed large amounts of energy continuously, and that gas could be used to "firm" up or guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres "if the sun stops shining or wind stops blowing". Tom Koutsantonis says gas would guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke ) As part of the strategy, new data centres would be required to supply their own power. Developer Quantum DC, who yesterday announced it was pausing its plans for a 1,200-megawatt data centre at Tungkillo , had previously estimated about 20 per cent of the energy it needed would be supplied by a gas power station to be built on a section of its 220-hectare Adelaide Hills block. The company had proposed that the rest of the centre's electricity requirement would be supplied by renewables. Apart from Tungkillo, plans are underway for at least three other major data centres in SA. Australian company Iren proposed a $10 billion 800MW facility at Bundey, near Robertstown in the state's Mid North, while AI giant Firmus previously announced plans for data centres near Tailem Bend and Port Augusta. Kirsty Bevan says using gas is a step backwards. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) Conservation Foundation of SA chief executive Kirsty Bevan said the use of gas to supply energy to SA's data centres would be a "step backwards" for the government and the climate. "South Australia has led the nation on renewable energy and is aiming for 100 per cent net renewable electricity by 2027, but that progress could be undermined by proposals to lock in more gas," she said. Ms Bevan said using gas would also be ignoring "community expectations". "With energy storage and other backup technologies available to support grid reliability, expanding gas supply for data centres and AI infrastructure is a step backwards," she said. When asked generally about the potential environmental impacts of using gas for data centres, Mr Koutsantonis said: "Well if you don't let them use gas, they'll use diesel or they'll use coal." Robert Simms is urging the SA government to reconsider its position. ( ABC News: Tony Hill ) SA Greens leader Rob Simms said green-lighting gas projects was a major step away from the government's previous policy. "This is outrageous," Mr Simms said. "We don't need more dirty gas here." "It's a total backflip from where the government was just a few months ago when they gave an assurance to the people of South Australia that these data centres would be self-sufficient, they'd be reliant on renewables." Mr Simms urged the government to reconsider its position, and proposed a moratorium on the construction of data centres in SA. In a statement, an SA government spokesperson said the Greens' suggestion of a policy backflip was "nonsensical". "Allowing large new energy demand without requiring it to be matched by new firmed renewable energy, as suggested by the Greens, would be a recipe for a more expensive and less reliable system," the spokesperson said. Political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development , and united in the upper house to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres.

events.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
events.summary: Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself . Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios. Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including: What will the investigations uncover? Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences. Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee. Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public. Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it. Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter. Who takes the permanent role as CEO? CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally and we are big fans of her strategically," tech bull Dan Ives wrote Thursday in a research note. Prediction markets point to Nvidia hyperscaling tech exec Ian Buck as the the leading candidate, but the political ramifications of Nvidia's position in the global economy may demand someone with more experience with geopolitics. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook, whom Ives also floated, but Kalshi traders rate that as a 1 in 25 shot. Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble? Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars — and Huang is at the center of that vast flywheel, Axios' Zachary Basu writes . Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says. "This Nvidia story is going to take a little air out of the balloon for the Anthropic IPO," he says. The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips: "The company was never the source of AI demand. It has been supplying the capacity to meet that demand," which remains "enormous," he wrote today. Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry? Competitors like AMD, Alphabet and Intel could benefit if chips customers are soured on working with Nvidia. "When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: did the clients sign with the banker — or with the bank? Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market," writes Mark Malek, CIO at Siebert Financial. What's the floor for Nvidia's stock? Nvidia shares were down another 5.7% just before 3pm Thursday and are now down 27% over the last month, having lost about $1 trillion in value. "With this kind of leadership uncertainty, it's very difficult to predict where shares go over the next several trading sessions," writes Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. "Sometimes huge news catalysts like this take all technicals out of the equation." The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang? Elon Musk has already hinted he could hire the former Nvidia chief as he moves toward a possible merger of SpaceX and Tesla . But it'll be hard for anyone to hire Huang unless and until the FBI probe in particular is resolved. The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

events.title: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
events.summary: Save and Invest Nvidia is buying back shares—here's what stock buybacks mean for investors Save and Invest What higher for longer interest rates mean for your investments Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Save and Invest My 401(k) fully vests this month—why my work anniversary is worth thousands Work Most job seekers don't ask this important question in interviews—but they should Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6. It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership. "The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable." While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says. Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says. In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy. When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management. Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?" If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount. "If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs." Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says. And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability. "Did Nvidia's prospects change as a result of [Huang's resignation]? There's no definitive answer for that," he says. Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund's fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. Even companies that have successfully replaced their founders, such as Apple and Microsoft , have failed to grow as quickly as under original leadership, he says. Investors will have to weigh the risk that Nvidia will lag without Huang at the helm against the firm's still impressive growth projections — the company will report third-quarter fiscal year earnings results on Nov. 17 — and their long-term belief in the firm's position as a top supplier of microchips that power AI. "One thing we do know is that AI demand hasn't changed," Hainlin says. events.title: Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang
events.summary: Whether she was a spy, a fixer, or just a paramour of Jensen Huang, the name Alice Huang (no relation) has roiled the business world this week following reports that the two were having an affair. The revelation snowballed into Jensen’s shocking resignation Wednesday. Now come reports that officials are looking into other companies Alice was working with. Bloomberg reported , based on an anonymous source, that the Department of Justice is running multiple probes into Nvidia . One is focused on antitrust issues and two others are focused on Megaspeed—where Alice Huang was a former top executive—and Super Micro Computer . Separately, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in alleged efforts to smuggle Supermicro hardware laced with Nvidia’s red-hot GPUs into China. It is unclear whether that probe is tied to smuggling cases already brought in the U.S. or Asia. Neither Jensen Huang, Nvidia, nor Supermicro have been formally charged with any wrongdoing. Supermicro stock tumbled 12% after U.S. markets opened this morning. The company did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.  Thus far, much of the speculation about Jensen Huang’s catastrophic downfall as the leader of Nvidia has centered on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that reportedly became one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Southeast Asia. But Supermicro, the San Jose server maker run by Charles Liang, Jensen Huang’s friend of three decades and an important partner to Nvidia, has been in under the microscope regarding export-control compliance and is being pulled along with Nvidia. Fortune has reported on the Supermicro case since before federal agents arrested its co-founder in March, and that reporting shows a company with a documented track record of governance and compliance failures. Despite its history, Supermicro has remained in lockstep with Nvidia. Liang and Jensen have shared the stage together at Computex in Taiwan, where Jensen was photographed in 2024 with Alice at a cocktail bar. In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with allegedly routing about $2.5 billion in servers laced with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China through a Southeast Asian front company. Bloomberg later reported the front company is OBON, a Bangkok-based AI infrastructure firm, which has not been charged. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme.  Liaw, who immediately resigned his executive and board roles at Supermicro following his arrest, has pleaded not guilty. His trial was pushed to March 2027 after Liaw’s lawyers told the judge in his case that subpoenas issued to Supermicro could be material to Liaw’s defense. Nelson Boxer, Liaw’s attorney, declined to comment. One of Liaw’s co-defendants in the smuggling case, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October, including to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app from his phone on the day of the arrests. Sun’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment, and it’s unclear if Sun has a cooperation agreement with the government.  There is no public evidence so far that the Supermicro and Megaspeed cases are directly connected but there are mounting threads. Thursday, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a statement noting that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had initiated investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang and in doing so sought information from Supermicro. Supermicro only offered “limited cooperation,” Singaporean authorities said. In a July 2025 meeting, Singapore officials raised this with U.S. authorities and asked for their assistance in getting Supermicro’s cooperation and have repeated the request “on several occasions” to the Department of Justice and the FBI.  “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement reads. Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Supermicro’s export-control problems did not start with Liaw’s arrest, Fortune ’s reporting has found. In 2006, the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai, mirroring the basic scheme prosecutors alleged in the Liaw case.  Liaw himself has been through the crisis wringer before. He left Supermicro in 2018 amid a board-led investigation tied to Supermicro’s Nasdaq delisting and an SEC probe of its accounting, which ended with a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned as a consultant in May 2021, became a full-time employee, and rejoined the board in December 2023.  In 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research accused Supermicro of accounting manipulation and export-control failures and the company denied the allegations. Ernst & Young then resigned as auditor mid-audit, saying it could no longer rely on management’s representations. A special committee recommended in December 2024 that Supermicro replace CFO David Weigand and the company agreed to do so “immediately .” The company didn’t name a successor until October.  As Fortune has reported, the Liaw indictment describes thousands of nonworking dummy servers staged in warehouses to fool auditors, contractors using hair dryers to peel off serial-number labels, and a compliance auditor who was off-site allegedly enjoying “entertainment” paid for by another company during an inspection. It also shows how the alleged scheme fed directly into Nvidia’s supply pipeline. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly told the front company that “the only way” to get Nvidia to commit B200 chip allocations was to create monthly forecasts. Nvidia is not accused of wrongdoing in the Liaw indictment.  After Liaw’s arrest, Supermicro’s board opened its own investigation, overseen by independent director Scott Angel and former audit committee chair Tally Liu (no relation to Liang’s wife and co-founder Sara Liu). In August, Supermicro said that probe found no evidence that current senior management knew about the alleged scheme to diver the chips. The investigation resulted in an unspecified number of terminations in sales, business development, and technical support, Supermicro said at the time, for failure to follow policies or the code of conduct. Supermicro has also disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls, along with subpoenas or inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities. Through all that has beleaguered Supermicro, the company’s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast. This will all become a test for Supermicro’s new CFO, Mark Long, a former Western Digital finance chief who took over from Weigand last month and reports to Liang. events.title: Meet Colette Kress, the finance chief steering Nvidia through its first CEO transition
events.summary: Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia, has been named interim CEO. Nvidia Nvidia has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned. Huang exited as Nvidia's board probed a foreign intelligence effort and his alleged affairs. Kress, seen as a potential successor, previously held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft. Nvidia's longtime finance chief Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as a widening scandal brings Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure to an end. Kress's appointment on Thursday follows Huang's resignation , which the board said was effective immediately. The board said it is initiating a search for a permanent CEO and will "consider internal and external candidates." Nvidia's share price dropped more than 10% in premarket trading after announcing Huang's resignation. Huang stepped down after Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." He also admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a memo. The New York Times reported that Huang had romantic relationships with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — whom US intelligence officials identified as a suspected Chinese spy — as well as Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia employee who served as vice president of healthcare. Insiders and analysts had previously pointed to Kress as a likely successor to Huang, citing her visibility among shareholders. She has worked at Nvidia for 13 years, joining in September 2013 and helping to lead the company's finances through the AI boom. "Nvidia's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in a statement on Thursday. Kress is one of Nvidia's most influential executives As Nvidia's chief financial officer, Kress is one of its most public-facing and influential executives, and she'll lead the coming earnings call on November 17. She took home about $14.3 million in total compensation last fiscal year, according to the company's annual filing. She also speaks at conferences and investor meetings, laying out the company's key strategies. Kress has previously spoken about how AI agents will be the next big driver of Nvidia's business. "Agentic AI is really where it is getting work done, work that can augment the work of many employees, many of our folks at home," Kress said at the Consumer Electronics Show in January. "All of these things are really important as we think going forward. Those transitions are going to take some time, and they're all occurring and creating an exponential growth in terms of our compute." As finance chief, Kress has also played a key role in Nvidia's partnerships with cloud giants, startups, and other compute partners. She previously said at CES that the AI boom has "created an exponential growth in the need for the amount of compute that's necessary." Kress "has built enormous credibility inside and outside the company; she now runs the most important one in the AI Revolution," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote in a note to investors. Nvidia has a flat leadership structure The board also announced that Harvey C. Jones will serve as its first chair. Jones, a semiconductor industry veteran, has served on Nvidia's board since the company's founding and is also a managing partner at Square Wave Ventures. Huang maintained a flat leadership structure with as many as 60 direct reports, and said he wanted to keep working for as long as possible, which complicated succession planning. Kress reported directly to Huang , Business Insider previously reported. Prior to joining Nvidia, Kress held finance positions at Cisco and Microsoft. events.title: Master carver to engrave crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball sold as mementos
events.summary: People who find themselves at the site of the iconic New Year's Eve ball drop can purchase one of the 5,280 Waterford crystals from the Constellation Ball that dropped in New York City last year in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026 Dropped in Times Square on New Year’s Eve, the Constellation Ball was created with 5,280 Waterford crystals that incorporated three different designs to represent life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026. On Thursday, people can buy one of those crystals and get their names engraved on it as a memento. They will be replaced with new crystals to ring in 2027 with a theme yet to be announced. It takes about three days to make each crystal by hand for the roughly 12-foot (3.7-meter) geodesic sphere that weighs 12,350 pounds (5,602 kilograms). The process involves the design, molding, kilning and the finishing of each crystal. Waterford, a longtime luxury crystal brand from Ireland, has designed the New Year’s Eve ball’s crystals for over 25 years. Some new crystals are swapped in every year. Richard White, a master cutter for Waterford, flew to New York City to engrave the crystals that vary in size from 1.5 to 4 inches in diameter. White will use a small electronic pen with a diamond tip to engrave names on the small crystal pieces Thursday. “To be actually here and to be up close, personal with it, is a real excitement for me,” White said of seeing the completed ball. Delfin Ortiz, general manager and senior vice president of One Times Square, the 26-story building from which the annual ball drops, said the crystals are part of “tomorrow's history.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Microsoft Outlook outage stretches on for hours Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE A New Year’s Eve ball was first dropped in Times Square in 1907. Built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr, the 700-pound (318-kilogram), 5-foot (1.52-meter) diameter ball was made of iron and wood and featured 100 25-watt light bulbs. Nine versions of the ball have been featured in the century-plus since that first celebration. The only years no ball drop occurred were 1942 and 1943, when the city instituted a nightly “dimout” during World War II to protect itself from attacks. Crowds instead celebrated the new year with a moment of silence followed by chimes rung from the base of One Times Square. One Times Square began offering crystals for purchase last year, though Thursday marks the first time they will be engraved. events.title: Only four government ministers have saved money this year. Here's who
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Only four ministers have achieved net savings this year, budget papers show Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher have flagged further savings in the mid-year budget update. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Four federal ministers have achieved net savings in their portfolios this financial year, according to ABC analysis of the May budget. The most significant savings were in the infrastructure portfolio. The government is searching for savings ahead of the mid-year budget update, but has not committed to a net save. Only four out of more than 20 government ministers have managed to save more than they have spent this year, pointing to challenges across the board as the cabinet works to rein in spending. Stung by the accusation from the opposition and some commentators that the federal budget is worsening inflation and fuelling interest rate hikes, ministers have indicated they are searching for fresh savings ahead of December's budget update. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has indicated the government is looking "across the board" for savings, but has declined to commit to a "net" saving — that is, big enough to offset any new spending. A net save of $8.2 billion was achieved in the May budget, measured over the full five years of budget forecasts. But the government failed to achieve a net save for this financial year, when inflation pressure is most acute. Looking at this year alone, the government spent $8.7 billion more than it saved. It also raised an extra $2.2 billion in revenue, meaning the budget was $6.5 billion worse off overall. Only Infrastructure Minister Catherine King, Education Minister Jason Clare, Agriculture Minister Julie Collins and Treasurer Jim Chalmers achieved net savings for the 2026-27 financial year, according to an ABC analysis of budget papers. Of these, only Ms King's portfolio had substantial net savings with $1.3 billion overall, mostly from the decision not to proceed with programs including Inland Rail. The largest net spend for 2026-27 was Health Minister Mark Butler, whose total includes measures the government describes as "unavoidable", including the listing of new PBS medicines and a major hospitals deal. This was despite some savings from the NDIS and the private health insurance rebate for older Australians, which is yet to win support in parliament. Defence Minister Richard Marles and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, whose responsibilities include Services Australia, both spent in excess of $1 billion. Catherine King achieved the largest net save this year, with nearly $1 billion. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The government has offered few specifics about areas it will target for mid-year budget savings, but Senator Gallagher confirmed last week the public service would be subject to "belt tightening". The Albanese government has overseen a significant expansion in public service headcount, from 173,558 before it came to office to 217,256 as of May, spread across multiple portfolios. The largest individual increases were the National Disability Insurance Agency (more than 5,000 new staff) and Services Australia (more than 4,000). Labor fought former Liberal leader Peter Dutton's bid to reverse that increase during the 2025 election campaign, but has made quiet moves of its own to contain public service spending since then. Peter Dutton campaigned unsuccessfully to return public service numbers to their pre-pandemic levels. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) In 2024, it opted not to give departments any extra money to cover the wage rises in a new pay agreement worth 11.2 per cent over three years. That effectively required departments to find 11.2 per cent of savings elsewhere. Several subsequently offered redundancy rounds last financial year, with at least 1,500 redundancies confirmed but an exhaustive tally not yet available. But an ABC analysis of budget papers show departmental staffing costs still increased by $792 million last year, only partly offset by a $687 million reduction in "supplier" costs, such as consultants. Annual reports indicate further cost overruns are likely. Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation. Earlier this year, ministers asked all departments and agencies to identify 5 per cent of their resourcing that was "low priority". Senator Gallagher emphasised at the time that this was meant as a savings shortlist, not as a 5 per cent overall cut.

events.title: David Jones closures present 'unique opportunity' for big shopping centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Economic pain of outer suburbs accelerated demise of David Jones, experts say Economic pain felt in outer suburban areas could have fast-tracked the problems that overtook David Jones. ( ABC News: Taryn Southcombe ) David Jones is closing 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the majority to close in metropolitan outer suburbs. Property analyst Howard Penny says outer suburbs were disproportionately feeling mortgage stress. According to retail expert Gary Mortimer, a changing business model is forcing major suburban centres to adapt to survive. Acute economic pain being felt in the outer suburbs may have accelerated the demise of David Jones, according to property and retail experts. The 188-year-old shopping giant announced on Wednesday that it would close 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the vast majority being in metropolitan outer suburban areas. Among those are stores in areas like Hornsby, Parramatta and Campbelltown in Sydney, Maribyrnong and Glen Waverley in Melbourne, and Robina on the Gold Coast. Howard Penny says retail challenges reflect negative consumer impacts in emerging areas. ( ABC News ) Howard Penny is the head of Real Estate and Infrastructure Research for Australia and New Zealand at Citigroup. He said that was a symptom of the financial strain in those areas after five interest rate hikes this year. S&P Global Ratings data this week revealed that households in some outer suburbs in Sydney, Melbourne and south-east Queensland are more than twice as likely to be experiencing mortgage stress than the national average. "It's new home buyers, it's young families, et cetera, and naturally the areas where these types of consumers are, are in the newer areas further out in the cities," Mr Penny said. The announcement has also raised questions about how large suburban shopping centres will fare losing a large anchor tenant. Nine of the stores that are closing are in Westfield shopping centres, owned by Scentre Group. Scentre had offered David Jones discounted rents to continue trading, after the department store stopped paying rent in September. Howard Penny said there was likely to be a short-term impact on Scentre Group, but that was unlikely to threaten the viability of its shopping centres in the outer suburbs. "Although we are, in the short term, a little concerned as to the short-term impacts on income and rent due to the disruption, in the medium term, we remain optimistic, and we believe that in 18 months, these shopping centres may actually look even stronger on the back of this," he said. After Wednesday's news, Scentre Group chief executive Eliott Rusanow was similarly confident. "Our business is practically full, with occupancy at 99.8 per cent and strong demand for space," Mr Rusanow said in a statement. "We have a unique opportunity at 17 Westfield destinations to introduce and grow local and international brands and experiences that our customers want." Gary Mortimer says the fall of David Jones comes as major suburban centres shift. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Gary Mortimer is a professor at the Queensland University of Technology who specialises in retail and marketing. He said the closures represent the changing business model of major suburban centres. "A big centre once might have included an anchor tenant, be that a department store, and possibly a discount department store and a supermarket," Professor Mortimer said. "Today, those centres have changed. Those centres are now underpinned by precincts: health precincts, services precincts, libraries, gyms, childcare, car wash facilities and a whole wide range of experiences and offers." He said the changes in the composition and socio-economic pressures in outer suburban areas require shopping centres to adapt to survive. "As the demography of those suburbs changes and the centre now is better representative of a Kmart, Target, Big W discount department store than a traditional department store, I think they'll have no problems filling that space," Dr Mortimer said.

events.title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
events.summary: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement. The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level. In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode. In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question. Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains. The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode. Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models. The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens. On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out. In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform. events.title: I'm a millionaire in California who supports taxing the rich. I'm disappointed Prop. 40 was rejected — people will suffer.
events.summary: Scott Ellis is a Silicon Valley-based millionaire who supports the taxation of the wealthy. Patriotic Millionaires Scott Ellis is a millionaire in Silicon Valley who supported a proposed wealth tax on billionaires . After the proposition was rejected by Californians this week, Ellis was disappointed but not surprised. He said he's glad it's started important conversations about wealth, and hopes for future efforts. This as-told-to essay is based on conversations with Scott Ellis, a 56-year-old millionaire who lives in Silicon Valley, about Proposition 40, California's proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax , which was rejected by California voters on November 9. Ellis is a member of Patriotic Millionaires, a group of wealthy Americans who advocate for a fair tax system, a livable wage, and equal access to political power. The following has been edited for length and clarity. (Editor's note: This article was first published in January 2026 and updated on November 12, 2026.) I'm disappointed, but I'm not surprised. The reality is that if people spend over $300 million opposing something and people spend about $30 million in favor, you get outspent by 10:1. That does matter. It was a big task to get it on the ballot in the first place, and I was really delighted that it was, because it at least started us on what I think is the right conversation: Let's talk about wealth. How much wealth do people have? Is there such a thing as too much? What should we do when people have too much? I've been talking about wealth and excessive wealth for a number of years. I feel like a few years ago, people were kind of humoring me. They're listening much more seriously now. There are conversations in my group chats with friends about wealth and wealth taxes. The conditions that led to this in the first place haven't suddenly gone away, and they will get worse. The massive federal funding cuts are working their way through states and local communities. This was on the ballot because of the health cost implications. Millions of people are going to lose their healthcare; there will be more suffering. There are tens of millions of voters in California who don't have a billion dollars. They're the ones who chose to do this, and I hope they're watching. I think it should be interesting for people to see how the wealthy responded. When I think about my concern about excessive wealth and how it distorts democracy and undermines our society, you couldn't ask for a clearer example than Sergey Brin spending over $100 million in one state election. The question I ask everybody is, "Are you worried?" I'm worried about the health of our economy, our society, our democracy. But I'm going to be fine — I've been very financially fortunate. I'm worried about you, your healthcare, and your kids. I'm very glad that this effort was made, and I hope that additional efforts will be made in the future . I came out here for business school because I wanted to be at Stanford, and because you could play golf during the winter. Now I love it here. It has nothing to do with taxes ; taxes have never been anywhere on our list of criteria for deciding where to live. I want to live where my family is and love the weather, the jobs, and the dynamism. Taxes are the price that we pay to live in a civil society. We have to do this together. There are examples all around the world of the power of effective government, and just like anything else, government needs to be funded. We should make it effective and efficient. I'm proud to pay the taxes I pay. I should pay taxes that are higher than other people because I have more wealth than other people — that makes sense. My wife and I achieved financial success in our careers A lot of our financial success has been due to my wife's success, as well as mine at the beginning of our careers. I went to Harvard undergrad, worked at McKinsey for three years, and then went to Stanford. I then worked at Hewlett-Packard for almost eight years. In 2007, my wife was a VP at Yahoo, and we had two small kids. I looked at my boss's job and the CEO's job, and decided I didn't ever want those roles. I thought, "Uh-oh, I'm on this ladder, and it's not really where I want to go." Ultimately, my wife and I decided that I would step back and be the stay-at-home parent. My wife continued her career, and she's been very successful in consumer internet at Yahoo, Google, and Pinterest. I developed an interest in social issues in college I studied poverty, urban America, housing, transportation, and sociology in college, and started thinking more about questions like: What does fairness look like? What does justice look like? What would it look like to build a great society? I got busy pursuing my career, meeting my wife, and raising our kids, but as time passed and we progressed in our careers, I got back into thinking about how we help others around us. I did a bunch of volunteer work in different contexts, eventually becoming the COO and then the CSO of a nonprofit called New Teacher Center, which does intensive mentoring programs for new teachers. Since 2012, I've started and run several nonprofits in the education space, and advised almost 200 individuals and organizations on things like strategy, finance, operations, and culture. I'm also really focused on addressing excessive wealth and its impact on society and thinking about a future vision for American democracy, which is how I came to Patriotic Millionaires , an organization of wealthy Americans who advocate for higher taxes on wealthy people like ourselves, a higher minimum wage, and a broader distribution of political power across our society. I've been struck by the massive accumulation of wealth In recent years, I've been struck by the massive accumulation of wealth enabled by the consumer internet space, globalization, and the structure of the finance industry. It's different from what it used to be in the '80s and '90s; this is a whole new ballgame. More recently, I've been looking around Silicon Valley at all these people who are so incredibly wealthy, talented, and successful, and realizing how few of them are thinking about choosing to build a better society together. They're excited about starting new companies and raising new funds, but these are all people who have more money than they could ever spend, and their next goal is to generate even more money, mainly for people who already have more money than they could ever spend. Meanwhile, 10% of our society is in poverty. It really feels unfair and wrong, and we can do better. events.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
events.summary: Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results. Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research. Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically. Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult. Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords. Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular. Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets. “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.” Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals. Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers. The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents. This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic. events.title: House Foreign Affairs chair: 'Very likely' chips restrictions make it into defense bill
events.summary: Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., talks with reporters outside the US Capitol. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The chair of the House committee overseeing export controls says chip guardrails in a coming defense bill are likely. Rep. Brian Mast cast doubt on whether ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang knew where his company's chips ended up. Mast is also pressing for Huang to testify soon about the scandal, Politico reported . House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said Thursday it is "very likely" a group of bills that would impose new guardrails on exports of advanced US chips to China will make it into a must-pass annual defense bill this year. The Florida Republican told reporters that the controversy involving Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's CEO earlier Thursday after revelations he had an extramarital relationship with a potential Chinese spy, has added momentum to the effort. "If he doesn't know who he's in bed with, he doesn't know where all the chips are going either, and we know that for a fact," said Mast, whose committee oversees export control policy. Lawmakers are discussing a trio of chip export control bills for the annual defense package, including the Chip Security Act , a measure that would crack down on smuggling by requiring advanced chips to contain location-verification mechanisms. Two other measures are in the mix as well. One would tighten restrictions on chip-making equipment and push foreign countries to match US restrictions. The other would give Congress a chance to review licenses for advanced sales of AI chips. President Donald Trump has been cool to the idea of tighter chip export restrictions and previously signed off on deals that allowed Nvidia to sell more of its high-end chips to China. Mast also said Thursday that he still has confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing growing scrutiny over his handling of the Trump administration's chips policy. But he declined to say the same for a key Lutnick deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, who heads the Commerce Department bureau in charge of export controls. Asked if he has confidence in Kessler, chief of the Bureau of Industry and Security, Mast said: "I'm not going to answer that yes or no. It's something that — you know, he's been most granular on this level and a lot of things about where chips can and can't be sold to. That's been more of an argumentative dynamic." He also said he "absolutely" wants to investigate BIS' role in the Nvidia controversy. A BIS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Mast is pressing for Huang to testify soon about the scandal. "We want to see him basically in a week," Mast said. "Sooner rather than later." He is in talks with the former CEO's team, but didn't rule out a subpoena. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "If negotiations shut off and we don't think they're in good faith, OK, fine, do that," he said. "I'll just subpoena you for the next day. No big deal." events.summary: Microsoft said its Outlook email service is currently experiencing an outage, preventing both business and consumer users from accessing their inboxes. The issue was initially flagged as affecting the U.S. and the Americas, and later expanded to affect “any region.” Microsoft hasn’t given a specific cause, but said that it was providing updates in its admin center , which wasn’t reachable at the time of publication. In a post on X for users who can’t access the admin center, Microsoft said some of its infrastructure was experiencing “elevated load,” and that it was “redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load.” In its latest update, Microsoft attributed this incident to “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” for reasons it did not explain. Microsoft said it continues to investigate the outage. Microsoft says its video conferencing tool Teams, file sharing platform SharePoint, and its AI tool Copilot are also unavailable. The company says its Defender XDR security system is also affected by the outage. Consumers are also unable to access their OneDrive storage, Office (for the web), and several other Microsoft services during the ongoing outage. TechCrunch will reach out to Microsoft for comment, as soon as our own email service has resumed. The company’s last major incident was in September , when a days-long outage hit Microsoft 365, its online productivity suite that includes Outlook. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service. events.title: Salmon deaths at 'eye-watering' levels in Macquarie Harbour
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mortality data for salmon farms in Macquarie Harbour revealed after RTI documents release Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour. ( Huon ) It's been revealed that almost 2,000 tonnes of salmon died in Macquarie Harbour over a 15-month period. Salmon Tasmania says it equates to about 8 per cent of fish farmed there during that time. The EPA is yet to issue new licences for companies to continue operating in the harbour. Almost 2,000 tonnes of farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour on Tasmania's west coast, new data shows. The Environment Protection Authority's (EPA) mortality data was obtained by conservation group Environment Tasmania, which submitted the Right to Information (RTI) request in December last year. But it took until this week for the information to be made public after salmon companies sought reviews of the EPA's decision to release the data, as they are entitled to do under RTI laws. The EPA regulates 10 salmon leases in the harbour. ( Supplied: Tassal ) The data shows a total of 1,907 tonnes of farmed salmon died in the harbour between October 2024 and December 2025. "Salmon has no place in Macquarie Harbour," Environment Tasmania campaigner Jess Coughlan said. The mortality data was obtained by Environment Tasmania. ( Supplied: Tassal ) Environment Tasmania said this would infer about 15 per cent of the total maximum haul had died. But Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said the maximum tonnage could not be used to determine a "mortality rate". "Mortality is measured by counting the number of fish that died, not their weight," Dr Whittington said. The new figures come after a separate RTI in late 2024 showed a total of 1,149 tonnes of salmon had died over a seven-month period between September 2023 and March 2024. Monthly data on salmon deaths doesn't show locations Since 2025, the EPA has released monthly data showing the total tonnage of mortality among salmon farms across the state, but it is not broken down by location. Macquarie Harbour, which is the only habitat for the endangered Maugean skate , makes up only a small portion of the salmon industry's annual production across Tasmania. Dr Whittington said mortality was "unfortunately part of all livestock farming". He said there was no standard "mortality rate" for farmed salmon. Salmon Tasmania CEO John Whittington said mortality was measured by numbers of fish not weight. ( ABC News: Madeleine Rojahn ) "As with other forms of farming, survival rates or losses vary by year, location and season," Dr Whittington said. "Salmon growers employ a range of strategies to maintain fish health and maximise survivability, including selective breeding, vaccination, specialised diets and growing fish larger on land so they spend less time at sea." The new RTI data did not include details about what caused the deaths of the salmon. Salmon Tasmania said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused other mass mortalities. ( ABC News: Sophie Zoellner ) But Dr Whittington said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused mass mortality in salmon pens in other parts of the state. As such, he said the industry had not applied to use the antibiotic florfenicol in Macquarie Harbour. Ms Coughlan said there had been "near complete opacity surrounding operations where disease and mortality are concerned" in the harbour. The EPA regulates salmon farming at 10 leases within Macquarie Harbour. However, the environmental licences issued to the three salmon companies that operate there expired almost a year ago. A map showing the location of salmon farm licences in Macquarie Harbour. ( ABC News: Magie Khameneh ) Prior to the expiration, the companies applied for new licences, meaning they can continue to operate pending the outcome of their applications. The EPA told the ABC it was continuing to assess the environmental conditions in Macquarie Harbour to inform future regulatory decisions about salmon farming in the region. events.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
events.summary: With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms. In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc . But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products. The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028. "I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said. Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance. "My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot." All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio. Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you." They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir , while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants. Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power , and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority ." At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement ," he wrote in his shareholder letter. It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process. Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company. He told CNBC: " If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir . Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection." In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough . "And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet. Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight. Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®
