events.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs B ritain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry. The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech. The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control. The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology. Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms , concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits. Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes. The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale. Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: I've cooked over 1,300 recipes from Ina Garten. Here are 10 of my favorites for Thanksgiving.
events.summary: Over the past few years, I've made all of Ina Garten's recipes. These are my favorite picks for a perfect Thanksgiving dinner. Trent Pheifer I've made more than 1,300 Ina Garten recipes. These are my favorite recipes for Thanksgiving .  Garten's make-ahead turkey gravy and autumn sangria are some of my favorites. Her Parmesan smashed potatoes, shaved Brussels sprouts with pancetta, and popovers are great sides. If Ina Garten's taught me anything, it's that a solid game plan is the key to a successful Thanksgiving dinner . I may go overboard by planning my dishes, timeline, and grocery list in early October, but my meal prep runs like a well-oiled machine every year. Fortunately, I have you covered when it comes to planning a menu . I've cooked all of the Barefoot Contessa's 1,300-plus recipes , and here are some of my absolute favorites for Thanksgiving dinner. Her autumn sangria packs a punch. Trent Pheifer " Cook Like a Pro ," page 24 When guests arrive, I love to kick things off with a seasonal cocktail . So many sangrias can be cloyingly sweet, but Garten's autumnal recipe is a perfectly balanced mix of cabernet sauvignon, apple cider, apple and pear brandy, and cinnamon syrup. Even better, you can make it days in advance to let the flavors meld. Be careful, though, as the Barefoot Contessa's drinks pack a punch. Making a turkey roulade is a good alternative to carving a whole bird. Trent Pheifer " Barefoot Contessa Back to Basics ," page 109 I'd always preferred dark-meat turkey until I tried this roulade. It's a deboned turkey breast packed with cranberry, sausage, and fig stuffing, then rolled, baked, and sliced. With this recipe, you don't need to carve an entire bird as your guests arrive. If you are choosing to go with a full bird, I'd suggest Ina's Accidental Turkey — the dry-brined method is a game changer! Her make-ahead turkey gravy with onions and sage is fabulous. Trent Pheifer " Make It Ahead ," page 103 I joke that I make extra of this gravy to sip on while making the rest of the Thanksgiving meal — it's that good. It can be made days in advance and then be rewarmed with turkey drippings on the day of the big meal. Even without the drippings, it's a fabulous gravy. Garten's mushroom-and-leek bread pudding is packed with flavor. Trent Pheifer " Foolproof ," page 188 For years, I never fully appreciated the appeal of dressing or stuffing. Sure, it was good, but with so many delicious Thanksgiving sides, I often only grabbed the smallest portion of it. That changed when Garten introduced me to savory bread pudding — stuffing's moister, much more flavorful cousin. This mushroom-and-leek one is my favorite. Parmesan smashed potatoes are pretty easy to make. Trent Pheifer "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook," page 158 Garten's truffle mashed potatoes are an absolute favorite of mine, but her Parmesan smashed potatoes are my go-to when I'm planning to smother my spuds in gravy. The potatoes contain sour cream, which adds a nice tang as the Parmesan takes these to the next level. One big perk of this recipe is that it lets you skip the annoying task of peeling potatoes. Her shaved Brussels sprouts with pancetta are loaded with flavor. Trent Pheifer Food Network If you grew up in the '80s or '90s, there's a good chance you hated Brussels sprouts, which were almost always boiled and never delicious. Now, they're one of my favorite veggies, and nothing complements them better than a little bacon or pancetta and syrupy balsamic vinegar. For this recipe, I recommend using a food processor to quickly shred your sprouts. Popovers can be sweet or savory. Trent Pheifer "Parties," page 189 These popovers are impressively puffy and can skew sweet or savory — serve them with jam or gravy. The key is to get the popover pan as hot as possible before adding the batter — I usually heat the pan for 10 minutes rather than the two minutes Garten recommends. Maple-roasted butternut squash is a great side dish. Trent Pheifer " Barefoot Contessa Back to Basics ," page 158 I take back all the bad things I said about butternut squash when I was growing up. It makes for a dreamy side dish when paired with pancetta, maple syrup, and sage in this recipe. Skip pie and opt for pumpkin-mousse parfaits instead. Trent Pheifer "Barefoot Contessa at Home," page 180 Forget making pumpkin pie this year and instead prep this show-stopping, light-as-air treat. The ethereal pumpkin mousse layered with whipped cream and spicy, crunchy crumbled ginger cookies is the perfect cap to an otherwise heavy meal. Pecan squares are a good alternative to the classic pie. Trent Pheifer "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook," page 188 Pecan pie was a must at Thanksgiving until I discovered these. Garten swaps the pie dough for a shortbread crust and tops it with a chewy, crunchy pecan mixture with a hint of orange. Go ahead and gild the lily by dipping the squares in the optional chocolate. This recipe yields a lot of bars — I usually cut it in half and make the dessert in a 9-by-13-inch casserole dish. events.title: Australia defends climate record after Greta Thunberg's 'snail' swipe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chris Bowen seeks pragmatic consensus heading into final COP31 talks Chris Bowen rejects suggestions Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter has damaged its standing in the negotiations. ( Reuters: Murad Sezer ) Chris Bowen has rejected criticism of Australia's climate leadership over its continued coal and gas exports. The climate change and energy minister says countries must be realistic about the transition to cleaner energy. Negotiations at COP31 will intensify next week as Australia seeks agreement on electrification and climate finance. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has defended Australia's credibility as a global climate negotiator and signalled a pragmatic approach to securing a deal at COP31 amid pressure for a stronger international commitment to move away from fossil fuels. Mr Bowen has questioned why the Coalition sought to diminish Australia's role on the world stage and singled out Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for attacking expenses introduced during his own time as minister. "Does he want one lump of hypocrisy or two with his coffee?" Mr Bowen told the ABC in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at the summit, putting Mr Bowen at the centre of efforts to secure agreement between more than 190 countries on the next steps to tackle climate change. "My job is to steer consensus to the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow," he said. Anthony Albanese (right) and Chris Bowen have defended Australia's decision to expand coal and gas production. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) That task has become more complicated as momentum builds behind a renewed push for a plan to transition away from fossil fuels. Fossil fuel road map lacks consensus Despite efforts by Brazil and others to advance work on a global road map for moving away from coal, oil and gas, the COP31 agenda remains predominantly focused on electrification, adaptation and climate finance. Mr Bowen described the fossil fuels transition as a "challenging issue" and noted the failure to get consensus on fossil fuels at last year's COP showed the enthusiasm of some governments was no guarantee of a collective agreement. He said there was "good spirit" around the negotiations at this year's summit before adding there was a "long way to go", with talks to ramp up next week. Mr Bowen also drew a connection between the road-map push and Australia's efforts to accelerate global electrification, arguing that reducing the use of fossil fuels would depend heavily on replacing them with electricity. Australia rejects fossil fuel hypocrisy claims Australia's role at COP31 has brought with it scrutiny of the nation's continued expansion of coal and gas production, with environment campaigners arguing the country's domestic policies undermine its climate credibility. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has criticised the pace of Australia's climate policy. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Speaking overnight at the summit, activist Greta Thunberg said even a "snail" would agree Australia was moving too slowly on climate action. But Mr Bowen emphatically rejected suggestions that Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter had damaged its standing in the negotiations. He said other governments understood the practical challenges of reducing dependence on fossil fuels, including their continued reliance on Australian exports. Mr Bowen said the argument Australia's exports undermined its leadership on climate was not one that "survives contact with reality in a COP negotiation". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also defended the government's approach, arguing resource companies contributed substantial tax revenue used to fund public services. Coal and gas policies under scrutiny at COP31 Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has put the Pacific at the centre of his COP31 pitch, but Australia's continued expansion of coal and gas is drawing criticism from climate advocates. Asked why he did not directly reference fossil fuels in his speech at the opening of the COP31 leaders summit, Mr Albanese said "you could pick out any number of things" that were not in the short address. Electrification presents its own challenges Australia is championing a commitment to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. But the proposal has attracted criticism because it does not explicitly require the additional electricity to come from renewable sources. Mr Bowen said linking electrification exclusively to clean energy would be difficult to achieve.

events.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability H alf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe. It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability. An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious. Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one. The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it. First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration , will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job. Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed. Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors. Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive. Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
events.summary: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. events.title: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services
events.summary: The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org ® . Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website . events.title: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us | Moira Donegan
events.summary: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us At a time when individual men wield massive power, the ramifications of the Nvidia CEO’s affair could be enormous O ne of the reasons you want to distribute power and responsibility in powerful organizations and high-stakes enterprises is so that the narcissism or myopia of one man do not come to carry outsized consequences. When power is spread out across multiple people, it matters less if one of those people is prone to flattery, or in the midst of a midlife crisis, or perhaps just a bit stupid; the limits on his power become limits on the fallout of his character flaws. A broad distribution of authority also has the virtue of making any one man disposable, replaceable: if he turns out to have poor judgement or counterproductive preoccupations, he can be dispensed with, and his role can be filled anew with someone better suited to its responsibilities. But if one man becomes synonymous with a company – or a country – then untold numbers of other people live and die by that man’s decisions. And when his decisions are bad – petty, selfish, shortsighted, small-minded or dumb – then it is other people who will pay the price. And the price is often quite steep. Because we live in an era of massive inequality, tightly consolidated corporate leadership, and rule by a billionaire class with large egos and deficient dignity, the US economy is now experiencing one of the latter scenarios, in the form of Jensen Huang , a Silicon Valley billionaire who this week confessed to having an extramarital affair. This would be tacky and embarrassing for Huang on its own. But because Huang is the longtime CEO of Nvidia , one of the country’s largest companies and the manufacturer of advanced chip technology that is powering the US’s AI boom, his petty midlife crisis – the kind of small-minded narcissism that can usually be dispensed with in the form of a red sportscar, or indeed with one of the cheesy leather jackets that Huang is prone to wearing – is now a problem for the US economy, and potentially for national security. Because Huang’s mistress was not just any of the interchangeable young women that such men usually go for. This one happened to be a suspected Chinese spy. It’s unclear how much the woman, Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang – no relation – learned from her relationship with the tech billionaire, or how the information she may have gathered could undermine US economic and military interests. Alice Huang worked in television in China before becoming an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company and one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Megaspeed was under investigation by the US commerce department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips to China, which is banned from importing them by US law. (Megaspeed said it had offered to cooperate with the US government’s investigation but those offers went unanswered.) According to the New York Times, the investigation was abruptly halted last year after the general counsel for Nvidia, Jensen Huang’s company, intervened. Among other things, Jensen Huang is known for his close relationship with Donald Trump. On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to an affair, and his company announced that it would be launching an investigation into the incident. “The Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” which is perhaps a bit too hopeful. On Thursday, Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO. But the statement itself is a reflection of the depth of Huang’s control over the country. If you or I had endangered corporate secrets and state security in a flight of reckless, narcissistic frivolity, the way Huang may have done, then our employers would not be announcing the investigation while we kept our jobs. Nvidia’s stocks were down when the markets opened on Monday. They may well go down further still. And yet the scandal is fitting for our current era of Silicon Valley, in which loyalty to Donald Trump has gone from a strategic move by major tech companies to ensure favorable contract and regulatory terms to much more full-throated embrace of the ideology and style of the far right. Following the lead of its major male executives, the tech industry has become reckless and irresponsible, proud of itself for accelerating technologies it plainly claims to be unable to control, demanding investments in datacenters and government contracts from taxpayers whom it smugly brags about putting out of jobs, and flooding our aesthetic and informational worlds with low-grade slop that is frequently factually inaccurate, often dangerous for vulnerable users, and uncanny in its unpleasantness, bearing a creepy and inhuman sheen in its images and language.

events.title: After Jensen Huang is Howard Lutnick the prime target of national security inquiry?
events.summary: When questioning the motives of certain public leaders, the Roman orator Cicero was said to have used as a shorthand, “cui bono?” meaning, whose interests come first? That line rings true as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick falls under rapidly escalating bipartisan scrutiny over his role in the flow of Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy , yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations . Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was an executive, was suspected of funneling advanced chips to China for years, yet the U.S. government took little action. Many are now asking: Who knew what, and when? And why is this surfacing only now? We have already described Nvidia directors’ exposure to shareholder lawsuits over their own failures of oversight. Now the scrutiny is shifting to Washington. How did the U.S. government look past so grave a threat to national security for so long, and let these sales go on? As the reporting accumulates, all roads lead to one person, who by multiple accounts blocked action over the objections of fellow cabinet members and leading voices in both parties in Congress: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He is now squarely on the hot seat, and it grows hotter by the day as more information comes to light. Untangling the Truth of a Muddled Timeline Megaspeed has long been a major target of U.S. government focus amidst pervasive allegations that the Singapore-based data center company helped Chinese firms evade U.S. export controls on sensitive Nvidia chips. The Department of Commerce’s own agents began investigating Megaspeed , the Singapore firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China, in 2024, under the Biden Administration. After the change of administration but amidst the ongoing probe, The New York Times reported that in 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel emailed those agents directly, citing permission from Lutnick’s export-control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, with Commerce soon pausing its work on the investigation. That sparked many concerns even within the GOP, with respected Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton writing to Lutnick directly , urging Commerce to investigate Megaspeed more carefully. Still, Megaspeed never landed on the entity list, the blacklist kept by the Department of Commerce that cuts suspect firms off from American technology; even though other agencies repeatedly agreed on proposing to add Megaspeed to the list, with the Financial Times reporting that the State Department, Treasury Department, Energy Department and the Pentagon were pushing particularly aggressively to add Megaspeed to the entity list. Despite these entreaties, Lutnick’s Commerce Department was unmoved, steadfastly refusing to add a single company to the entity list for more than a year . Then came the memo. This spring, the New York Times reports , Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified assessment built on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. Its conclusion was as stark as can be: China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang and on America’s AI chips, and she had grown close to the Nvidia CEO. U.S. officials assessed that Beijing’s aims may have gone further, to steering Nvidia into pressing Washington for greater Chinese access to its most advanced chips. The memo went to a handful of senior officials before President Trump’s May trip to China, with Axios reporting that Lutnick was among those who received the memo directly. Perhaps not coincidentally, Jensen Huang was originally left off the delegation of business leaders traveling to China with Trump, before being added at the very last possible minute during an Alaska refueling stop . That same month, Reuters reported that Commerce had cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s. Perhaps even more alarmingly, but less widely known than the existence of the memo; Axios also reports that President Trump approved a crackdown on chip diversion to China no less than three times, in May, in August, and on Nov. 5, with even Elon Musk supportive, and that Lutnick and his deputies had resisted carrying out each order. As Maria Curi and Marc Caputo of Axios reported pithily , “One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick,” noting that virtually every other Administration official was supportive of these crackdowns. Just last week, after news of the Jensen Huang spy scandal broke, Axios reported that Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal, with virtually all other Admin officials siding with Bessent; yet Lutnick apparently continued to stall. Already, there has been speculation that the leaks over the last week that felled Huang came from sources within the Trump Administration, perhaps from within the National Security Council, who were frustrated at Lutnick pushing what they perceived to be pro-China policies, with many remarking about the suspicious timing of these leaks right after midterm elections, even though the original memo was circulated in May this year, six months ago. Lutnick Loses Cabinet Confidence and GOP Trust What makes this scrutiny so hot is who is turning up the temperature. Lutnick’s chief antagonists on the issue of China chip controls are almost entirely his own colleagues within the administration, ranging from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, all of whom reportedly favor a far tougher approach than Lutnick has been willing to impose. Lutnick’s Republican detractors are plenty outside the administration as well, particularly within the GOP congressional ranks. Republican Sen. John Kennedy says Lutnick must explain himself “ in front of God and country .” Rep. Bill Huizenga has attacked Lutnick’s lack of responsiveness to Congress as “frustrating,” and the Republican chairs of the House China and Foreign Affairs committees, Rep. John Moolenaar and Rep. Brian Mast, have made their unhappiness with Lutnick just as vivid. All these intraparty critics join legions of Democratic senators who are demanding records from Lutnick, and after last week’s midterms , their party takes the committee gavels in January with detractors making clear that Lutnick is one of their top targets – for reasons extending far beyond merely his role in sensitive U.S. technology making their way to China. events.title: THC drink companies rush to sell inventory as Illinois ban takes effect
events.summary: Many hemp companies are shipping their remaining inventory to Wisconsin, Minnesota and Tennessee, which have different regulations At midnight this morning in Illinois , hemp-derived THC drinks transformed from grocery store commodities into illegal narcotics, and manufacturers have been rushing to sell their inventory or ship it out of state. Republicans tacked a last-minute provision on to last year’s spending bill that ended the government shutdown, banning all hemp-derived THC products, including the THC-infused alcohol alternatives sold at liquor stores and grocery stores . Under the new law, no container can have more than 0.4mg THC total. In June, Illinois passed a state-level law intended to align with the federal ban, initially set to go into effect this month. While Congress delayed the federal ban until December, Illinois did not change its state-level effective date. There has been some confusion around the Illinois ban because of a lawsuit filed last week by the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association, a hemp lobbying trade group that includes approximately 250 Illinois businesses. Some headlines suggested the lawsuit effectively paused the Illinois hemp ban until 19 November, but that pause only applies to businesses that sued . The timing of the ban is unfortunate for Playdate, a non-alcoholic wine company that launched its first product, a THC-infused, NA rosé, less than two months ago. With less than two weeks to go before the ban, Playdate cofounders Sammy Dorf and Brian Ward were still unsure how to handle their remaining inventory. It’s possible the federal government will ultimately leave hemp-derived THC regulation to the states, mirroring their approach to medical and recreational cannabis. Many hemp companies are strategically shipping their remaining inventory to Minnesota and Tennessee, which already have their own hemp regulations. After selling off Playdate wine at a steep discount, Dorf and Ward said they have less than a truckload left, which they’ll ship to states where they can still sell it. If the hemp ban remains in place, Ward and Dorf intend to shift their focus to plain NA wine, minus the THC. Joe Chura, CEO and founder of Go Brewing in Naperville, Illinois , got into the business the other way around. Chura’s initial goal was to create the world’s first gluten-free, NA beer. He launched Easy Man, a THC-infused option, just last year, hoping to provide an alternative buzz without the health consequences of heavy drinking. “Probably a month ago, we made our last batch,” Chura said. “We were planning another one that we ended up cancelling, because we didn’t want to get stuck with it.” The last of the Easy Man left sold out on Friday, Chura added: “Had I known the demand would have been as great at the end, I probably would have made [the cancelled batch.] But it was cutting it close.” Perfectly Dosed, a Chicago-based company that sells THC emulsions to beverage companies, didn’t have the option to dispense their remaining inventory in a fire sale, as they sell it to other companies in bulk. They had a metric ton of emulsion leftover, containing more than 100m milligrams of THC, according to cofounder and CEO Alexander Choi. “We’re hopeful that more reasonable regulations will pass, and so we’d like our stuff closer to home than further,” Choi said. They shipped their metric ton of emulsion to Wisconsin. Companies outside Illinois have another month to off-load their product. Joe Gerrity, CEO of Crescent Canna, has been selling beverages off to individual consumers by the pallet. He has some sense of who’s buying. “When someone’s buying thousands of dollars worth of product, you want to do some due diligence,” Gerrity said, adding that several former NBA players bought pallets. One of the most difficult things about planning for the ban is the uncertainty around how it’s going to be implemented and enforced. “It was hard for us to tell when distributors were going to stop selling our products, when retailers were going to ask them to be off the shelves,” Gerrity said. While many in the industry don’t expect the federal government to strictly enforce the ban, alcohol distributors will probably still refuse THC beverages if there’s any possibility they could lose their license, Gerrity explained. Gerrity is also working to figure out how to destroy inventory if necessary. “You can’t just click a button and destroy thousands of pallets,” he said. Choi, meanwhile, has been reformulating his emulsions to be chemically stable in case they need to be diluted to comply with federal regulations. Despite the volatility of the industry, Chura said that he’s still hopeful that the bans will be reversed, and is even thinking about a THC beer compliant with federal regulations – that is, one that only contains 0.4mg of THC. It’s still unclear whether such a product would be legal.

events.title: How Nvidia's Veterans Day video inadvertently sealed Jensen Huang's fate amid scandal
events.summary: A seemingly wholesome social media post from Nvidia on Veterans Day inadvertently showed why keeping embattled Jensen Huang as chief executive was almost impossible. On Wednesday, as the US observed Veterans Day, Nvidia employees gathered and watched Marines methodically unfold and raise the US flag at the company's California headquarters. "This Veterans Day, we honour all who have served, including veterans across our Nvidia community ," read the caption accompanying the video on several of the company's social media platforms. "Thank you for your service." During any other time in Nvidia's history , and if just about any other company had posted something similar, the reaction would have mostly been positive. But its now former chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to infidelity with an accused Chinese spy, and reports that he also had an affair with a former Nvidia executive, opened the company's Veterans Day event to criticism. View this post on Instagram "Ironically, the Marines motto is 'Semper Fidelis', which means 'Always Faithful'. You can't script this," wrote one of about 160 people who commented on the post. "You should maybe take a break from posting," wrote another. About the same time as Nvidia's Veterans Day video was posted on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that people close to the company were claiming Mr Huang had another affair, with a former Nvidia executive. "What about Kimberly Powell?" read another comment on Nvidia's Veterans Day video post. Top executives have survived such media coverage in the past, but the problem for Nvidia and Mr Huang proved to be the national security concerns related to AI . For several years, Mr Huang has criticised export bans preventing US technology from being acquired and used by China , which the US has regarded with increased hostility over the past decade. Republicans and Democrats often criticised Mr Huang for his public statements that the strict export laws hurt the US more than helping, and that the policies should be changed. He was familiar with the Oval Office, where he seemed to successfully convince President Donald Trump late last year to relax some of the export policies affecting China . Republicans and Democrats were irked, but even more so after the revelation on Sunday about Mr Huang's romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a technology executive who US officials say was a spy for China. Subsequent media reports implied that he was doing everything he could to try to undermine US export laws, and that various companies in China were able to circumvent them. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank in Washington, told Bloomberg on Monday that Mr Huang and Nvidia should be held accountable. "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him – it really needs to be looked into," Mr McGuire said. So Rubio himself is worried about Jensen’s romantic relationship with the Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, meaning the intel was validated at the highest levels of government. But still, Commerce has done nothing to limit AI chip shipments to Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. Why? https://t.co/AkaxnPMKcB — Chris McGuire (@ChrisRMcGuire) November 8, 2026 In a post on X, Mr McGuire said some members of the Trump administration had tried to convey that Mr Huang had been compromised, while others seemed to disregard it. One year ago, during Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, the company wrapped itself in the US flag. Mr Huang walked on stage in front of thousands after a video played highlighting US achievements in technology. “It’s difficult not to be sentimental about America after watching that video,” he said. Last Sunday, however, Mr Huang's admitted affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese spy confirmed his critics' worst fears. On Veterans Day, Nvidia's video with the Marines showed that the repercussions of Mr Huang and his company's alleged actions were not going away any time soon. "Where is the Chinese flag?" another comment read adjacent to the video. "What about Chinese veterans?" wrote another. Others, however, were quick to say the main focus of all the anger directed towards Nvidia was that the company did not seem to mind its most powerful chips being used by China. "I'm not a Chinese spy, can I have a 5090?" another person commented, referring to the graphics processing unit that Nvidia describes as the "most powerful" consumer GPU "ever made". Nvidia's attempt to show that it was committed to US national security and the soldiers that protect it, had backfired. On Thursday, less than 24 hours after the Veterans Day video was posted, Nvidia's board of directors announced that Mr Huang had resigned. Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, will act as interim chief executive.

events.title: Google DeepMind Staff Tap the UK Government to Escalate Their Unionization Fight
events.summary: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab. On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application with the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions. The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm that the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership. The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression that their demands weren’t being taken seriously. “They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.” “We respect the right of employees to make an informed decision about whether or not to join a union,” Google DeepMind spokesperson Tom Hewett tells WIRED in a statement. “We have consistently listened to both those seeking to unionize and those opposed, and have acted in good faith from the outset. We remain committed to constructively participating in this process, and have maintained open and transparent communication with our employees and the unions throughout.” The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Alphabet, Google’s parent company, removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development. “When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.” The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts. “We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee. The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations. “We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.” In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote. The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK. “It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.” Update 11/12/26 3:50pm ET: This story has been updated to add a statement from Google DeepMind. events.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
events.summary: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month , eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort. eMudhra has since left the CA racket , saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue. What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of. eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing. By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task. “Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.” The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers. As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work. “It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo. It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads. “The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.” As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself. “I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained. We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

events.title: Worried doctors urge action on frequent shortages of critical drugs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lifesaving medicines repeatedly in short supply and doctors are worried New ABC analysis has revealed the important medicines that have repeatedly been in shortage, highlighting supply chain weaknesses that could get worse. If you've never heard of Bicillin L-A, count yourself lucky. It's a long-lasting penicillin and a lifesaver for many Australians with syphilis or rheumatic heart disease. Trouble is, there's a global shortage and Australia's emergency supplies ran out in September. And, as it turns out, this isn't the first time this important medicine has been in short supply. Medicine shortages are reported on the Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) website. For this story, we tracked shortages going back to 2015, including some that were expected to continue into next year. Bicillin L-A 1.2 million units went into shortage in April 2025, and isn't expected to be back to normal until March next year. It's been labelled a critical shortage, which means there could be a risk of life-threatening or serious impacts. It also means there's not enough supply or no other suitable replacement on the Australian market. But we found multiple shortages of this drug, and most of them were critical . The current shortage is the longest recorded for this drug, and the company says it's due to manufacturing issues. And this is far from the only drug in critical shortage. Another is Creon, which is used to help people digest food, including patients with cystic fibrosis. Two different doses of this drug have been in shortage for more than a year, due to an unexpected increase in demand. One dose, Creon 25,000, has been in shortage multiple times in recent years. We found a low impact shortage in 2015, followed by four medium impact shortages. Like Bicillin, the current shortage is the longest and most severe. These are only two of the 40 medications recently in critical shortage. Our analysis revealed more than half of them have had at least one recorded shortage before. And 13 medications, or about a third, have been in critical shortage multiple times. We've put them together here, ordered by the number of previous shortages and the length of the current one. It's important to note that some of the medicines relate to a specific dose or formulation, and there are ways the health sector manages shortages, which we'll come back to. (If you're concerned your medication is in shortage, you can check the TGA website ). Most of the shortages continued beyond October 2026, when the data was last collected. Bicillin and Creon are among the medicines that have the most shortages recorded, with six each. The other drugs at the top of our list include a nuclear medicine used to assess how blood moves through the heart (Radpharm PYP), and an injection that reduces high blood pressure in late pregnancy (among other uses). The list also includes the only vaccine available for Q fever — a bacterial disease that can result in serious illness. Australia is due to run out of the vaccine this week. While many of us are lucky enough to never have heard of these drugs, some on the list are ones you'd commonly get from your pharmacy. They include the EllaOne morning after contraceptive pill, which is known as the gold standard , and Lyclear scabies cream. Some medicines haven't had as many shortages, but that's because they've spent several years in one continuous shortage. Again, the reasons given by the suppliers are either increased demand or manufacturing issues. And it's not just the repeated critical shortages causing headaches for medical staff and patients. More than 420 shortages were recorded between late September and early October, with critical ones making up the smallest share. Royal Australasian College of Physicians spokesperson and internal and addiction medicine professor John Saunders said repeated medicine shortages — including medium-impact ones — caused "great frustration" among doctors. While there were often alternatives available, he said sometimes they weren't as good, or were simply not available at all. "It's not something that I can say, 'Oh there, there, don't worry about it, it'll be alright' — far from it," he said. "Switching medications when this isn't part of a plan … is a very difficult thing for [patients] to experience." University of Adelaide pharmacy lecturer and pharmacist Jack Janetzki said the medicines on our "critical" list spanned a wide range of essential uses, such as treating life-threatening and severe fungal and viral infections.

events.title: Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month
events.summary: On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned from the company that had become, in many ways, synonymous with its chief executive. Less than an hour later, when the markets opened, Nvidia’s stock had lost roughly $546 billion in market value. Though it has rebounded somewhat, the last weeks of scandal—including a reported second affair with an Nvidia employee—have tanked the chipmaker’s valuation by more than $1 trillion. Huang’s very public downfall began in late October, when The New York Times reported that the CEO had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed and an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. (The two are not known to be related.) At that time, Nvidia’s market cap was around $5.2 trillion. On November 8, Nvidia announced it was investigating its CEO, after Jensen publicly acknowledged the affair. By the following morning, roughly $1 trillion had been erased since the scandal started. If you hang out with a certain type of person who thinks of themselves as a daytrader, they might have talked about “buying the dip” over drinks last weekend. If you believe Nvidia can thrive without Huang, there’s still time! The dip has dipped even further. But the early consensus seems to be that this could be more of a prolonged plunge. “Huang is irreplaceable,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, told WIRED last week. “He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution.” There are very real questions about what the end of Huang means for the global economy. Not only are Nvidia’s chips used to train most major AI models, but the company has also invested billions in a number of other tech companies. As of an August regulatory filing , Nvidia owned nearly $30 billion worth of Intel stock and roughly $21 billion of SpaceX stock. For now, Nvidia’s loss is other chipmakers’ gain. AMD shares are up 28 percent over the past five days, and Broadcom is up nearly 16 percent. Nothing to see here. More Numbers That Illuminate Huang’s Value: Nvidia’s market share of chips used in training frontier AI models: roughly 90 percent ; AI companies in which Nvidia has invested at least $100 million: eight, as of its August filing; Huang’s pay last year : $36 million; Portion of Nvidia owned by Huang: 3.5 percent, as of March—which means the scandal has devalued Huang’s own share of the company by more than $50 billion; PR firms hired with expertise in sex scandals: at least one ; Huang relatives employed by Nvidia: one son, one daughter, and one son-in-law ; Leather jackets owned: several, including a $960,000 Tom Ford number ( but not that vintage Saint Laurent jacket everyone was talking about on X ). Update 11/12/26 2:50pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that a third Jensen Huang affair has been reported. events.title: Dewa posts record nine-month profit on increased demand for its services
events.summary: The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority has posted record profit in the first nine months of 2026, underpinned by increased demand for its utility services in the emirate. Net profit attributable to owners of the company in the nine months to the end of September jumped 11 per cent year-on-year to more than Dh7.1 billion ($1.93 billion), Dewa said in a regulatory filing on Thursday to the Dubai Financial Market , where its shares are traded. Revenue for the period also hit a record, growing 3.3 per cent to about Dh25.7 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a key metric of profitability, climbed 2.5 per cent to Dh13.43 billion. Dewa attributed revenue growth to increased demand across its electricity, water, district cooling and other businesses. "We continue to advance our journey towards net zero by 2050, while strengthening our contribution to Dubai’s sustainable economic growth and global competitiveness,” said Saeed Al Tayer, chief executive of Dewa, referring to the UAE's economic and societal push to zero emissions. For the third quarter of 2026, net profit grew 8.3 per cent annually to Dh3.9 billion, as revenue rose 5.4 per cent to nearly Dh10.9 billion and Ebitda inched down more than 1 per cent to Dh6.11 billion. The three months through to the end of September highlighted the continued expansion in Dubai's economy, which was reflected in rising electricity demand, increased clean energy generation and improvements in operational efficiency, Dewa said. "As the emirate continues to develop, Dewa remains committed to providing the essential power and water services and innovative smart and digital solutions needed to support households, businesses and economic activity," the utility said. Dewa continues to boost its portfolio with an increased focus on clean energy generation. The utility has announced plans for the seventh phase of the Mohammed bin Rashid Solar Park, which Dewa operates, that includes incorporating large-scale battery storage. Dewa also operates a network of electric vehicle charging stations, as more motorists opt for EVs. Dewa's moves demonstrate its "ability to keep pace with Dubai’s growing energy needs while steadily increasing the contribution of clean energy", Mr Al Tayer said. Dewa has also previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced. In June, the utility established Dewa International to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. The company aims to work with governments, developers and financial institutions to identify investment opportunities and participate in projects outside the UAE. Earlier this month, Dewa International signed an agreement with China's Shanghai Electric to explore energy and water investments in global markets, as the emirate seeks to expand its footprint in the international utilities sector. Shares of Dewa ended 1.11 per cent higher at Dh2.74 on the DFM on Thursday.

events.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
events.summary: CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world? Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run. This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading. Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft , Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes. What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself . One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments. In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips. None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms. Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets. Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI , to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts. Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island. As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date. Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies. Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades. Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open. This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy.

events.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025. “This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X. This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026 The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance. As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space. After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models. The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned. Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.” Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated. For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026 In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
