events.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
events.summary: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media , or doing their Duolingo lesson. Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns —practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also ensure ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster, make tiered pricing transparent; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service. The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference. The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo. Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act , which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.” Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook . If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act , says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds. The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities. Correction: 11/12/2026, 10:15 GMT. WIRED updated this article to correct that Ticketmaster does not use dynamic pricing in the EU. events.title: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
events.summary: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. Millions more HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank , Russia's largest private bank. ®

events.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico ) + It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $) + John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian ) + But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $) + What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $) + Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $) + Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge ) + Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $) 3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible” Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $) + This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian ) 5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica ) 6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $) + Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP ) 7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $) + “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC ) 9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta ) 10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here’s what it’s taught us Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “What a dereliction of duty. He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.” —Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy. One more thing How refrigeration ruined fresh food Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus. According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.  Read the full story on her research . —Allison Arieff We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world. + Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos . + Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year. + Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael’s “Careless Whisper.”

events.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
events.summary: Evelyn at the grave of her twin, Ginnifer The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms. Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon. Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him. Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.) No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born. Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma. The living room in the house where Ginnifer was born and died. Dozens of Followers of Christ members filled the home that day, but none called 911. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office Followers anoint the ailing with olive oil. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin? There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive. In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper. He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves. Evelyn, at 14 days old, was still so small she could fit into dolls’ clothes. Courtesy of the Phillips family Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death. The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn? Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn. Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him. Jennifer and Marshall Phillips For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves. Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question. Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura and Samantha Swindler/The Oregonian For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population. The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother. Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.” Evelyn in her room Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care. events.title: CoreWeave reports positive Q3 results, but faces tough road ahead
events.summary: One solid quarter does not make a rebound. CoreWeave, the battered AI computing provider, surprised Wall Street yesterday by posting better-than-expected earnings and raising its annual forecast. But shares are still down nearly 40% so far this year, and the company is still not throwing enough cash off its business to cover its roughly $41 billion of net debt. “Narratives shifted, sentiment swung, and people scrutinized the build-out of AI,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said in a blog post that pledged to “calibrate investment” to demand, regulatory winds, and, probably most importantly, the availability of money. Intrator said the company would no longer be turning to unsecured borrowing to fund its business. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Anthropic IPO could lead to 'large correction' in markets, Fed official says
events.summary: Just as the proverbial ink was drying on Anthropic’s updated prospectus for the frontier lab’s expected $1.4 trillion IPO, a Federal Reserve official warned of a “large correction” in stock prices if AI returns fall short of expectations. Citing $800 billion in AI-related debt, plus off-balance-sheet liabilities and the circular financing powering the AI trade, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said any “shock would likely slow the AI buildout” and “soften” the economy. Nowhere are expectations loftier than at Anthropic, the first frontier lab to go public. Its valuation has already come in below initial expectations. It’ll still be one of the biggest listings of all time, pegged at $90.4 billion, but any wobbles around the IPO — set to price on Nov. 18 and start trading the next day — “might mean a selloff of the AI theme around the IPO,” said Tore Opsahl, head of quantitative solutions advisory group at Nomura. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
events.summary: Walter White baptizes a Followers of Christ member in 1951. He led an Oregon City, Oregon, offshoot of the sect. Courtesy of the Phillips family It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said. “They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon. The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches. White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.” Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.” White’s grave in the Followers’ cemetery outside of Oregon City Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings. The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho , focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences . Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated. White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t. In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl. Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households. White, second from left in the back (in suspenders), with Followers leaders in Oregon City in 1937. By 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Courtesy of the Phillips family White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other. As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.) White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.” White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups. In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space. events.title: Tracking how Jensen Huang changed his stance on China
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s public rhetoric on China became more admiring, and his stance on export controls more critical, after the US restricted Nvidia’s made-for-China chip in 2025 — and as he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. A Semafor analysis of 42 podcast interviews with Huang since early 2022 shows how Huang’s argument around global chip policy evolved in a series of long-form, unscripted, and often friendly settings: Huang talked up China’s strengths and cast Beijing as a formidable competitor as he argued more forcefully for a careful balance between protecting US interests and making US technology the backbone of global AI development. Whether the Nvidia CEO’s position was shaped by his affair with an executive at a Singapore-based data center firm with alleged ties to Beijing is now a matter for the company’s board, which hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate, and for Congress, who plan hearings on the matter. But his stance on China and chip controls is freshly in the spotlight. Semafor identified dozens of exchanges about China across the interviews and used a pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to score each one on Huang’s stance on export restrictions and how he regarded China. Before China’s DeepSeek burst onto the global stage and Washington put new limits on Nvidia’s sales to the country in early 2025, Huang spoke on podcasts about export restrictions in a largely neutral tenor, framing them as a matter of compliance, according to our review. Mentions of China in Huang’s interviews rose roughly sixfold after those 2025 curbs, as the chip CEO argued that the restrictions hurt the US more than China. “If we leave a market altogether, there’s no question somebody else would step in ,” he told Michael Milken in May 2025. In 14 interviews since the 2025 curbs, he talked up China’s AI researchers, open-source models, and manufacturing, often as reasons the US can’t afford to cut the country off, or rejected the idea of treating it as an enemy. He invoked the “American tech stack” 34 times across eight interviews since July 2025, arguing that the world’s developers should build on US technology. In eight interviews he said that 50% of the world’s AI researchers are Chinese or in China, suggesting the country’s tech talent can’t be ignored. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: A top lobbyist returns to the White House
events.summary: The News A conservative firebrand who helped craft the Trump administration’s campaign against Ivy League universities has returned to the White House to help chief of staff Stephen Miller build his team, a move that will test the administration’s efforts to contain the influence of lobbyists within the White House. May Mailman, who left her post as Trump policy adviser in 2026 to launch her own lobbying firm, will join the White House on a temporary basis as a special government employee, Axios first reported and Semafor confirmed. In recent months, Mailman had built a healthy stable of corporate clients with active matters before the Trump administration, including Vestis, a uniform supplier which has pushed the FTC to block a rival’s acquisition, people familiar with the matter said. The FTC is poised to block that deal , Semafor earlier reported. Other companies she’s worked for include Netflix, Meta, HPE, Comcast, and KKR, according to the people. Mailman, as well as the firms, either declined to provide a comment for this story or did not return a request for comment. Mailman served as a policy adviser early in Trump’s tenure, helping Miller go after Harvard and Columbia for what the administration called indifference to antisemitism on college campuses. She decided to return to the administration in recent days after Miller was named chief of staff, with Miller asking her to help him staff up his team and find ways to optimize relationships between government entities. Mailman ruled out a policy role when discussing her return to public service, though, in part over concerns that it would fuel a perception of impropriety, one person with knowledge of her thinking said. Still, the revolving door between the White House and lobbying work raises questions around how much Mailman stands to benefit personally from her new role and about the level of influence that corporations have held over this White House. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Mailman informed clients of her new role within recent days, and has instructed her firm — which she has taken a leave of absence from — to not engage with the White House while she is serving there for the next few weeks, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Americans on both sides of the aisle have grown frustrated with the level of influence big corporations have over this administration — with a CNBC survey of voters finding that corruption was the number one issue going into the midterms. That perception has only been fueled by the list of Trump-connected lobbyists who have gone in and out of the White House, perhaps the only bipartisan move left in DC. Mailman, perhaps uniquely, has shied away from the kind of publicity that some lobbyists have courted. And her efforts to create a firewall between her clients and her firm, as she returns to government service, stand in contrast to other administration power brokers, who openly tout their relationships with administration officials.

events.title: Apple tells its Support Community to STFU
events.summary: Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026. Users seeking help with their gizmos from other Apple customers were greeted with the message : "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. "We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Need help? Head to the official Apple Support site. Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device? This is no longer the forum for you. Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5. Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular. Other places to seek advice remain, and useful answers were never guaranteed. As one user put it on X : "rip to every thread that ended with 'same problem here' and zero solutions." Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions. Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure. The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination. The company has yet to respond. ®

events.title: UK’s Cheval Collection launches Dubai project in expansion push
events.summary: Cheval Collection , the UK-based luxury hospitality firm, has launched a development in Dubai, with plans to expand in the UAE and the region as property demand increases. The project in Dubai South will have 98 serviced hotel apartments ranging from studios to three-bedroom units, and 95 one-, two-, and three-bedroom branded residences. It is scheduled to open in 2030. Cheval South Bay is the fourth development for the company in Dubai and its sixth in the Middle East. It has two more under-construction properties being built in Saudi Arabia. Sales for Cheval South Bay are expected to start next year. Prices and the total value of the project have yet to be disclosed. “Announcing this project today shows what our confidence is like in Dubai, our confidence in the UAE, and our confidence in the wider GCC [Gulf Co-operation Council],” Nick Pilbeam, Cheval Collection’s chief commercial officer, told The National. “Cheval already operates two properties in Dubai, Cheval Maison The Palm, Cheval Maison Expo City Dubai … in the last six months, in the current situation, they've [performed] well. They've outperformed the market, certainly in occupancy because of this long-stay angle.” Cheval Maison The Palm and Cheval Maison Expo City, opened in 2023 and 2025, offer serviced apartments. The company also launched a branded residence development in Dubai Island in April. Cheval's latest announcement comes as property developers continue to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled a 3.8 million-square-metre residential development next to Palm Jebel Ali, with a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments. It will also have education, health care, sport and leisure facilities across 15 neighbourhoods in southern Dubai, with two schools, a hospital and six mosques. In September, Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, and Sharjah-based Arada revealed plans to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion ($4 billion). Cheval is also exploring opportunities to start a new project in Abu Dhabi as the emirate’s property market has been performing strongly this year, with real estate transactions surging. A total of 38,483 transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis. “There's a lot going on in the Abu Dhabi real estate market,” Mr Pilbeam said. “I can't talk anything concrete just yet, but it is certainly a city and an area that we're looking at and interested in.” The privately owned company is also looking to expand in other parts of the Middle East and North Africa region, with a new property launch being planned “in a few weeks time” expected to take its portfolio to about 1,000 units. “We're clearly on a growth journey. However, we're still very selective about the projects that we go in for. We want to be in prime locations, in tier-one locations, tier-one destinations. We are negotiating multiple projects,” he added.

events.title: UAE's Landmark Group probes data breach in Shukran loyalty programme

The customer information involved includes names, contact details and dates of birth, the Dubai-based retail and hospitality conglomerate said. Cyber breaches are increasing as bad actors try to make financial gains or steal user data, prompting companies to strengthen their network defences. As well as financial damage, attacks on systems can have reputational consequences. According to IBM's latest Cost of a Data Breach report, the average cost of a data breach for organisations in the Middle East hit $8 million this year. Artificial intelligence has made cyber attacks more complex and agile. IBM said lost business remained the largest cost category in the region, averaging $3.57 million per breach. The UAE has put in place advanced cyber defence systems to fend off any attacks to protect the economy and society. On one Tuesday in September, the Emirates faced 640,000 attacks, national cyber security chief Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said.

events.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
events.summary: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said . "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill , owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register , Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

events.title: Subdued sales for Singles' Day, China's online shopping festival
events.summary: Early signs suggest China’s biggest annual online shopping festival is failing to persuade anxious consumers to spend more, despite discounts HONG KONG -- Early signs suggest China ’s biggest online shopping event is struggling to persuade anxious consumers to spend more, despite discounts. The Singles’ Day festival, a major discount campaign comparable to Black Friday and Cyber Monday in the U.S., centers on Nov. 11. But it begins weeks earlier and is seen as a barometer of the broader economy. Retail data platform Syntun said cumulative sales as of Oct. 31 totaled just over 1 trillion yuan ($154 billion), broadly in line with the same period last year. Retailers have increased sales mainly by extending the festival. Total Singles’ Day sales in 2025 reached a record of almost 1.7 trillion yuan ($254 billion). Consumer demand in China remains subdued, however, as a prolonged property downturn and other pressures weigh on confidence. “Optimism over a recovery in domestic demand has faded,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board. “Improvements in sentiment have repeatedly proved short-lived.” E-commerce giants such as Alibaba have turned to artificial intelligence to encourage frugal shoppers to spend more. Alibaba integrated its Qwen AI into its Taobao and Tmall platforms to help shoppers place orders and find products. Plans offering AI tokens are also being prominently promoted during Singles’ Day for the first time. This month, a livestream by Li Jiaqi, dubbed the “Lipstick King” for his huge lipstick sales, sold plans covering roughly 2 trillion tokens within half an hour, according to Chinese media. Singles’ Day originated as “Bachelors’ Day,” a celebration of being single. The nationwide shopping festival began in 2009 and now targets everyone. While China’s broader economy continues to grow at a relatively robust pace, expanding 4.6% from a year earlier in January-September, much of that momentum came from a boom in exports . Retail sales of consumer goods rose just 1.1% over the same period. China’s vast domestic market has struggled as a yearslong real estate downturn has left households feeling less wealthy. Home prices have fallen roughly 20% or more from their 2021 peak, with smaller cities and the resale market seeing steeper declines. Although home prices appear to be stabilizing in larger cities, many homeowners remain concerned they could fall further, said Andy Rothman, founder and CEO of the advisory firm Sinology. In the southern furniture manufacturing hub of Foshan, 24-year-old Gabby Liang said she was feeling cautious. “I’ve been buying much less online, especially when it comes to non-essential items,” she said. “During the Singles’ Day festival last year, I bought quite a bit of skincare products. But this year I expect to buy fewer.” Other shoppers are also reining in spending. “I’m perhaps not as keen on pursuing famous or high-end brands as I used to be,” said Beijing resident Kong Min, referring to this year’s Singles’ Day. Middle-class Chinese consumers have lost confidence, and many festival discounts are less generous than they once were, said Shaun Rein, managing director of China Market Research Group in Shanghai. More shoppers are experiencing “discount fatigue,” said Yaling Jiang, founder of market research company ApertureChina. With discounts available year-round, Singles’ Day may be losing its power to boost spending, she said. “Looking at what Singles’ Day originally was: a shopping festival where people used to expect the largest discounts of the year,” she said. “That is not true any more after it was extended to multiple platforms, then to a monthlong thing.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Microsoft Outlook outage stretches on for hours Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Liang, who works in furniture sales, said extras such as cameras and game consoles were off her shopping list this year. “We’re undergoing a consumption downgrade,” she said. “Even the amount that we earn has somehow been downgraded.” Business has stalled as Chinese shoppers tighten their belts, Liang said, despite rising exports to markets such as the Middle East and Africa. An oversupply of goods, from cars and TVs to shoes and other electronics, has intensified competition in China’s crowded domestic market, pushing manufacturers to expand overseas. Exports overall surged 35% from a year earlier in October, driven by high-tech products such as semiconductors and electric vehicles. China is on track to surpass last year’s record trade surplus of $1.2 trillion . Domestic demand for big-ticket items, including cars and some luxury goods, has been particularly weak. Passenger car sales in China have fallen for most of this year, dropping almost 25% in January-September, according to industry data. The decline partly reflects cuts to government subsidies .

events.title: UAE corporate tax revenue jumps by a third to Dh46.5bn in 2025
events.summary: Corporate tax revenue collected by the UAE rose by nearly 34 per cent in 2025, amid a rise in on-time compliance. The Federal Tax Authority collected approximately Dh46.5 billion ($12.7 billion) in corporate tax for periods ending in the 2025 financial year, up from Dh34.75 billion a year earlier. That brought total revenue collected from the introduction of corporate tax to the end of 2025 to Dh81.27 billion, the FTA said in a statement on Wednesday. The federal corporate tax took effect on June 1, 2023, and became the most significant tax after the UAE introduced the 5 per cent value added tax in 2018. VAT revenue distributed to the UAE federal government and the governments of the seven emirates for the tax periods between January and August 2026 amounted to about Dh28.27 billion, while excise tax over the same period amounted to Dh1.4 billion. “The growth in collected tax revenues, including the significant increase in corporate tax revenues, reflects the efficiency of the FTA’s operations and its ongoing efforts to develop its procedures and services,” said the authority's director general, Abdulaziz Al Mulla. The FTA said the filing rate reached 91 per cent this year, compared to 87 per cent in 2025, as the on-time payment rate hit 97 per cent, signalling increased and improved participation from taxpayers. The rate for the timely filing of VAT returns was at 83 per cent in 2026, up from 81 per cent last year, while its on-time payment rate rose to 98 per cent. The return filing rate for excise tax hit 92 per cent in 2026, compared to 91 per cent in 2025, with the on-time payment rate at 98 per cent. “The authority continues to raise tax awareness, strengthen its engagement with taxable persons, and provide the information and guidance needed to fulfil their obligations,” Mr Al Mulla said. “These efforts contribute significantly to enhancing their compliance with tax legislation and procedures and facilitate the timely filing of tax returns and payment of tax due.” The UAE's introduction of corporate income tax was seen as a step that will not only help the Arab world’s second-largest economy broaden its revenue base, but will also help the country achieve its long and short-term economic growth objectives. Analysts had said the move will increase the country's taxation scope beyond VAT and different custom duties and complements government efforts to diversify its economy from oil. “Tax compliance and taxable persons’ engagement with tax legislation and procedures have also improved significantly, supported by greater awareness and a stronger tax culture,” Mr Al Mulla said. “The FTA remains committed to maintaining regular communication with stakeholders in the tax sector to understand their views and suggestions, and to strengthen their contribution to the sustainable development of the tax system.”

events.title: Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python
events.summary: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing. A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory. No Python here In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel." Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here. XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators . Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch . Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime , which supports an open graph format with Python bindings. Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

events.title: Distant wars pose risks for Africa’s digital services
events.summary: The News When users in Côte d’Ivoire of the popular ride-hailing and food-ordering app, Yango, started experiencing delays booking taxis and deliveries last month, the glitches were not to do with local bandwidth or power outages but the impact of problems elsewhere in the world. Though temporary, the issue was a reminder of Africa’s vulnerability as a result of being reliant on internet infrastructure beyond the continent. Yango licenses technology from Russian company Yandex, whose data centers in Russia were hit by Ukrainian drone strikes in October. While rumors spread among Ivorians that this was the cause of Yango’s issues, a spokesperson for the Dubai-based company told Semafor the disruptions were down to infrastructure changes in the Gulf. Hadil Elmaki said it had to move operations to a different data center after a partner company said in September that the infrastructure affected by Iranian attacks could no longer support Yango’s work. “Moving interconnected systems between data centers is a complex process,” Elmaki said, while describing the disruptions as temporary “affecting certain functions of our services in Côte d’Ivoire. These were not widespread outages, but intermittent issues.” Yango runs some of its operations using Amazon’s cloud-computing infrastructure, including servers in the UAE, according to public records reviewed by Semafor. In mid-September, Amazon said it could not restore access to one of its three data center zones there after Iranian drone strikes in March. Egyptian news publisher EnterpriseAM , which also used UAE-based servers, is another company that said it was affected as its website went offline for more than a day in March. It restored operations after moving to another hosting location and recovering missing data from its own systems. Digital infrastructure has now become a target in conflict and with many African businesses leaning on overseas servers and the cables connecting them to the continent, the recent attacks raise questions about the resilience and control over their own data. The vital internet cables linking Africa and Europe have also been disrupted amid fighting. In 2024 these under-water pipes in the Red Sea were damaged and attacks on commercial ships by Yemen’s Houthi forces complicated repairs. That conflict is also holding back new capacity — Meta has yet to build the southern Red Sea section of 2Africa, a cable designed to ring the continent. “This is the new line of warfare,” Jane Munga, a technology policy researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Semafor. “Something happening across the world can affect Africa.” ‘Digital sovereignty’ Increasing numbers of African businesses are moving operations to the cloud, but as there is a lack of in-country servers, many are hosted abroad, said Amreesh Phokeer, research director at non-profit advocacy group the Internet Society. For Phokeer, this is now a policy question for the continent’s governments: “Do they invest locally to build more resilience, or do they create even more dependence on the outside?” Governments and companies want more infrastructure at home. Under the banner of “digital sovereignty,” they are expanding local data centers and cloud services to gain more control over their data and digital economies. Mauritania launched a national cloud service in June to support public administration, and Gabon inaugurated a data center built by pan-African technology company ST Digital in July to host government and business services. Africa’s ambitions to build its own AI industry are adding to that demand. About 1,250 companies applied to be part of the first cohort of Askya AI Growth Platform, a program for African AI startups run by Lagos-based venture capital firm Askya Investment Partners, which began in October. “How are you going to build sovereign cloud or sovereign AI if you don’t have local infrastructure?” Phokeer asked. Ruben’s view Africa’s growing reliance on digital services demands greater transparency about the infrastructure behind them. On Facebook, Yango reassured users in Côte d’Ivoire that it was working to resolve their problems. In response to my questions, the company did not identify the infrastructure partner involved or say where the services had moved. As African countries put more banking, public services and state records in the cloud, unanswered questions of this kind carry greater weight. Governments and companies should explain what happens when the systems supporting these services fail, who is responsible and how continuity is ensured. Users should not have to investigate a company’s infrastructure to know whether they can rely on its services. “That is the work of government. That is the work of the regulator,” Munga told me. She also argued that journalists, civil society, and elected representatives can help citizens demand answers. Regulators should require providers to demonstrate how they would keep essential services running through a disruption. Companies should explain significant failures and what they have done to prevent a repeat. That would give the public something more useful than assurances that an app is working again. Room for Disagreement Building local data centers alone will not protect African digital services from disruption. Experts argue that governments and businesses should spread their systems across several sites, with backup locations both inside and outside national borders. “What if the war is local?” Munga said. “It needs to be a strategy that thinks about diversification.” Phokeer pointed to Ukraine, whose internet proved resilient after Russia’s 2022 invasion because it was not concentrated in a few strategic sites and could route traffic through several neighboring countries. “Good practice says you shouldn’t keep your data in just one place,” he said. “You need to be able to put it in several places.” Notable High data costs and a lack of local infrastructure are placing a ceiling on AI implementation in Africa, according to a paper from ACET

events.title: Don Leonard isn't a House member yet. He's already rocking Capitol Hill.
events.summary: Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) hasn't been sworn in yet, but he's making a name for himself on Capitol Hill as one of the most outspoken anti-establishment progressives in the incoming freshman class. Why it matters: That's an unlikely position for a Democrat who represents a rural Ohio district that President Trump carried by 10 percentage points in 2024. Leonard is archetypal of a burgeoning breed of swing-district House Democrats — populist in style, receptive to left-wing policies and unbound by traditional political norms — that will be well-represented in the 120th Congress. "I'm really vibing with my class," he told Axios in a Tuesday interview on Capitol Hill. "These are everyday citizens who heard the same call I heard and stood up." State of play: Leonard, a professor of city planning who defeated Republican Rep. Mike Carey in last Tuesday's midterm elections, was turning heads on Capitol Hill before he even arrived for freshman orientation on Sunday. He told his local CBS affiliate the day after the election he will "be shopping for a new leader" unless House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) changes his pro-Israel positions. He made an even bigger splash on Tuesday with a video he posted to social media saying he met with "senior members" who warned him his life would be a "living hell" and that he would lose reelection if he opposes Jeffries for speaker of the House. The other side: House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), asked about Leonard's video at a press conference Tuesday afternoon, told reporters, "I don't know what senior Democrats he's talking about." "I think all of us here can attest to the work, the time, the energy that Hakeem Jeffries put into helping us build this majority," Aguilar said. Aguilar predicted Jeffries will be "overwhelmingly selected" as speaker and that he doesn't "lose any sleep over that." "Members could have ideas and interests and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question," he added. What they're saying: Leonard, in his interview with Axios later on Tuesday afternoon, characterized the conversation described in his video as a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" talk with "folks who have been on the Hill for a really long time." "They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff ... the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'" In addition to cutting U.S. aid for Israel, Leonard said he wants Jeffries to commit to supporting a Constitutional amendment to ban super PACs. "The time for half-measures is over," he told Axios. "I hear people, even members of the Progressive Caucus, talking about, 'Maybe we just tax super PACs.' Y'all, we need a 28th Amendment." Between the lines: Leonard said he has also found himself irked by House Democrats' seniority system, which makes it difficult for freshman members to get onto some of the most coveted committees. "I'm just a little confused and frustrated right now by why the Democratic caucus is so hierarchical when it comes to these committees," he told Axios. Leonard added: "When we're less democratic than the Republican Party ... that raises questions for me." What's next: The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk. "I shook his hand and I asked him for six minutes," he said, telling Axios he wants to "look him in the eye, let him know that [I] respect his capacity as a leader ... but I need something to take back to my district that shows that my party understands the magnitude of the crisis we face." "I'm going to hope that I can persuade him in the six minutes that we don't have to cross that bridge, but my constituents aren't bluffing and neither am I."

events.title: The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry
events.summary: This article is brought to you by Innomotics . In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics , a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants. 1866: The breakthrough that powered the future The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century. This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. Innomotics The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today. One principle. Millions of motors. More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems. Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations. Innomotics Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades. Award-winning innovations Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award. Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements. Innomotics AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency. Perfect Harmony GH180: Proven drive technology for modern industry For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production. Winding lifetime analysis: The service to know more and risk less Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime. The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance. Innomotics 160 Years Later. Still Running. What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today. As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance. Video: Innomotics For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19 th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half. Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running. events.title: A 13-Year-Old Asked AI About Suicide on Her School Laptop. It Didn’t Get Flagged for Weeks
events.summary: A 13-year-old girl spent three months using her school-issued laptop to discuss depression, research suicide, and plan her funeral before self-harm-monitoring software finally prompted school officials to alert her parents, who intervened and stopped her, according to a lawsuit filed this month by her parents. The lawsuit alleges that Google and parent company Alphabet were negligent in their rollout of a Gemini model, claiming that the AI chatbot “coached” the North Carolina teenager to consider taking her own life. The case, which was previously reported by The New York Times, is one of several that allege harm from AI chatbot use, including claims of delusions and suicide . But it also illustrates the limitations of surveillance tools that thousands of schools have adopted in recent years, which are ostensibly designed to protect students from themselves when browsing and chatting online. Andrew Liddell, a lawyer for the family, tells WIRED that, according to information the school provided to the family, the alert went to the personal phone of a former counselor who had left the school nine months before. The ex-employee was diligent in passing the alert along to current staff, who then notified the girl’s mother, he says. As classrooms continue to rely on Google’s low-cost offerings, including Gemini, their ability to keep up with the potential risks is front and center. Just last week, parent and teacher groups across the country decried Google’s new requirement that schools must turn on generative AI features if they want to use Search. US senator Ed Markey cited Emma’s lawsuit in a letter to Google demanding the company let schools disable AI Mode and AI Overviews, writing that “Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage.” According to the lawsuit, the North Carolina girl, identified as Emma Doe, descended into “a severe psychological crisis” after Google Search routed her to Gemini on her school-issued Google Chromebook. Though Emma’s school had blocked the stand-alone Gemini website, the lawsuit alleges that she was steered into interacting with the chatbot through AI Mode, which lets people ask follow-up questions about a query or begin an unrelated conversation. Emma queried AI Mode about mental health issues starting last December. She asked about “severe depression” and “reasons to live,” and by late January she was asking about suicide, per the lawsuit. Over the course of two days around Valentine’s Day, she began writing a 1,500-word eulogy for herself with help from AI Mode in a Google Doc titled “Funeral.” The lawsuit says she worked on the document for more than four weeks while continuing to interact with the Gemini tool thousands of times. After school on St. Patrick's Day, she deleted most of the file and restarted. But Liddell says the themes and thoughts the girl expressed didn't materially change. Around 7:30 pm, her mother allegedly received a message from the school indicating that her daughter was in “imminent danger,” the lawsuit states. Her mother used her phone to log in to Emma’s school account and “watched her daughter compose a suicide note in real time,” according to the lawsuit. Google spokesperson José Castañeda says that the company is seriously “reviewing the claims in the lawsuit” and that its systems, including AI Mode, “aim to prevent users from engaging in harmful conversation.” "We’ve worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it,” Castañeda says. Lawyers for the family have sought to withhold the school's name to protect Emma's privacy. WIRED was able to identify the school, which did not return requests for comment. In recent months, the school added links to suicide prevention resources to the bottom of its website, according to WIRED’s review of the Internet Archive. Liddell tells WIRED that Emma’s school only learned about her mental health crisis because it used at least one third-party student-activity-monitoring system. Citing information that was allegedly previously provided to the school’s parents, he says these may have included products from the companies GoGuardian and Gaggle. Liddell says that the family lacks a definitive answer because the school’s “window of cooperation” with them was brief. GoGuardian spokesperson Natalia Switala tells WIRED that the company cannot “discuss any individual student or district” due to “student privacy obligations.” Gaggle did not immediately return WIRED’s request for comment. The screening tools generally work by capturing keystrokes or scanning files and using algorithms and human review to identify potentially concerning content . It’s unclear whether the school’s third-party screening tools monitor AI Mode interactions or, if they do, how well they actually work.

events.title: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
events.summary: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware." Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic." So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®
